We demonstrate that model compression can enhance the population risk of a pre-trained model by analyzing the balance between reducing generalization error and increasing empirical risk through compression. Initially, we establish that model compression diminishes an information-theoretic limit on generalization error, offering a perspective of compression as a regularization method to prevent overfitting. Subsequently, we quantify the rise in empirical risk caused by model compression using rate distortion theory. Our findings suggest that population risk may be reduced through model compression when the reduction in generalization error surpasses the rise in empirical risk. Through a linear regression case study, we illustrate that such a reduction in population risk via model compression is feasible. Additionally, our theoretical insights indicate that the Hessian-weighted $K$-means clustering compression method could be enhanced by regularizing the spacing between cluster centers. We corroborate these theoretical claims with experiments involving neural networks.

In the field of visual decoding, reconstructing images from human brain activity captured via functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) poses significant challenges, particularly with natural images. This process involves conditional image generation based on fMRI data, for which generative adversarial networks (GANs) have recently been adapted to produce natural images. Despite advancements, the quality and realism of the reconstructed images remain suboptimal, largely due to limited fMRI data samples and the inherent instability in GAN training. To address these issues, we introduce a novel GAN-based Bayesian visual reconstruction method (GAN-BVRM). This approach incorporates a classifier to interpret categories from fMRI data, a pre-trained conditional generator for creating natural images within specific categories, and a combination of encoding models and an evaluator to assess the generated images. Utilizing the advanced pre-trained generator from BigGAN, GAN-BVRM produces a wide array of natural images and selects those that most accurately correspond to the brain activity, using encoding models to reconstruct the original image stimuli. Here, the semantic content and intricate details of the reconstructions are managed by decoded categories and encoding models, respectively. Additionally, GAN-BVRM adopts a Bayesian approach to harmonize the naturalness and fidelity of the output.

This study introduces an innovative end-to-end deep learning framework designed to concurrently detect demand baselines and model incentive-driven agent demand responses using net demand measurements and incentive signals. The framework is divided into two distinct modules: 1) a differentiable optimization layer that simulates the decision-making process of a demand response participant, using incentive signals as input to forecast the user's response; 2) a conventional neural network model that predicts the user's baseline demand based on relevant features. These two predictions are combined to estimate the net demand. Additionally, we propose a gradient-descent method to propagate errors from the net demand forecast back to update the parameters of both the agent model and the baseline demand forecast simultaneously. The efficacy of our method is validated through computational experiments involving synthetic demand response data and a comprehensive real-world demand response dataset. The findings demonstrate that our method successfully identifies the demand response model with high accuracy, even in the absence of prior baseline demand information.

Precise hardware performance models are essential for optimizing code generation. Compilers utilize these models to guide heuristic choices, superoptimizers use them as a benchmark for minimization, and autotuners rely on them to identify the best configuration for specific applications. Nevertheless, creating these models is challenging due to the complexity of modern processors and the growing demand for deep learning accelerators, which adds to the development workload. We present a technique for developing performance models by training on a collection of tensor computation graph programs tailored for Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) instances. Our findings reveal that our trained model surpasses a highly optimized analytical performance model in two areas—tile-size selection and operator fusion—and it also aids an autotuner in identifying quicker programs in scenarios where TPU access is either restricted or costly.

We develop and evaluate an algorithm for first-order stochastic optimization applicable to a broad category of functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Specifically, we focus on \emph{variationally coherent} functions, which may be either convex or non-convex. For these functions, the iterates of our algorithm almost surely converge to the global minimizer $\boldsymbol{x}^*$. Moreover, using the same algorithm and hyperparameters, after $T$ iterations, we ensure that for convex functions, the expected suboptimality gap is limited to $\widetilde{O}(\|\boldsymbol{x}^* - \boldsymbol{x}_0\| T^{-1/2+\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon>0$. This algorithm is the first to simultaneously achieve these dual characteristics. Additionally, the convergence rate for convex functions is comparable to that of parameter-free algorithms. Our approach is a variant of the Follow The Regularized Leader framework, incorporating \emph{rescaled gradients} and dynamic linearithmic regularizers.

In this study, we introduced and tested a fully automated pipeline for generating hippocampal surfaces using a 3D U-net integrated with active shape modeling (ASM). The pipeline primarily involved three stages. Initially, a 3D U-net was applied to each magnetic resonance image to automatically segment the hippocampus in each hemisphere. Next, ASM was conducted on a set of previously acquired template surfaces to establish a mean shape and derive shape variation parameters via principal component analysis. Finally, a hybrid particle swarm optimization technique was employed to identify the ideal shape variation parameters that align closely with the segmentation. From these, the hippocampal surface was constructed using the mean shape and the determined shape variation parameters. The results demonstrated that our pipeline successfully produced hippocampal surfaces for both hemispheres with high precision, accurate anatomical topology, and adequate smoothness.

Image repurposing is a prevalent tactic for disseminating misinformation on social media and online platforms, where unaltered images are paired with falsified metadata to spark rumors and promote propaganda. Although manual fact-checking is feasible due to the wealth of verified information online, the growing frequency and simplicity of such semantic distortions necessitate the creation of reliable automated systems to evaluate the semantic accuracy of multimedia content. In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach for detecting image repurposing, modeled on the real-world conflict between a malicious actor who manipulates image metadata and a vigilant overseer who checks the consistency between images and their associated metadata. Both parties utilize a reference dataset of authenticated content to pursue their objectives. Our method delivers top-tier results in verifying location-identity, subject-identity, and painting-artist associations, demonstrating its effectiveness across a wide range of applications.

There is a growing fascination with developing algorithms that facilitate interaction between humans and machines. One of the most intuitive methods for obtaining human feedback is through comparison-based queries. However, a significant hurdle in crafting these interactive learning algorithms is managing noisy responses. The typical solution of repeating a query multiple times is often impractical due to high costs and the unrealistic expectation that noise remains independent across repeated queries. In this paper, we present a novel weak oracle model in which a non-malicious user answers a pairwise comparison query only when confident about the response. This model effectively replicates human behavior in areas susceptible to noise. Additionally, we explore the use of this weak oracle model in the context of content search, a variation of the nearest neighbor search problem, using comparisons. Specifically, our goal is to develop efficient algorithms that can pinpoint a target object within a database using a dissimilarity metric by engaging the weak comparison oracle. We introduce two algorithms, WORCS-I and WORCS-II (Weak-Oracle Comparison-based Search), which are proven to identify the target object with a number of comparisons that is comparably low.

This research focuses on predicting glaucomatous visual field loss using datasets from patients with the disease. Our objective is to precisely forecast the disease's progression in individual patients. Given the limited number of measurements available per patient, creating effective individual predictors is challenging. A newly introduced clustering-based approach improves prediction accuracy by grouping patients with similar spatiotemporal patterns and building predictive models based on the collective data within each cluster. However, the accuracy of these predictions heavily relies on the quality of clustering, and determining the optimal clustering technique remains problematic. To address this, we introduce a novel method that combines multiple cluster-based predictors to achieve superior accuracy compared to using a single cluster-based prediction. Additionally, our approach demonstrates exceptional results by hierarchically integrating experts derived from various clustering methods. Using real-world datasets, we show that our technique significantly outperforms traditional clustering-based and individual regression methods, thanks to a hierarchical aggregation strategy that allows effective predictors within smaller groups to excel.

Long Short-Term Memory networks, trained through gradient descent and back-propagation, have achieved remarkable success across a variety of applications. However, estimating the network weights through point estimation often leads to overfitting and fails to capture crucial uncertainty information related to these estimates. While exact Bayesian neural network approaches exist, they are computationally infeasible and impractical for real-world use. In this study, we introduce a method to approximate weight uncertainty using the Ensemble Kalman Filter, which can efficiently handle a large number of weights. Additionally, we enhance the ensemble update step by optimizing the noise distribution covariance through maximum likelihood estimation. To evaluate our proposed algorithm, we test its effectiveness in detecting outliers across five real-world events sourced from the Twitter platform.

Interpretable machine learning has recently attracted significant interest. To effectively explain decisions made by black-box systems, it is crucial to balance brevity and comprehensiveness, ensuring that a wealth of information is conveyed succinctly. However, current methods in interpretable machine learning often overlook this balance, resulting in overly detailed and redundant explanations. We introduce the Variational Information Bottleneck for Interpretation (VIBI), a versatile and interpretable approach that delivers concise yet thorough explanations, independent of the specific system used. VIBI employs the information bottleneck principle, an information-theoretic framework, to identify optimal explanations. For each case, VIBI identifies critical features that are both highly compressed regarding the input (ensuring brevity) and highly informative about the decision made by a black-box system for that input (ensuring comprehensiveness). We tested VIBI on three distinct datasets and benchmarked it against leading interpretable machine learning techniques, assessing both interpretability and fidelity through human evaluations and quantitative measures.

We present an innovative technique for creating text, specifically song lyrics, by leveraging the speech-like acoustic properties of a provided audio file. Our approach adapts a vocal source separation algorithm and an acoustic model originally designed to identify isolated speech, but we apply it to instrumental music or ambient sounds instead. By processing the "errors" produced by the vocal separator through the recognizer, we generate a transcription of words that are \emph{perceived} to be spoken within the audio input. We outline the core elements of our method, offer preliminary analysis, and explore its potential for fostering machine-assisted collaboration in creative endeavors.

Denoising poses a significant challenge in scientific imaging. Deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) represent the cutting-edge approach for denoising natural images, achieving remarkable outcomes. Yet, their application in scientific imaging remains largely untapped. Typically, denoising CNNs are trained using real natural images that have been artificially degraded with synthetic noise. Conversely, in scientific contexts, access to noiseless ground-truth images is often unattainable. To overcome this, we introduce a simulation-based denoising (SBD) framework, where CNNs are trained using simulated images. We evaluate this framework using data from transmission electron microscopy (TEM), a key imaging method in fields like material science, biology, and medicine. SBD significantly surpasses existing methods on both a simulated benchmark dataset and real-world data. Beyond producing denoised images, SBD also creates likelihood maps to illustrate the consistency between the denoised image structure and the input data. Our findings highlight limitations in current denoising architectures, such as their limited field-of-view. By expanding the field-of-view of the CNNs, we enable them to leverage non-local periodic patterns in the data, which proves essential at high noise levels. Furthermore, we assess the generalization potential of SBD.

We address the challenge of selecting high-dimensional Ising (graphical) models. A straightforward algorithm for structure estimation is proposed, which relies on thresholding empirical conditional variation distances. We introduce a new criterion for manageable graph families, where this approach proves efficient, characterized by the existence of sparse local separators between pairs of nodes in the underlying graph. For these specific graphs, the algorithm requires a sample complexity of $n=\Omega(J_{\min}^{-2}\log p)$, with $p$ representing the number of variables and $J_{\min}$ denoting the minimum (absolute) edge potential in the model. Additionally, we derive nonasymptotic necessary and sufficient conditions for accurate structure estimation.

Melanoma is regarded as the deadliest type of skin cancer. The resemblance between malignant and benign cancerous lesions often requires doctors to dedicate significant time to diagnosis. Currently, malignancy assessment relies mainly on invasive histological analysis of suspicious lesions. Creating an effective classifier for early and accurate detection could reduce the adverse impacts of skin cancer, enhance monitoring, and improve patient survival rates. This study introduces a multi-class classification approach utilizing the CoAtNet architecture, a hybrid model that integrates the depthwise convolution operations of conventional convolutional neural networks with the advantages of Transformer models and self-attention mechanisms to deliver superior generalization and capacity. The proposed classifier demonstrates impressive results, achieving a precision of 0.901, a recall of 0.895, and an AP of 0.923, showcasing its strong performance relative to other leading-edge networks.

Simulation holds the promise of revolutionizing the creation of reliable algorithms for mobile agents in high-stakes environments. Yet, the limited photorealism and the absence of varied sensor options in current simulation platforms pose significant challenges to unlocking this potential. We introduce VISTA, an open-source, data-driven simulator designed for autonomous vehicles, incorporating a range of sensor types. By leveraging high-quality, real-world data, VISTA accurately models and simulates RGB cameras, 3D LiDAR, and event-based cameras, facilitating the quick creation of new perspectives in a virtual setting. This capability enhances the data pool for policy learning by including rare scenarios that are hard to replicate in reality. With VISTA, we have successfully trained and evaluated perception-to-control policies across different sensor modalities and demonstrated the effectiveness of this method through implementation on a full-scale autonomous vehicle. The policies developed in VISTA show seamless sim-to-real transfer without adjustments and display superior resilience compared to policies trained solely on real-world data.

Poor sitting habits are recognized as a significant risk factor for musculoskeletal disorders and lower back pain, particularly among the elderly, individuals with disabilities, and office workers. In today's digital age, many people spend the majority of their time seated at computer desks, whether for leisure or work, which can lead to spinal issues and associated discomfort. Consequently, there is a critical need for systems that can alert individuals to their sitting posture and suggest corrective measures, such as physical exercise. While much research has focused on standing posture recognition, seated posture analysis has been comparatively overlooked. Existing studies on posture recognition have utilized various methods, including wearable sensors, pressure or force sensors, and video or image analysis. This study aims to develop Machine Learning models to classify an individual's sitting posture by examining data obtained from a chair equipped with two 32x32 pressure sensors on the seat and backrest. The models were constructed using five different algorithms: Random Forest (RF), Gaussian Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, and Deep Neural Network (DNN). Each model was assessed using the KFold cross-validation method. This paper details the experiments conducted with two distinct datasets—controlled and realistic—and provides a discussion of the findings.

One-shot Neural Architecture Search (NAS) seeks to reduce the computational cost involved in identifying top-performing models. Recently, however, the effectiveness of simple random search has been highlighted, showing results comparable to those of advanced NAS algorithms within the same search domains. In response to this, we investigate the impact of significantly broadening the NAS search space and introduce Bonsai-Net, an effective one-shot NAS approach tailored for this expanded search area. Bonsai-Net incorporates a refined differential pruner and reliably identifies superior architectures that outperform random search while using fewer parameters than other leading methods. Moreover, Bonsai-Net conducts model search and training concurrently, greatly decreasing the overall time required to develop fully-trained models from the ground up.

Numerous critical data analysis applications encounter significantly imbalanced datasets concerning the target variable. A prime example is medical image analysis, where positive samples are rare, yet performance is often measured by the accurate identification of these positive cases. We tackle this issue by redefining it as an anomaly detection problem using generative models. Our approach involves training a generative model without supervision on the 'negative' (more common) data points, then utilizing this model to assess the likelihood of new, unseen data. A well-performing model enables the identification of 'positive' cases as data points with low likelihood. In this position paper, we explore the application of cutting-edge deep generative models, specifically GANs and VAEs, to estimate data likelihood. Our findings indicate that both GANs and VAEs successfully distinguish between 'positive' and 'negative' samples in the MNIST dataset. However, in the case of the NLST dataset, neither GANs nor VAEs managed to grasp the data's complexity or detect anomalies with the precision required for this task. These outcomes suggest that, despite various successful applications of generative models reported in the literature, significant challenges persist in this domain.

We investigate networks of learning agents that communicate and collaborate to address a shared nonstochastic bandit problem. These agents rely on a communication network to exchange information about the actions chosen by their peers, discarding any messages that have traveled more than $d$ hops, where $d$ represents a delay threshold. We propose \textsc{Exp3-Coop}, a cooperative adaptation of the {\sc Exp3} algorithm, and demonstrate that with $K$ possible actions and $N$ agents, the average regret per agent over $T$ rounds is bounded by an order of $\sqrt{\bigl(d+1 + \tfrac{K}{N}\alpha_{\le d}\bigr)(T\ln K)}$, where $\alpha_{\le d}$ denotes the independence number of the $d$-th power of the connected communication graph $G$. Furthermore, we establish that for any connected graph, setting $d=\sqrt{K}$ yields a regret bound of $K^{1/4}\sqrt{T}$, which outperforms the minimax regret of $\sqrt{KT}$ observed in noncooperative settings. By selecting $d$ more strategically, the regret bounds can approach the full-information minimax regret of $\sqrt{T\ln K}$ in dense graphs. In cases where $G$ contains sparse components, we demonstrate that a modified version of \textsc{Exp3-Coop}, which allows agents to adjust their parameters based on their centrality within $G$, significantly reduces regret. Lastly, as a secondary outcome of our study, we offer the first characterization of minimax regret for bandit learning under delay constraints.

Prediction markets are employed in various real-world scenarios to forecast outcomes like presidential elections. This paper introduces a mathematical framework for artificial prediction markets aimed at supervised learning of conditional probability estimators. This innovative approach facilitates the integration of predictive insights from features or trained classifiers, with the resulting fusion represented as the contract price for potential outcomes. The market can be dynamically trained by adjusting participants' budgets based on training data. Drawing inspiration from actual prediction markets, the governing equations are formulated from straightforward and logical assumptions. Efficient numerical algorithms are developed to solve these equations. The resulting artificial prediction market is demonstrated to be a maximum likelihood estimator, extending beyond linear aggregation methods found in boosting and random forest, as well as logistic regression and certain kernel techniques. Additionally, the market mechanism supports the integration of specialized classifiers that engage only in specific cases. Experimental results indicate that artificial prediction markets frequently surpass random forest and implicit online learning in performance on both synthetic data and real UCI datasets. Furthermore, a comprehensive assessment for detecting pelvic and abdominal lymph nodes in CT data reveals that the prediction market enhances Adaboost's detection accuracy from
Proceedings of the 2019 BMVC Workshop on Interpretable and Explainable Machine Vision, held in Cardiff, UK, on September 12, 2019.

Data collection and annotation in machine learning are often time-intensive, particularly when addressing large-scale challenges. A typical strategy to mitigate this issue involves transferring knowledge from a related, labeled domain to a target domain. Two widely used methods to accomplish this are adversarial learning and self-training. In this article, we initially explore the issues of training instability and erroneous confusion that occur during the adversarial learning process. Subsequently, drawing inspiration from domain confusion and self-ensembling techniques, we introduce a hybrid model called Domain Confusion with Self-Ensembling (DCSE), which learns representations that are invariant to both features and classes. Our experiments demonstrate that this proposed method outperforms existing empirical approaches across various unsupervised domain adaptation benchmarks.

Deep generative modeling with flow-based approaches has become increasingly popular due to their ability to provide exact log-likelihood estimation alongside efficient training and synthesis. Nevertheless, a significant drawback of flow models is their reliance on a high-dimensional latent space, equivalent in size to the input space. To address this issue, Dinh et al. (2016) introduced a multi-scale architecture that iteratively factors out a portion of the dimensions at consistent intervals. Previous studies on generative flow models with multi-scale architectures have utilized static masking for dimension factorization. In contrast, we propose an innovative multi-scale architecture that employs data-dependent factorization to determine which dimensions require additional flow layers. To support this, we develop a heuristic that assesses each dimension’s contribution to the overall log-likelihood, reflecting the relative importance of each dimension. This heuristic is seamlessly integrated into the flow training process, facilitating the flexible application of our likelihood contribution-based multi-scale architecture across various flow models. We demonstrate its implementation in several leading flow models, showing enhanced log-likelihood scores and improved sampling quality on standard image datasets. Additionally, we perform ablation studies to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

Cyber-physical systems (CPS) and Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices are increasingly utilized in a wide array of applications, spanning from healthcare tools and wearables to vital infrastructures such as nuclear power plants, autonomous vehicles, smart cities, and smart homes. However, these devices often lack robust security across their entire software, hardware, and network layers, creating a broad attack surface that hackers can target. In this article, we introduce a groundbreaking method for identifying unknown system vulnerabilities, managing them effectively, and enhancing incident response when these vulnerabilities are exploited. The uniqueness of our approach stems from analyzing data from documented real-world CPS/IoT attacks, converting this information into regular expressions, and applying machine learning (ML) techniques to this collection to uncover new attack vectors and security flaws. Our findings reveal that we can generate 10 new attack vectors and 122 new vulnerability exploits capable of compromising CPS or IoT environments. The ML approach boasts an accuracy of 97.4% and significantly reduces the search space by 87.2%, enabling efficient prediction of these threats. We showcase the practical application of our technique through a case study on hacking the in-vehicle network of a connected car.

ICD coding serves as the global benchmark for documenting and reporting health conditions and diagnoses, playing a crucial role in healthcare revenue cycle management. However, the manual assignment of ICD codes is susceptible to human error, largely due to the extensive code set and the subtle distinctions between similar codes. As machine learning approaches depend on accurate ground truth data for training, the inconsistencies among human coders introduce noise into the labeling process. This noise complicates both the training and evaluation of ICD classifiers. This paper explores the nature of noise in manually assigned ICD-10 codes and proposes a novel approach to develop robust ICD-10 classifiers despite such labeling discrepancies. Our findings reveal that the noise in ICD coding is systematic rather than random. Unlike most existing methods that assume label noise is independent of features or labels, this does not hold true for ICD data. Consequently, we introduce a new method to train classifiers that can withstand systematic noise. Our approach involves identifying ICD-10 codes that are frequently misused or confused by human coders, taking into account their positions in the ICD-10 hierarchy, the code types, and the prediction patterns of a baseline classifier. We then devise an innovative training strategy to address these challenges.

In this study, we address the challenge of $\ell_{p}$ norm linear regression, a problem with significant applications in areas like sparse recovery, data clustering, and semi-supervised learning. Although the problem is convex, it lacks a closed-form solution. Existing algorithms, which are iterative in nature, often encounter convergence difficulties; they may diverge for p>3 or exhibit sensitivity to initial conditions in reaching the optimal solution. Moreover, these methods are not universally applicable across all values of $p$. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an iterative algorithm named Parallel IteRative AlgOrithM for $\ell_{P}$ norm regression via MajorizaTion Minimization (PROMPT), which operates on the principle of Majorization Minimization. We demonstrate that PROMPT ensures monotonic progression and guarantees convergence to the optimal solution for any value of $p$. Additionally, this algorithm facilitates parallel updates of each component of the regression variable, enabling efficient processing of large-scale data—a critical advantage in today's data-rich environment. We further illustrate that PROMPT is adaptable to graph-based semi-supervised learning tasks. Through numerical simulations, we confirm that PROMPT consistently converges to the optimal solution regardless of the starting point and outperforms existing approaches.

Examining the structure of cells in microscopy images can reveal important details about the effects of compounds or the roles of genes. To tackle this challenge, it is essential to develop methods that extract relevant biological data from the images while disregarding technical discrepancies, such as variations in experimental methods or differences in the equipment used for capturing the images. We introduce Treatment ExemplArs with Mixture-of-experts (TEAMs), a novel embedding learning strategy that employs a group of experts, each trained to recognize specific technical variations in our dataset. During testing, TEAMs combine the insights of these specialists to generate results. This allows TEAMs to create robust embeddings with reduced bias from technical noise by mitigating the impact of variations across experts. For training, we utilize Treatment Exemplars, which help our model encapsulate the diversity of the entire dataset within each minibatch, ensuring compatibility with GPU memory constraints. We tested our method on three datasets for applications like drug discovery, achieving a 5.5-11% improvement in accurately determining the mechanism of action of cell treatments compared to the leading methods.

$(j,k)$-projective clustering extends the concepts of $k$-clustering and $j$-subspace clustering. It involves a set of points $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where the objective is to identify $k$ flats of dimension $j$—that is, affine subspaces—that optimally align with $P$ according to a specified distance metric. In this work, we introduce the first algorithm that produces an $L_\infty$ coreset with a size that is polynomial in $d$. Additionally, we present the inaugural strong coreset construction for general $M$-estimator regression. Specifically, our method enables efficient coreset constructions for a variety of regression models, including Cauchy, Welsch, Huber, Geman-McClure, Tukey, $L_1-L_2$, and Fair regression, as well as loss functions that are generally concave or power-bounded. Lastly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experimental results derived from real-world datasets.

The remarkable success of adversarial attacks in deceiving deep neural networks presents a significant barrier to the broad implementation of deep learning in fields where safety and security are paramount. Although various defense strategies have been developed since the vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial attacks was first identified, fully comprehending and mitigating this problem remains a distant goal. In this research, we propose that one key factor behind the potency of adversarial attacks is their ability to subtly access and manipulate the gradient flow within a deep neural network. This inherent capability to exploit gradient flow renders defense against such attacks particularly difficult. Building on this theory, we suggest that if a deep neural network architecture could actively utilize its own gradient flow during training, it could substantially enhance its defensive strength. Drawing from this insight, we present self-gradient networks, an innovative deep neural network architecture crafted to offer greater resilience to adversarial disruptions. By incorporating gradient flow data, self-gradient networks attain improved stability against perturbations, surpassing the outcomes of conventional training methods. We also perform a theoretical analysis to deepen our understanding of the dynamics of the proposed architecture.

In this study, we address the challenge of clustering very short text collections through subspace clustering. This issue is relevant in various contexts, including product categorization, fraud detection, and sentiment analysis. The primary difficulty stems from the high-dimensional and extremely sparse nature of short texts' vectorial representations, caused by the vast array of unique terms in the corpus and the minimal word count per text without repetition. We introduce a novel, straightforward subspace clustering algorithm based on linear algebra to effectively group such data. Tests conducted on product names from the US Amazon website to determine product categories demonstrate that our algorithm performs comparably to leading clustering methods.

Machine learning models can jeopardize the privacy of individuals whose data is used for training. Recent attacks, such as model inversion or attribute inference attacks, have successfully extracted sensitive information from these models, uncovering specific private details about participants in the training data. Research indicates that the risk of model inversion increases due to various factors, including the influence of particular features. It is evident that not all features carry the same degree of privacy or sensitivity; some, deemed particularly sensitive, are more vulnerable to inversion attacks. To address this issue, we propose a method to mitigate model inversion attacks in tree-based models by diminishing the impact of sensitive features. This approach remains underexplored, with only preliminary efforts made previously to employ it as a defense against attribute inference. Our findings demonstrate that it is often feasible to train models in alternative ways, adjusting the influence of different features without compromising the model's accuracy. We have successfully utilized

Children continuously learn by inquiring about topics that pique their curiosity. Similarly, as robots become increasingly embedded in our society, they too must persistently acquire knowledge about unfamiliar concepts by posing questions to humans. This paper examines a cutting-edge method for continual learning and introduces a self-supervised strategy to identify most uncertain objects in an environment using cluster representations of previously learned categories. We evaluate our method on a standard dataset for continual learning in robotics. Our findings demonstrate that our curiosity-driven approach to continual learning outperforms both random sampling and softmax-based uncertainty sampling in terms of classification accuracy and the overall number of classes mastered.

We introduce ARLPCG, a novel method called Adversarial Reinforcement Learning for Procedural Content Generation, which dynamically creates and evaluates new environments using an auxiliary input as a control mechanism. Training reinforcement learning (RL) agents in unfamiliar settings is a well-known challenge. A common strategy to enhance the adaptability of these agents is to procedurally generate a variety of environments. ARLPCG, however, employs an adversarial framework featuring two RL agents: a Generator, which creates the environments, and a Solver, which attempts to navigate them. The Generator is rewarded based on the Solver’s performance, incentivizing the creation of environments that are tough yet feasible. To boost the diversity and manageability of the generated environments, we incorporate auxiliary inputs for the Generator. This approach offers dual advantages: it enhances the Solver’s ability to generalize by facing varied challenges crafted by the Generator, and it allows the trained Generator to produce innovative, solvable environments alongside the Solver. We validate our approach by designing two distinct 3D environments reflective of popular gaming genres—a third-person platformer and a racing game. Our results demonstrate that ARLPCG achieves a significantly higher solve ratio, with the auxiliary inputs effectively shaping the complexity of the levels.

Probabilistic classifiers generate confidence scores alongside their predictions, and these scores ought to be well-calibrated, meaning they should accurately represent the prediction's reliability. When confidence scores are optimized to minimize metrics like the expected calibration error (ECE), they effectively gauge average reliability across an entire population. However, assessing the reliability of a specific, individual prediction remains generally unfeasible. In this study, we introduce the local calibration error (LCE) as a bridge between average and individual reliability. The LCE evaluates the average reliability of a group of similar predictions for each individual prediction, with similarity defined by a kernel function in a pretrained feature space and a binning approach based on predicted model confidences. We demonstrate theoretically that the LCE can be efficiently estimated from data and empirically show that it uncovers more detailed miscalibration patterns than the ECE can identify. Our primary contribution is a novel local recalibration technique, LoRe, designed to refine confidence scores for individual predictions and reduce the LCE. Through experiments, we prove that our recalibration approach yields more precise confidence scores, enhancing downstream fairness and decision-making in classification tasks involving both image and tabular data.

This paper addresses the challenge of identifying the most suitable options through pairwise comparisons, even when these comparisons are not necessarily transitive. Within this context, we explore a reinforcement urn model. We demonstrate that convergence to the optimal solution is achieved when reinforcement of the winning alternative takes place after evaluating three randomly selected alternatives. However, the more straightforward approach of reinforcing the winner of a randomly chosen pair does not guarantee convergence and may result in cyclic behavior.

The swift dissemination of information via social media significantly impacts quantitative trading and investment strategies. The rising trend of speculative trading in highly volatile assets, such as cryptocurrencies and meme stocks, introduces new challenges in the financial sector. Examining these "bubbles"—episodes of abrupt, abnormal market behavior—is essential for gaining deeper insights into investor psychology and market trends. However, the extreme volatility and the overwhelming flood of disjointed social media content, particularly for lesser-known assets like cryptocoins, create obstacles for current analytical approaches. As an initial step toward applying Natural Language Processing (NLP) to cryptocoins, we introduce CryptoBubbles, a pioneering multi-span identification task for detecting bubbles, accompanied by a comprehensive dataset of over 400 cryptocoins from nine exchanges across five years, encompassing more than two million tweets. Additionally, we have crafted a series of sequence-to-sequence hyperbolic models tailored for this multi-span identification task, drawing on the power-law dynamics of cryptocurrencies and social media user behavior. We also evaluate the performance of these models in zero-shot scenarios using a test set of Reddit posts related to 29 "meme stocks," which experience spikes in trading volume fueled by social media excitement. Our analysis, covering both quantitative and qualitative aspects as well as zero-shot testing on Reddit and Twitter data for cryptocoins and meme stocks, offers valuable insights.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are effective generative models, yet they often face challenges with training instability. The Wasserstein GAN (WGAN), a recent advancement, improves the stability of GAN training, though it occasionally produces low-quality outputs or fails to converge. We have identified that these issues frequently stem from the weight clipping technique used in WGAN to impose a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, which can result in problematic behavior. As an alternative to weight clipping, we suggest penalizing the gradient norm of the critic relative to its input. Our approach outperforms the traditional WGAN and facilitates stable training across a diverse range of GAN architectures with minimal need for hyperparameter adjustments, including 101-layer ResNets and language models handling discrete data. Additionally, we have obtained high-quality results on the CIFAR-10 and LSUN bedrooms datasets.

Texture segmentation involves dividing an image into distinct regions based on varying textures, where each region comprises pixels with similar characteristics. The process relies on identifying discontinuities in filter outputs and analyzing their statistical attributes to segment and classify images with diverse texture areas. In this research paper, texture segmentation of chili X-ray images is achieved using a Gabor filter. The resulting segmented textures from the Gabor filter are processed through three texture filters: Entropy, Standard Deviation, and Range filters. Following texture analysis, features are extracted using statistical approaches. This study employs Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrices and First Order Statistics as methods for feature extraction. The extracted features from these statistical techniques are then input into a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier. The findings indicate that texture segmentation, when paired with the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix for feature extraction, achieves a superior accuracy rate of 84% compared to the First Order feature extraction method. Key Words: Texture segmentation, Texture filter, Gabor filter, Feature extraction methods, SVM classifier.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have garnered significant interest, largely due to their ability to produce high-quality, original samples in visual domains. However, most existing approaches restrict user involvement in the image creation process to minimal interactions. In this study, we introduce a groundbreaking GAN framework that integrates human input directly into the image generation workflow. Our method allows users to iteratively provide relative constraints, such as "Create an image that resembles image A more than image B." Following each input, the GAN generates new images for the user to review, shaping subsequent feedback. This feedback helps tailor the GAN's output within a customizable semantic space that can represent various similarity metrics, including classes, attributes, object relationships, and color. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework produces images of quality comparable to those from unsupervised GANs, while successfully adhering to numerous user-specified constraints. This transforms the GAN into a tool for interactive image generation, maintaining high image quality alongside enhanced user control.

Employing a high Update-To-Data (UTD) ratio, model-based approaches have recently surpassed the sample efficiency of earlier model-free techniques in continuous-action Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) benchmarks. In this paper, we present Randomized Ensembled Double Q-Learning (REDQ), a straightforward model-free algorithm, demonstrating that it matches or exceeds the performance of a leading model-based algorithm on the MuJoCo benchmark. Additionally, REDQ accomplishes this with fewer parameters and reduced wall-clock run time compared to its model-based counterpart. The high performance of REDQ is enabled by three meticulously combined components: (i) a UTD ratio significantly greater than 1; (ii) a collection of Q functions; and (iii) in-target minimization over a randomly selected subset of Q functions from the ensemble. Through thoughtfully crafted experiments, we offer an in-depth evaluation of REDQ and other related model-free algorithms. To our knowledge, REDQ represents the first successful model-free DRL algorithm for continuous-action spaces that utilizes a UTD ratio substantially greater than 1.

Over the last few years, machine learning (ML) has seen remarkable progress and has been effectively applied to a wide array of tasks, including the detection of phishing attempts. Nevertheless, creating a robust ML-based detection system remains a complex endeavor, necessitating the expertise of data scientists well-versed in the specific field. In recent times, Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) frameworks have gained significant traction, allowing individuals without deep ML expertise to develop machine learning models. This raises a compelling question: can AutoML surpass the outcomes achieved by human data scientists? Our study evaluates the performance of six prominent, cutting-edge AutoML frameworks across ten distinct phishing datasets to determine if AutoML-driven models can exceed the capabilities of manually engineered machine learning models. The findings suggest that AutoML-based models indeed surpass manually crafted models in intricate classification tasks, particularly with datasets featuring indistinctive features, overlapping categories, or significant non-linear characteristics. However, constructing a practical phishing detection system with AutoML frameworks presents ongoing challenges, including their limitation to supervised classification tasks which require labeled data, and the lack of functionality for incremental updates to the models. This highlights the continued importance of expert involvement in certain aspects of model development and deployment.

We explore the challenge of reconstructing a high-rank matrix that is only partially observed, where the columns adhere to a nonlinear structure, such as a union of subspaces, an algebraic variety, or are organized into clusters. The problem of recovery is defined as minimizing the rank of a nonlinear feature map applied to the original matrix. This is subsequently approximated through a constrained non-convex optimization problem on the Grassmann manifold. We introduce two categories of algorithms: one based on Riemannian optimization and the other employing an alternating minimization approach, each featuring both first- and second-order variants. These algorithms come with theoretical assurances. Specifically, for the alternating minimization approach, we demonstrate global convergence and provide bounds on worst-case complexity. Moreover, leveraging the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, we prove that the alternating minimization converges to a singular limit point. We present comprehensive numerical experiments for scenarios involving union of subspaces and clustering, under conditions of entry sampling and dense Gaussian sampling. Our approaches perform comparably to existing methods, with notably high accuracy observed in recoveries using second-order Riemannian methods.

We present an algorithm for completing an order-$m$ symmetric low-rank tensor using its multilinear entries, with a runtime roughly proportional to the total number of tensor entries. This tensor completion algorithm is utilized to address the challenge of learning mixtures of product distributions over the hypercube, yielding novel algorithmic outcomes. For product distributions with linearly independent centers, our method successfully recovers distributions with up to $\Omega(n)$ centers in polynomial time and sample complexity. In the general scenario, it recovers distributions with up to $\tilde\Omega(n)$ centers in quasi-polynomial time, resolving an open question posed by Feldman et al. (SIAM J. Comp.) for distributions with incoherent bias vectors. The core of our approach relies on repeatedly applying a low-rank matrix completion algorithm designed for matrices with adversarially missing entries.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) serve as aerial base-stations, facilitating the transmission of time-critical data packets from IoT devices to nearby terrestrial base-stations (TBS). Ensuring that the packets from IoT devices remain current at the TBS poses a significant challenge in UAV-relayed IoT networks. This issue requires managing two concurrent processes: (i) the collection of data packets from IoT devices by UAVs (hop-1), and (ii) the delivery of these collected packets from UAVs to the TBS (hop-2). To tackle this, we introduce Age-of-Information (AoI) scheduling algorithms tailored for two-hop UAV-relayed IoT networks. Initially, we present a straightforward AoI scheduler named MAF-MAD, which adopts the Maximum AoI First (MAF) approach for data collection at the UAV level (hop-1) and the Maximum AoI Difference (MAD) approach for data delivery to the TBS (hop-2). We demonstrate that MAF-MAD achieves optimal AoI scheduling under ideal conditions, including lossless wireless channels and on-demand data generation at IoT devices. Conversely, for more complex scenarios involving lossy channels and inconsistent periodic data generation at IoT devices, we propose a deep reinforcement learning approach using a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based scheduler. Simulation outcomes reveal that the PPO-based scheduler surpasses other methods such as MAF-MAD, MAF, and round-robin across various general conditions.

Deep Learning has proven to be a powerful tool in addressing numerous complex challenges that were unimaginable just a few decades ago. However, alongside its many advantages, it also poses potential risks to society. One significant issue is the creation of deep fakes, which has become increasingly accessible with smartphone applications allowing anyone to produce fake images or videos. This accessibility underscores the urgent need for effective countermeasures to determine the authenticity of such content and to combat the erosion of trust in online information. Although deep fakes generated by neural networks can appear incredibly lifelike, they often leave behind subtle spatial and temporal clues or signatures after manipulation. While these traces are imperceptible to the human eye, they can be identified by neural networks specifically trained for deep fake detection. In this paper, we examine and compare several cutting-edge neural networks, including MesoNet, ResNet-50, VGG-19, and Xception Net, to assess their effectiveness in this critical task.

The correct initialization of weights plays a vital role in the efficient training and rapid convergence of deep neural networks (DNNs). Previous studies in this field have primarily concentrated on equalizing the variance of weights within each layer to ensure the stability of (i) the input data as it moves forward through the network and (ii) the loss gradients as they are backpropagated. However, this common heuristic overlooks the interdependencies of gradients across different layers and only accounts for first-order effects. In this paper, we introduce and explore an initialization method grounded in a detailed assessment of the global curvature of weights across layers, achieved by estimating and managing the norm of their Hessian matrix. This systematic approach not only aligns with prior findings for DNN activations like smooth functions, dropouts, and ReLU, but also enhances them. Our experiments with Word2Vec and the MNIST/CIFAR image classification tasks demonstrate that monitoring the Hessian norm serves as an effective diagnostic tool, aiding in the more precise initialization of weights.

Although various approaches address different forms of distribution shift, including label shift (such as adversarial attacks) and domain shift, the challenge of handling a joint shift remains unresolved. By examining a joint distribution shift that combines both adversarial and domain-specific perturbations, we demonstrate that this combined shift degrades model performance more severely than individual shifts. Additionally, we find that using a similar domain negatively impacts performance more than a dissimilar one. To mitigate this decline, we explore perturbation sets guided by constraints in input and parameter spaces and employ a meta-learning approach (via hypernetworks) to adapt model parameters based on test-time inputs, thereby improving performance.

A fundamental trait of human intelligence is the capacity to share knowledge with others in a concise manner. Yet, despite their predictive capabilities, many current machine learning models remain opaque, hindering humans from gaining meaningful insights. In the realm of sequential decision-making, we have developed a new machine learning algorithm that communicates its insights to humans through understandable "tips." This algorithm identifies the tip that most effectively narrows the performance gap between human users and the optimal strategy. We tested our method via randomized controlled user studies, where participants operated a virtual kitchen. The results demonstrate that the tips provided by our algorithm significantly enhance human performance compared to standard intuitive approaches. Furthermore, we explore several empirical observations that could guide the creation of algorithms for human-AI interaction. For example, we discovered that participants do not merely follow our tips unquestioningly; rather, they integrate these suggestions with their personal experiences to uncover new ways to boost their performance.

A critical issue in deep learning revolves around the privacy and security of neural networks (NNs). Historically, these two elements have been examined independently. The effect of privacy-focused training on the resilience of NNs remains largely unclear. This paper conducts an experimental analysis to assess how training with Differential Privacy (DP), a common approach for safeguarding privacy, influences model susceptibility to a wide array of adversarial attacks. Findings indicate that models trained with privacy protections exhibit lower robustness compared to those without such measures. Moreover, adversarial examples are more likely to transfer effectively between DP-trained models than between models with and without privacy protections. In-depth comparisons of DP and non-DP models also reveal notable disparities in their gradients. Additionally, this study is the first to highlight that inappropriate parameter selection in DP training may cause gradient masking, leading to a false perception of security.

Society increasingly depends on algorithms, such as classifiers, for critical decision-making, highlighting the importance of ethical assurances like fairness. Fairness is generally understood as ensuring that a classifier’s key metrics are roughly equivalent across protected demographic groups. This paper reviews existing fairness strategies and uses them as a foundation to propose algorithms that embed fairness within genetic programming for classification tasks. We introduce two innovative concepts: the first integrates a fairness goal into multi-objective optimization, while the second modifies lexicase selection to dynamically create cases based on intersections of protected groups. We explain why lexicase selection is particularly effective in encouraging models to perform consistently across the potentially limitless subgroups where fairness is required. Employing a modern genetic programming framework, we build models on four datasets necessitating fairness constraints and compare their performance against earlier game-theoretic approaches. The evaluation focuses on the methods' capacity to produce Pareto-optimal trade-offs between subgroup fairness and accuracy. Our findings indicate that genetic programming techniques, especially random search, are highly effective for this purpose.

We investigate the concept that writing a piece of text is an exercise in maximizing one's expected utility. To illustrate this concept, we focus on the critical decisions made by the Supreme Court of the United States. A substantial body of research in quantitative political science offers a foundation for empirically analyzing the decisions of justices and their connection to textual content. We integrate texts written by amici curiae—individuals or groups, distinct from the litigants, who aim to influence the court's rulings—into such a framework, and explicitly represent their objectives within a random utility model. We highlight the advantages of this method through enhanced vote prediction accuracy and the capacity to conduct counterfactual analysis.

Pathologist-defined labels serve as the benchmark for histopathological datasets, despite recognized inconsistencies in certain tasks. Currently, several datasets focusing on mitotic figures are accessible and have facilitated the creation of advanced deep learning algorithms. To evaluate the durability of these algorithms and the repeatability of their techniques, testing across multiple independent datasets is essential. The impact of varying labeling approaches in these datasets remains unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce a new set of labels for the images in the auxiliary mitosis dataset from the TUPAC16 challenge. Beyond traditional manual screening for mitotic figures, we implemented a novel, algorithm-assisted labeling method to reduce the likelihood of overlooking rare mitotic figures in the images. Two pathologists independently reviewed all potential mitotic figures. This newly available label set, now public, includes 1,999 mitotic figures (a 28.80% increase) and also encompasses 10,483 labels of cells closely resembling mitotic figures (termed hard examples). A comparison using a conventional deep learning object detection framework revealed a significant disparity in F_1 scores between the original label set (0.549) and our alternative label set (0.735).
