The study of large graph properties through sampling has been a significant topic in statistical network analysis since the pioneering efforts of Goodman \cite{Goodman1949} and Frank \cite{Frank1978}. We revisit a challenge posed by Frank \cite{Frank1978} concerning the estimation of the number of connected components in a vast graph using a subgraph sampling approach. In this method, a random subset of vertices is selected, and the resulting induced subgraph is analyzed. A critical issue is whether precise estimation is feasible in the \emph{sublinear} regime, where only a diminishing fraction of vertices are sampled. Our findings indicate that accurate estimation is unattainable if the original graph includes vertices of high degree or extended induced cycles. However, for chordal graphs—where induced cycles of length four or greater are not permitted—we define the optimal sample complexity within constant factors and develop linear-time estimators that demonstrably meet these limits. This work broadens the scope of prior research, which primarily concentrated on unbiased estimators and specific graph types like forests or cliques. The development and evaluation of our approach hinge on the combinatorial characteristics of chordal graphs and specific identities related to induced subgraph counts, which are also crucial in substantiating our results.

Automatic speech recognition systems typically depend on spectral-based features like MFCC or PLP, which are derived from prior knowledge of speech perception and/or production. Recent advancements have demonstrated that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can estimate phoneme conditional probabilities in a fully data-driven approach by directly using raw temporal speech signals as input. This approach has achieved comparable or superior results to HMM/ANN-based systems in phoneme recognition and large-scale continuous speech recognition tasks, while utilizing fewer parameters. Inspired by these findings, we explore the application of a simple linear classifier within a CNN-based framework. In this setup, the network learns linearly separable features directly from raw speech. Our results indicate that this system delivers performance that matches or exceeds that of MLP-based systems which rely on cepstral-based features as input.

Finding approximate nearest neighbors in high-dimensional spaces is a fundamental challenge in large-scale data mining, with significant implications for machine learning and data science. One of the most effective and widely used methods for approximating nearest neighbors is locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). In this paper, we focus on developing LSH schemes tailored for distance functions that quantify the separation between probability distributions, with a specific emphasis on f-divergences and an extension to address mutual information loss. We begin by presenting a comprehensive framework for designing LSH schemes for f-divergence distance measures, and within this framework, we construct LSH schemes for both the generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence and triangular discrimination. Additionally, we demonstrate a two-sided approximation result for the generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence using the Hellinger distance, a finding that could hold independent significance. Furthermore, we introduce a general approach to transform the problem of creating an LSH scheme for a Krein kernel—expressed as the difference between two positive definite kernels—into a maximum inner product search problem. We illustrate this approach by applying it to mutual information loss, which is particularly relevant due to its applications in areas such as model compression.

Representation learning in knowledge graphs (KGs) has predominantly targeted the task of responding to straightforward link prediction queries. In this study, we tackle the more complex issue of predicting answers to conjunctive queries that involve several missing entities. We introduce Bi-Directional Query Embedding (BIQE), a novel approach that utilizes bi-directional attention mechanisms to embed conjunctive queries. Unlike previous methods, bi-directional self-attention effectively captures the interactions between all components of a query graph. Additionally, we present a new dataset designed for answering conjunctive queries and demonstrate through experiments that BIQE substantially surpasses existing state-of-the-art baselines.

Selecting an appropriate approximate posterior distribution is a fundamental challenge in variational inference. Typically, variational inference relies on basic families of posterior approximations to facilitate efficient computation, often using mean-field or other straightforward structured approximations. However, this limitation significantly affects the accuracy of the inferences drawn from variational methods. We propose a novel method for creating adaptable, highly complex, and scalable approximate posterior distributions. Our method utilizes normalizing flows, where a basic initial density is converted into a more intricate distribution through a series of reversible transformations until the necessary complexity is achieved. By adopting this perspective on normalizing flows, we categorize finite and infinitesimal flows and offer a cohesive framework for developing detailed posterior approximations. We show that the theoretical benefits of posteriors that more closely resemble the true posterior, paired with the scalability of amortized variational techniques, lead to notable enhancements in the performance and utility of variational inference.

Policy gradient methods represent a popular category of model-free reinforcement learning algorithms that employ a state-dependent baseline to minimize the variance of gradient estimators. Recent studies have proposed extending this baseline to incorporate both state and action dependencies, claiming that this adjustment substantially lowers variance and enhances sample efficiency without biasing the gradient estimates. To explore this advancement, we analyze the variance of the policy gradient estimator and demonstrate through numerical analysis that, contrary to expectations, learned baselines dependent on both state and action do not reduce variance compared to solely state-dependent baselines in widely tested benchmark environments. This surprising finding is supported by an examination of the open-source code from these earlier studies, revealing that specific implementation choices lead to discrepancies from the methodologies described in the papers, accounting for the previously reported empirical improvements. Additionally, our variance analysis identifies potential enhancements, which we exemplify by proposing a straightforward modification to the standard value function parameterization that markedly boosts performance.

Over the past ten years, computer vision has garnered significant interest within the field of computer science, yet its application to enhance engineering design research remains underexplored. With the advent of advanced datasets and technologies, researchers can now collect and utilize a vast array of observations and video content, making analysis the primary bottleneck. This paper explores the integration of machine learning, specifically object detection techniques, to facilitate the analysis of physical prototypes. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset comprising 5,950 images from 850 prototypes captured during early development phases, the authors examine potential applications for dissecting this data. They adapted two established object detection models from the TensorFlow Object Detection API and Darknet frameworks, customizing them with image sets of physical prototypes. Consequently, the paper presents a proof-of-concept featuring four trained models: two designed to identify wood-based sheet materials and two for recognizing microcontroller-containing samples. Each model’s performance is assessed using conventional object detection metrics, and the paper discusses the relevance of employing such models in engineering design research. The findings suggest that these models effectively categorize both material types and specific components.

A collaborative strategy was employed to enhance devices, circuits, and neural network architectures, effectively mitigating performance decline in a Fe-FinFET-based artificial neural network caused by changes in junction temperature. We established that the binary nature of the neural network, where the "0" state is set deep in the subthreshold region and the "1" state operates in strong inversion, is essential for reliable deep neural network (DNN) inference. A software-only binary neural network (BNN) served as a reference, achieving a 96.1% accuracy rate on the Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (MNIST) dataset for handwritten digit recognition. In comparison, the Fe-FinFET-based BNN, accounting for device-to-device variations at 300 K, attained a 95.7% inference accuracy on the same dataset. While significant accuracy drops due to temperature fluctuations were noted in a nonbinary neural network, the BNN using optimized Fe-FinFETs as synaptic devices showed remarkable resilience to temperature variations, sustaining a minimum inference accuracy of 95.2% across a temperature spectrum from -233K to 398K following optimizations in gate stack and bias. Nonetheless, reprogramming to modify device conductance was required for temperatures exceeding 398K.

This research explores the potential of using phonological features in text-to-speech systems to produce both native and non-native speech in English and Mandarin. We developed a mapping from ARPABET/pinyin to SAMPA/SAMPA-SC, and subsequently to phonological features. Our study tested whether this mapping could effectively generate native, non-native, and code-switched speech in these languages. Two experiments were conducted, one utilizing a small dataset and the other a larger one. The findings confirmed that phonological features are a viable input method, though further research is required to enhance model performance. Additionally, the accented speech output from the TTS models provides valuable insights into human second language acquisition processes.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a novel approach in machine learning, enabling model training without the need to centralize data on a single server. Typically, FL research focuses on a centralized system where one server holds the authority to manage numerous devices, guiding them through iterative model training. However, this centralized structure faces scalability challenges due to severe communication and bandwidth limitations as the device count increases. To overcome this, we introduce a ConFederated Learning (CFL) framework in this paper. Our CFL model incorporates multiple servers, each linked to a unique group of devices similar to traditional FL setups, while promoting decentralized cooperation among servers to effectively utilize the dispersed data across the network. We have devised an algorithm for CFL based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). This algorithm features a random scheduling strategy that selects a subset of devices at random to connect with their servers during each cycle, significantly reducing the data upload burden from devices to servers. We provide a theoretical analysis to support the efficacy of this approach. The numerical outcomes demonstrate that our method achieves convergence.

Regularization techniques are commonly used in deep learning neural networks (DNNs) to combat overfitting. In penalty-based regularization for DNNs, convex penalties are often preferred due to their assured optimization properties. However, recent theoretical studies indicate that nonconvex penalties, which meet specific regularity criteria, can also achieve strong performance with conventional optimization methods. In this paper, we explore both new and existing nonconvex penalties for DNN regularization. We offer theoretical support for the novel penalties introduced and evaluate the effectiveness of all penalties through DNN analysis across seven different datasets.

The Bayesian framework offers a promising solution to fundamental challenges in deep neural networks, such as inadequate calibration and data inefficiency. However, applying Bayesian inference to expansive weight spaces often necessitates limiting approximations. In this study, we demonstrate that accurate predictive posteriors can be achieved by conducting inference on only a small subset of model weights, while maintaining the remaining weights as point estimates. This subnetwork inference approach allows the use of sophisticated, otherwise impractical, posterior approximations on these subsets. Specifically, we introduce subnetwork linearized Laplace as a straightforward, scalable method for Bayesian deep learning: initially, we calculate a MAP estimate for all weights, followed by inferring a full-covariance Gaussian posterior over a chosen subnetwork via the linearized Laplace approximation. We also present a strategy for subnetwork selection designed to retain the model's predictive uncertainty to the greatest extent possible. Our empirical results show that this method outperforms ensembles and less detailed posterior approximations applied to entire networks. The subnetwork (linearized) Laplace approach is available in the laplace PyTorch library at https://github.com/AlexImmer/Laplace.

In recent times, the increasing complexity of neural networks has spurred significant research into compression methods to address the challenges posed by their large scale. The majority of these studies fall into three main categories: Knowledge Distillation, Pruning, and Quantization. Despite consistent advancements in this field, the practical application and commercial integration of these methods have not kept pace with the research. We introduce KD-Lib, a user-friendly, open-source library built on PyTorch, featuring cutting-edge, modular implementations of techniques from these three categories across various abstraction levels. KD-Lib is designed to be independent of specific models or algorithms and offers enhanced capabilities for hyperparameter optimization through Optuna, as well as logging and monitoring via Tensorboard. Access the library at https://github.com/SforAiDl/KD_Lib.

AI systems are increasingly integral to various applications within financial services. As these systems play a larger role in critical decision-making, the demand for compliance and robust model governance has intensified. Existing governance practices, rooted in traditional financial applications and modeling approaches, often fall short in addressing the unique traits of AI, such as uncertainty in assumptions and the absence of explicit programming. The governance of AI models typically involves intricate review processes and a heavy dependence on manual interventions, leading to significant issues in efficiency, cost, complexity, and speed. Moreover, the rapid increase in AI model complexity raises concerns about the long-term viability of current governance methods. This paper examines the challenges associated with AI model governance in the financial services sector. Looking ahead, we propose a system-level framework to enhance self-regulation, focusing on robustness and compliance. This framework seeks to unlock potential solutions by boosting automation and incorporating monitoring, management, and mitigation features. Additionally, it offers enhanced capabilities for model governance and risk management, enabling better handling of model risks during implementation.

We are living in a time of expansive data catalogs, making statistical analysis tools for handling large datasets, like machine learning, increasingly vital. A prime example is the Sloan Moving Object Catalog (MOC), which compiles astrometric and photometric data for all moving objects within the Sloan field of view. A significant benefit of this telescope lies in its array of five filters, which enable taxonomic analysis of asteroids through color studies. However, the impact of phase angle changes on color variation has previously been overlooked. In this paper, we tackle this oversight by utilizing absolute magnitudes for classification purposes. Our goal is to develop a new taxonomic classification for asteroids based on their magnitudes, independent of variations due to phase angle changes. We chose 9481 asteroids with absolute magnitudes of Hg, Hi, and Hz, derived from the Sloan Moving Objects Catalog using the HG12 system. Using these, we determined the absolute colors. For the taxonomic classification, we employed an unsupervised machine learning algorithm called fuzzy C-means, a valuable soft clustering method ideal for datasets where

Graph generative models represent a dynamic and rapidly evolving area of machine learning. As new, increasingly sophisticated models continue to emerge, there is a pressing need for a robust framework to evaluate and compare their performance. In this paper, we outline the essential criteria for an effective comparison metric and review the current landscape of graph generative model assessment, which primarily depends on the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) method. We conduct a detailed analysis of MMD's application in comparing graph generative models, identifying potential challenges and common pitfalls that researchers might unintentionally face. Through an in-depth study of MMD's behavior on synthetically altered graphs and recently developed graph generative models, we propose a practical approach to address these issues. Our insights are compiled into a set of actionable recommendations for researchers evaluating graph generative models.

The backpropagation of error algorithm, central to the achievements of deep learning, is pivotal in training deep neural networks. Yet, its reliance on sequential backward updates and non-local computations poses significant challenges for large-scale parallelization and contrasts with the brain's learning mechanisms. In response, neuroscience-inspired learning algorithms like predictive coding, which employ local learning strategies, offer a promising alternative to surpass the constraints of current deep learning methods. Initially conceptualized in theoretical neuroscience as a model for cortical information processing, predictive coding has recently evolved into a versatile algorithm capable of training neural networks through exclusively local computations. This survey examines literature that has shaped this viewpoint, elucidating the profound theoretical parallels between predictive coding and backpropagation. Additionally, it highlights the numerous benefits of predictive coding models compared to neural networks trained via backpropagation. We specifically underscore the remarkable adaptability of predictive coding networks, which outperform equivalent deep neural networks by simultaneously functioning as classifiers, generators, and associative memories, and can be structured on diverse graph topologies. Lastly, we evaluate direct performance comparisons of predictive coding networks in machine learning classification tasks, demonstrating their potential.

Federated learning has become a promising approach for massively distributed training of a shared deep learning model across numerous edge devices, while ensuring that private user data remains on the device. In this study, driven by the need to promote fairness among users and enhance robustness against malicious threats, we reframe federated learning as a multi-objective optimization problem and introduce a novel algorithm, FedMGDA+. This algorithm is designed to converge to Pareto stationary solutions with ease of implementation, minimal hyperparameter tuning, and without compromising the performance of any participating user. We analyze the convergence characteristics of FedMGDA+ and highlight its links to existing methods. Comprehensive testing across diverse datasets demonstrates that FedMGDA+ outperforms current leading techniques.

Although real-world data streams often exhibit frequent, nonstationary changes, most deep learning approaches focus on optimizing neural networks using training data, resulting in significant performance drops when dataset shifts occur. However, manually labeling or examining newly incoming data is often impractical, highlighting the need for unsupervised detection of model drift during inference. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to estimate model drift by leveraging batch normalization layer statistics from unlabeled test data. To address potential sampling errors in streamed data, we apply low-rank approximation to each representational layer. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in detecting dataset shifts and selecting models from a collection of candidates or training trajectories in an unsupervised manner. Additionally, we validate the reliability of our method by comparing model drift scores across various network architectures.

Bayesian inference tasks often involve sampling or approximating complex, high-dimensional probability distributions. This paper centers on the innovative Stein variational gradient descent approach, a set of algorithms that employ repeated steepest descent steps based on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space norm. This method results in interacting particle systems, whose mean-field limit represents a gradient flow within the space of probability distributions, characterized by a specific geometric framework. By adopting this perspective, we aim to clarify the convergence characteristics of the algorithm, particularly focusing on the challenge of selecting an appropriate positive definite kernel function. Our investigation suggests the use of certain nondifferentiable kernels with modified tails. Through various numerical experiments, we showcase the substantial performance improvements these kernels offer.

Current algorithms for spatial object recommendation often rank objects uniformly, disregarding their inherent heterogeneity due to differing spatial granularity. For instance, while one user might seek a recommendation for a broad area like Manhattan, another might want a specific spot like a restaurant. Moreover, a single user's preferences might shift during different phases of data exploration. This paper explores the facilitation of top-k spatial object recommendations across diverse granularity levels, accommodating objects from expansive cities to specific suburbs or buildings as Points of Interest (POIs). To address this, we introduce the POI tree, a structure that encapsulates the spatial hierarchy among POIs. We propose a novel multi-task learning framework named MPR (Multi-level POI Recommendation), where each task targets the recommendation of top-k POIs at a specific granularity level. Each task is divided into two components: (i) attribute-based representation learning, which extracts feature representations of users and POIs directly from their profiles; and (ii) interaction-based representation learning, which integrates user-POI interactions into the model. Furthermore, MPR offers explanations for the recommendations provided.

With the widespread use of smartphones and wearable devices, mobile health (mHealth) technologies hold significant potential to positively transform people's health on a large scale. Current advanced decision-making approaches in mHealth often depend on idealized assumptions, treating users as either entirely uniform or entirely distinct. In reality, however, a user may share similarities with certain individuals but not with everyone. In this paper, we introduce an innovative group-driven reinforcement learning approach for mHealth. Our goal is to explore how information can be effectively shared among similar users to transform limited individual data into more precise reinforcement learning (RL) policies. Specifically, we utilize the K-means clustering technique to categorize users based on similarities in their trajectory data and develop a shared RL policy for each group. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art RL methods in mHealth.

Normalization techniques are crucial for enhancing the efficiency and often the effectiveness of training deep neural networks. Rather than using traditional methods to directly normalize activations, we propose incorporating an additional loss term. This novel loss term promotes stability in the variance of activations, preventing significant fluctuations across different random mini-batches. We demonstrate that this approach leads to activations clustering around a limited number of distinct modes. Furthermore, we illustrate that when inputs originate from a mixture of two Gaussians, our proposed loss term either merges the two distributions or optimally separates them in the LDA framework, based on prior probabilities. Additionally, we establish a connection between this new regularization term and the batch normalization method, offering a regularization viewpoint. Our experiments reveal that this approach yields superior accuracy compared to batch normalization for both convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fully connected networks.

In recent years, deep learning has gained immense popularity, largely thanks to advanced computing hardware like GPUs. However, implementing these sophisticated models on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and embedded systems poses significant challenges. To address the high computational and memory demands, we introduce a new lightweight deep learning framework named LPRNet, which utilizes low-rank pointwise residual (LPR) convolution. The core idea of LPR is to apply low-rank approximation in pointwise convolution to minimize the module's size, while maintaining depthwise convolutions as a residual component to support the LPR module. This approach is vital when low-rank approximation impacts the convolution process negatively. We have integrated our design into MobileNet and ShuffleNetv2 by substituting modules with matching input-output dimensions. Our experiments on visual recognition tasks, such as image classification and face alignment across well-known benchmarks, demonstrate that LPRNet delivers competitive results while significantly lowering Flops and memory usage compared to leading deep models designed for model compression.

Adversarial training enhances the training dataset with perturbations to reduce robust error (against worst-case perturbations), yet it frequently results in higher standard error (on unperturbed test data). Past explanations for this balance have hinged on the notion that no predictor within the hypothesis class achieves both low standard and robust error simultaneously. In this study, we meticulously analyze the impact of augmentation on standard error in linear regression, specifically when the ideal linear predictor exhibits zero standard and robust error. We demonstrate that standard error may still rise, even if the augmented perturbations include noiseless observations from the optimal linear predictor. Furthermore, we establish that the recently developed robust self-training (RST) estimator enhances robust error without compromising standard error in noiseless linear regression. Experimentally, with neural networks, we observe that RST, when combined with various adversarial training approaches, enhances both standard and robust error against random and adversarial rotations, as well as adversarial $\ell_\infty$ perturbations in the CIFAR-10 dataset.

This study introduces Principal Trade-off Analysis (PTA), a decomposition technique similar to Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which enables the depiction of any game as a weighted combination of disc games (continuous Rock-Paper-Scissors games). By applying PTA to tournament graphs derived from empirical data, a series of embeddings into orthogonal 2D feature planes is created, each representing distinct strategic trade-offs. These trade-offs manifest as modes of cyclic competition. Similar to PCA, PTA offers optimal low-rank approximations of the tournament graphs, which can be truncated for simplification. The extent of cyclic competition complexity is measured by determining the number of significant cyclic modes. We demonstrate the utility of PTA through its application to two games (Blotto and Pokemon). The resulting 2D disc game visualizations are shown to be highly effective for interpretation. In Blotto, PTA uncovers game symmetries and highlights strategic trade-offs linked to specific win conditions. For Pokemon, the PTA embeddings reveal clusters in the feature space that align with Pokemon types, reflecting the game's inherent design of cyclic trade-offs.

Owing to the effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in handling graph-structured data, numerous GNN-based approaches have been developed for learning from knowledge graphs (KGs). In this study, we re-examine notable works through the perspective of propagation paths to uncover the critical elements driving these GNN-based methods. Our analysis reveals that while the target entity may be near the queried entity, the dependency on information can span a considerable distance. Consequently, enhanced reasoning outcomes are achievable by investigating extended propagation paths. However, detecting such long-range dependencies in KGs poses a challenge, as the number of associated entities increases exponentially. This challenge inspires us to develop an adaptive propagation path learning approach that eliminates irrelevant entities while retaining potential targets throughout the propagation process. Initially, we implement an incremental sampling mechanism to retain nearby and relevant targets. Subsequently, we devise a learning-driven sampling distribution to pinpoint targets with minimal entity involvement. This strategy enables GNNs to delve deeper, capturing distant information effectively. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our approach is not only efficient but also delivers top-tier results in both transductive and inductive reasoning contexts, thanks to deeper propagation capabilities.

Motivated by the remarkable achievements of deep learning across various fields, the concept of data-driven design for metamaterials has surfaced as an innovative approach to harness the capabilities of multiscale structures. Nevertheless, current model-focused strategies often miss robust methodologies for producing high-quality data. By relying on space-filling designs in the realm of shape descriptors, existing datasets for metamaterials tend to exhibit property distributions that are either significantly unbalanced or misaligned with relevant design objectives. In response, we introduce t-METASET, a sophisticated framework for intelligent data collection that prioritizes task-specific dataset creation. This framework addresses a common but often ignored challenge in the initial phases of design: managing a vast library of shapes (approximately on the order of 10^4) that lacks evaluated properties. Our primary strategy involves utilizing a data-driven shape descriptor derived from generative models, employing a sparse regressor as an initial predictive tool, and using diversity metrics to steer data collection towards regions that support designers in achieving their objectives. We test the efficacy of this framework across three simulated deployment scenarios, covering general, task-specific, and customizable applications. Two extensive mechanical metamaterial datasets, consisting solely of shapes, serve as the testing ground. The findings indicate that t-METASET successfully enhances task-oriented datasets incrementally. With its applicability to a wide range of design representations, t-METASET promises to propel future innovations in the field.

Domain adaptation (DA) and domain generalization (DG) have become key strategies for tackling the issue of domain shift, where the distributions of source and target data differ. DG presents a greater challenge than DA since the target data remains completely unavailable during the training phase in DG settings. Although adversarial techniques dominate the current state-of-the-art methods, they are seldom applied to DG challenges. Moreover, these methods often overlook correlation alignment, a technique proven to significantly reduce domain discrepancies. In this paper, we introduce a novel correlation-aware adversarial framework for DA and DG. This approach integrates correlation alignment with adversarial learning to align the features of source and target data, thereby enhancing the model's domain-agnostic capabilities. By combining these techniques, our method effectively minimizes domain differences even with unlabeled target data. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The development and elimination of agents in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) remain a significantly underexplored research domain. Most existing MARL algorithms operate under the assumption that the number of agents in a group stays constant throughout an experiment. Yet, in numerous real-world scenarios, an agent might cease to function before others in the team. This issue of early termination poses a unique challenge: the terminated agent needs to derive learning from the collective success or failure of the group, which occurs after its own termination. We define the process of transferring value from rewards gained by surviving teammates to terminated agents as the Posthumous Credit Assignment problem. Presently, MARL approaches address this by relegating terminated agents to an absorbing state until the whole group meets a termination criterion. While absorbing states allow current algorithms and APIs to manage terminated agents without alterations, they introduce challenges related to practical training efficiency and resource utilization. In this study, we initially show that sample complexity rises with the number of absorbing states in a simplified supervised learning task for a fully connected network, whereas attention mechanisms exhibit greater resilience to inputs of varying sizes. Subsequently, we introduce a novel architecture for a leading MARL algorithm that employs attention in place of a fully connected layer with absorbing states.

Interpreting neural signals to understand behavior, perception, or cognitive states is crucial for brain-computer interface research and has significant implications for systems neuroscience. Over the past ten years, deep learning has emerged as the leading approach in numerous machine learning tasks, from speech recognition to image segmentation. Its success in various fields has sparked a surge of applications within neuroscience. This article examines deep learning methods applied to neural decoding, detailing the architectures employed to extract meaningful features from diverse neural recording types, such as spikes and EEG. Additionally, we discuss how deep learning facilitates the prediction of outputs like movement, speech, and vision, emphasizing the integration of pretrained deep networks as priors for intricate decoding tasks, including acoustic speech and imagery. Deep learning proves to be a powerful asset in enhancing the accuracy and adaptability of neural decoding across various applications, and we highlight potential areas for future research and advancement.

We investigate the bandit problem in which arms are linked to stationary phi-mixing processes, resulting in dependent rewards. This setup raises the question of whether independence can be restored by disregarding certain reward values. As we will demonstrate, the bandit problem we address necessitates balancing the trade-off between exploration, exploitation, and independence. To tackle this, we propose a UCB strategy accompanied by a comprehensive regret analysis for scenarios where the size of the independence blocks (the disregarded rewards) is predetermined. Furthermore, we advance our approach by developing an algorithm that dynamically determines the size of these independence blocks based on the data. Lastly, we analyze our bandit problem in the restless scenario, where the time counters for all mixing processes progress simultaneously.

We present a method for developing optimal control policies for a large, linear particle accelerator by integrating deep reinforcement learning with a high-fidelity physics engine. This approach features an AI controller that employs deep neural networks to represent state and action spaces, learning optimal strategies through reward signals supplied by the physics simulator. In this study, our focus is limited to managing a small segment of the accelerator. Even so, preliminary findings suggest that our system can outperform human capabilities in controlling particle beam current and distribution. The overarching aim of this research is to dramatically decrease the tuning time for such systems by orders of magnitude and move towards near-autonomous operation.

How can we develop a universal method to select the most appropriate samples for training a classifier, especially when prior knowledge is minimal? Active learning, often viewed as an iterative optimization process, is crucial for building an enhanced training set to boost classification accuracy across various fields like text analysis, image recognition, and social network modeling. While integrating the representativeness and informativeness of samples has shown promise in active sampling, existing top-tier methods tend to excel only with specific data structures. Is it possible, then, to combine these two active sampling criteria without making assumptions about the data? This paper introduces a versatile active learning framework that seamlessly merges these criteria. Drawing inspiration from a two-sample discrepancy issue, we have carefully crafted triple measures to ensure that the selected samples are representative of the unlabeled data while also capturing the diversity of the labeled data. These triple measures can be constructed using any suitable similarity metric. Additionally, an uncertainty measure is utilized to establish the informativeness criterion, which can be implemented in various forms. Based on this framework, a practical active learning algorithm is developed, incorporating a radial basis approach.

We introduce a distributed Newton method with cubic regularization for large-scale convex optimization across networks. This method relies solely on local computations and communications, making it ideal for federated learning applications across diverse network structures. We demonstrate a convergence rate of $O(k^{-3})$, where $k$ represents the number of iterations, under the condition that the cost function is convex with Lipschitz continuous gradient and Hessian. Additionally, we establish network-specific bounds for the communication demands at each algorithmic step. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

While deep neural networks (DNNs) have seen significant advancements in recent times, they remain susceptible to threats in adversarial settings. A harmful backdoor can be inserted into a model by contaminating the training data, aiming to cause the compromised model to produce incorrect predictions during inference upon encountering a specific trigger. To counteract the risks posed by backdoor attacks, a range of detection and defense strategies have been developed. Nevertheless, most current methods depend on access to the tainted training data or a white-box model, which are often not accessible in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a black-box backdoor detection (B3D) approach that can detect backdoor attacks with merely query access to the model. We employ a gradient-free optimization technique to reverse-engineer potential triggers for each class, thereby uncovering the presence of backdoor attacks. Beyond detection, we also suggest a straightforward method for making dependable predictions with models identified as backdoored. Comprehensive experiments across numerous DNN models trained on various datasets validate the efficacy of our approach in the black-box context against diverse backdoor attacks.

In the field of data analysis and machine learning, a fundamental challenge is to identify the vertices of a convex hull from a given set of data points, especially when noise is present. Numerous algorithms have been devised with the premise that each vertex has at least one closely associated data point. Among these, vertex component analysis (VCA) and the successive projection algorithm (SPA) are notably popular. This premise is referred to as the pure-pixel assumption in blind hyperspectral unmixing and as the separability assumption in nonnegative matrix factorization. Recently, Bhattacharyya and Kannan introduced an algorithm for learning a latent simplex (ALLS) at the ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms in 2020, which operates under the condition that multiple data points are near each vertex. Under such conditions, ALLS demonstrates greater probabilistic robustness to noise compared to algorithms that rely on the separability assumption. Drawing inspiration from ALLS, this paper introduces smoothed VCA (SVCA) and smoothed SPA (SSPA), which extend the traditional VCA and SPA by presupposing the existence of multiple data points close to each vertex.
