In this study, we explore various deep learning approaches to address inverse problems. We categorize the current deep learning methods for inverse problems into three groups: Direct Mapping, Data Consistency Optimizer, and Deep Regularizer. To evaluate the effectiveness of these categories, we select a representative example from each type of inverse problem and conduct a statistical comparison of their resilience. Our extensive testing includes the traditional issue of linear regression and three prominent inverse problems in computer vision—image denoising, 3D human face inverse rendering, and object tracking—each chosen as a typical example for the respective inverse problem classes. The comprehensive results and statistical evaluations reveal that the robustness of each solution category varies according to the specific inverse problem domain, particularly influenced by the presence of measurement outliers. Drawing from our findings, we conclude by recommending the most resilient solution category for each class of inverse problem.

When concept drift occurs during the classification of a data stream, a typical solution is to retrain the classifier within a framework. However, this approach discards valuable knowledge if the classifier has effectively mastered the current concept, which might reappear later. Although some frameworks store and reuse classifiers, selecting the most suitable one for reuse can be a slow process. Moreover, these frameworks often fail to achieve the precision of leading ensemble methods. Speed is crucial for many data stream applications, necessitating frameworks that are both rapid and accurate for time-sensitive tasks. We introduce the Enhanced Concept Profiling Framework (ECPF), designed to identify recurring concepts and reuse a previously trained classifier, ensuring precise classification right after a drift. The innovation of ECPF lies in its method of comparing classifications on new data between a newly trained classifier and existing ones to swiftly determine the most effective classifier for reuse. It consistently trains both a new and a reused classifier, keeping the more accurate of the two when drift is detected. Additionally, ECPF duplicates reused classifiers to prevent a classifier tailored to a recurring concept from being altered by training on a different concept. Our experiments demonstrate that ECPF achieves significantly higher classification accuracy.

Over recent decades, scene text recognition has attracted significant interest from both academic researchers and practical users because of its critical role in numerous applications. Despite progress in optical character recognition, scene text recognition continues to pose challenges due to inherent issues like distortions and irregular layouts. Many current methods primarily rely on recurrent or convolutional neural networks. However, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) often face drawbacks such as slow training times due to sequential processing and issues like vanishing gradients or bottlenecks, while convolutional neural networks (CNNs) must balance complexity with performance. In this paper, we present SAFL, a self-attention-based neural network model incorporating focal loss for scene text recognition, designed to address the shortcomings of existing methods. By using focal loss instead of negative log-likelihood, the model prioritizes training on low-frequency samples. Additionally, to handle distortions and irregular text, we employ a Spatial Transformer Network (STN) to correct text alignment before it is processed by the recognition network. We conducted experiments to evaluate the proposed model against seven benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate that our model outperforms all others.

In multi-label classification, evaluating predictions is more complex compared to single-label classification, leading to the development of various significant yet distinct loss functions. Ideally, the learning algorithm should be adaptable to a specific performance metric. Gradient boosted decision trees, a prominent modern implementation of boosting, are particularly attractive in this context. However, their application is generally restricted to single-label classification, making them incompatible with multi-label loss functions unless these can be broken down by label. In this study, we extend the gradient boosting framework to handle multi-output scenarios and introduce an algorithm designed for multi-label classification that can optimize both decomposable and non-decomposable loss functions. By examining the Hamming loss and subset 0/1 loss as key examples, we explore the strengths and limitations of our method using synthetic data and assess its predictive accuracy on multi-label benchmark datasets.

The strength of machine learning algorithms lies in their ability to identify valuable features from vast datasets. As the scale of models and datasets grows, dataset distillation techniques that shrink extensive datasets into much smaller, yet highly effective versions will gain importance for enhancing training efficiency and feature extraction. In this context, we implement a cutting-edge distributed kernel-based meta-learning approach to achieve top-tier results in dataset distillation, utilizing infinitely wide convolutional neural networks. For example, with just 10 data points (0.02% of the original dataset), we achieve a test accuracy exceeding 65% on the CIFAR-10 image classification task, markedly surpassing the previous best accuracy of 40%. Our leading results are consistent across various datasets including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. Additionally, we conduct initial analyses of our distilled datasets to explore how they diverge from naturally occurring data.

The pursuit of learning disentangled representations has garnered significant interest recently, centering on a competition that utilizes a novel real-world disentanglement dataset (Gondal et al., 2019). Several approaches employing variational auto-encoders have been developed to address this issue, focusing on ensuring independence in the representations and adjusting the regularization term within the variational lower bound. Nevertheless, recent findings by Locatello et al. (2018) indicate that these methods are significantly affected by randomness and hyper-parameter selection. In our study, rather than creating a new regularization term, we enhance the FactorVAE by boosting reconstruction performance, expanding the network's capacity, and extending the training duration. This approach proves highly successful, securing the top position in the competition.

Students participating in online courses produce vast amounts of data that can be leveraged to tailor the learning experience and enhance educational quality. In this paper, we introduce the Latent Skill Embedding (LSE), a probabilistic framework that models both students and educational materials to suggest customized lesson sequences aimed at preparing students for targeted assessments. Similar to collaborative filtering techniques used in recommendation systems, this algorithm does not rely on predefined features for students or content but instead learns representations from interaction histories. We frame this challenge as a regularized maximum-likelihood embedding of students, lessons, and assessments based on past interactions between students and content. A comprehensive evaluation using extensive data from Knewton, a company specializing in adaptive learning technology, demonstrates that this method predicts assessment outcomes on par with leading models and effectively distinguishes between lesson sequences that result in mastery versus those leading to failure.

We explore a compelling variation of the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem, termed the Fair-SMAB problem, in which each arm must be pulled for at least a specified fraction of the total rounds available. We examine the relationship between learning and fairness, guided by a predefined vector that specifies the minimum fractions of pulls for each arm. We introduce a new fairness-aware regret metric, named $r$-Regret, which incorporates these fairness constraints and builds upon the traditional concept of regret. Our main contribution lies in defining a category of Fair-SMAB algorithms characterized by two factors: the tolerance for unfairness and the underlying learning algorithm employed as a black-box. We establish a fairness guarantee for this category that remains consistent over time, regardless of the learning algorithm chosen. Specifically, when the UCB1 algorithm is used, we demonstrate that our approach achieves an $r$-Regret of $O(\ln T)$. Lastly, we assess the impact of enforcing fairness on the traditional measure of regret.

Deep neural networks frequently assign high confidence scores to predictions for samples from unseen classes, which ideally should be flagged for expert review. Existing novelty detection algorithms struggle to accurately detect such near out-of-distribution (OOD) points without access to labeled data resembling these novel samples. In this paper, we introduce a novel ensemble-based method for semi-supervised novelty detection (SSND) that effectively utilizes a combination of unlabeled in-distribution (ID) and novel-class samples to deliver strong detection performance. Specifically, we demonstrate how to induce disagreement exclusively on OOD data through early stopping regularization. Although this principle is proven for a simplified data distribution, our comprehensive experiments indicate its applicability to more intricate cases: our method substantially surpasses leading SSND techniques on benchmark image datasets (SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) and medical imaging datasets, with only a minimal increase in computational overhead.

Research indicates that many hazards go unnoticed, placing construction workers at significant risk of unexpected safety issues. Recent findings also reveal a strong link between workers' viewing patterns, monitored through eye-tracking technology, and their ability to identify hazards. Consequently, examining these viewing patterns is crucial for enhancing our understanding of hazard recognition capabilities. This paper introduces a novel approach for automatically linking gaze fixations, gathered via a wearable eye-tracker, to specific areas of interest. The method employs computer vision-based segmentation and transfer learning to identify these areas or objects (namely, hazards). The resulting fixation data is analyzed to assess workers' viewing behaviors and determine their attention distribution. To test the effectiveness of this method, it is applied in a case study on a road under construction.

As deep neural networks (DNNs) gain popularity, there is an increasing need for hardware accelerators to enable real-time performance. However, the lengthy design cycles and rapidly evolving nature of DNN models pose significant challenges in meeting time-to-market demands for hardware evaluation. This paper introduces a pre-RTL DNN hardware evaluator that accommodates both traditional layer-by-layer processing and fused layer processing to minimize external bandwidth requirements. The evaluator is compatible with two leading accelerator architectures and identifies the optimal hardware configuration and layer fusion groups. Experimental results demonstrate that the layer fusion approach reduces memory bandwidth by 55.6%, improves latency by 36.7%, and decreases energy consumption by 49.2% compared to conventional layer-by-layer processing.

The challenge of fairness in machine learning arises because historical data frequently reflects biases against certain underprivileged groups, whether in the past or present. One potential solution is to use fair representation learning algorithms that eliminate biases from the data, rendering groups statistically indistinguishable. In this paper, we propose a novel fair representation learning algorithm that maps individuals from different groups into a unified group. This is achieved by training a duo of Normalizing Flow models while ensuring that essential ground truth information is preserved through the addition of a ranking or classification model. The resulting "chained" model is invertible and features a tractable Jacobian, enabling the connection of probability densities across different groups and facilitating the transformation of individuals between groups. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach is competitive with existing fair representation learning algorithms and offers enhanced invariance concerning the sensitive attribute.

Artificial neural networks require rapid decision-making with minimal latency for critical applications like navigation, tracking, and real-time machine action systems. This necessitates machine learning hardware capable of processing multidimensional data at high throughput. Convolution operations, the primary computational method for data classification, are hindered by complex run-time scaling challenges. However, by applying the convolution theorem homomorphically through a Fourier-optic display-light-processor, a non-iterative O(1) runtime complexity is achieved for data inputs exceeding 1,000 x 1,000 matrices. Using this method, we present a Fourier Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN) accelerator for data streaming multi-kernel image batch-processing. We demonstrate passive batch processing of large-scale matrices with 2 million dot-product multiplications executed by digital light-processing modules in the Fourier domain. Moreover, by leveraging multiple spatio-parallel diffraction orders, we enhance the parallelism of this optical FCNN system, achieving a 98-fold throughput increase compared to leading FCNN accelerators. A detailed analysis of practical challenges at the system's performance limits addresses issues such as crosstalk in the Fourier domain and resolution scaling constraints. By harnessing the immense parallelism of display technology to accelerate convolutions, this approach introduces a non-von Neumann-based paradigm for machine learning acceleration.

Traffic speed prediction plays a vital role in intelligent transportation systems (ITS). With the swift advancement of deep learning and transportation data science, an increasing number of innovative traffic speed prediction models have emerged, delivering high accuracy and the ability to forecast on a large scale. Nonetheless, current research faces two significant drawbacks. Firstly, predictions are made for aggregated traffic speeds instead of lane-specific speeds; secondly, many studies overlook the influence of other traffic flow parameters on speed prediction. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a two-stream multi-channel convolutional neural network (TM-CNN) model for multi-lane traffic speed prediction, incorporating the effect of traffic volume. In this approach, we initially propose a novel data transformation technique that converts raw traffic speed and volume data into spatial-temporal multi-channel matrices. Subsequently, we meticulously construct a two-stream deep neural network to adeptly capture features and relationships across individual lanes, within spatial-temporal dimensions, and between speed and volume. Furthermore, we develop a new loss function that accounts for the impact of volume on speed prediction. A case study utilizing one year of data confirms the effectiveness of the TM-CNN model and showcases its superior performance. This work contributes to two key research domains: (1) traffic speed prediction and (2) the study of multi-lane traffic flow.

Variational Autoencoders are highly effective for unsupervised learning, yet training deep models with multiple layers of dependent stochastic variables poses significant challenges, often hindering the full potential of these expressive models. We introduce the Ladder Variational Autoencoder, a novel inference model that iteratively refines the generative distribution through a data-driven approximate likelihood, inspired by the recently introduced Ladder Network. Our results demonstrate that this model achieves top-tier predictive log-likelihood and a more precise log-likelihood lower bound compared to traditional bottom-up inference in layered Variational Autoencoders and other generative frameworks. Through an in-depth examination, we reveal that our inference approach is fundamentally distinct, leveraging a more complex and distributed hierarchy of latent variables. Additionally, we find that batch normalization and a deterministic warm-up strategy (gradually increasing the KL-term) are essential for effectively training variational models with numerous stochastic layers.

A frequent issue with density models trained as variational autoencoders is their tendency to disregard latent variables when modeling data, making these variables ineffective. Research has previously explored two key reasons for this problem independently: the model's underspecification and the slackness of the variational lower bound. In this work, we integrate these lines of inquiry by combining tighter Monte-Carlo objective bounds with constraints on the mutual information between observable data and latent variables. Traditional methods of estimating mutual information, such as averaging the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the readily available variational posterior $q(z|x)$ and the prior, are incompatible with Monte-Carlo objectives since $q(z|x)$ no longer closely approximates the true posterior $p(z|x)$ of the model. To address this, we develop estimators for the Kullback-Leibler divergence of the true posterior from the prior by reusing samples from the objective. This approach allows us to train models with both continuous and discrete latent variables, achieving significantly better rate-distortion performance and avoiding posterior collapse. Although this mitigates the issue, the inherent tension between accurately modeling the data and effectively utilizing latent variables persists. Therefore, we advocate for the evaluation of inference methods across a spectrum of mutual information values.

To address the unpredictability of variable renewable resources, two readily available machine learning tools are utilized to predict the solar power output of a photovoltaic system. Support vector machines are employed to produce the forecasts, while a random forest serves as an ensemble learning approach to integrate these predictions. Typically, ensemble methods in wind and solar power forecasting involve merging meteorological data from multiple sources. However, in this research, both current and historical solar power forecasts from various models, along with relevant meteorological data, are fed into the random forest to enhance the precision of day-ahead solar power predictions. The effectiveness of this integrated model is assessed over a full year and benchmarked against other combination strategies.

Deep learning dominates as the primary method for numerous machine learning applications such as image recognition, machine translation, and speech recognition. It has surpassed traditional approaches across multiple domains, achieving remarkable success. However, the mechanisms behind its effectiveness are still not fully understood. Establishing a theoretical foundation for deep learning is of paramount importance. In this study, we offer a geometric perspective to elucidate deep learning: we demonstrate that its success fundamentally hinges on the manifold structure inherent in data. Specifically, natural high-dimensional data tends to cluster near a low-dimensional manifold, and deep learning effectively captures both the manifold and the probability distribution over it. Additionally, we introduce the notion of rectified linear complexity to assess the learning capacity of deep neural networks and to gauge the learning difficulty of an embedding manifold. We further prove that for any deep neural network with a fixed architecture, there exists a manifold that the network is incapable of learning. Lastly, we suggest employing optimal mass transportation theory to regulate the probability distribution within the latent space.

Over the last ten years, significant strides have been made in developing new RecSys methods. Despite these advancements, the RecSys research community continues to face a critical challenge: the scarcity of applied datasets and standardized benchmarks with clearly defined evaluation criteria and metrics to assess these innovative techniques. In this paper, we introduce the TTRS - Tinkoff Transactions Recommender System benchmark, a dataset focused on financial transactions. It encompasses over 2 million interactions among nearly 10,000 users and over 1,000 merchant brands spanning 14 months. To our knowledge, this is the first financial transactions dataset made publicly available. To enhance its applicability, we offer a thorough overview of the data collection process, preprocessing steps, and detailed statistics of the resulting dataset. Additionally, we provide an in-depth comparison of current leading RecSys methods applied to the task of next-period recommendation, along with a comprehensive evaluation of their performance across various metrics and datasets.

Forecasting the geographic location of social media users, such as those on Twitter, is valuable for applications like health monitoring, crisis response, content customization, and broader social research. In this study, we advance the field by developing and testing innovative approaches that integrate weighted multigraph literature with cutting-edge deep learning methods. Our proposed techniques build on a common framework (an enhanced network of mentions and/or followers) while employing varied strategies for processing information. These include information dissemination via transductive and inductive algorithms, such as RGCNs and GraphSAGE, as well as node embeddings using Node2vec+. Additionally, we incorporate attention mechanisms to integrate users' textual data into our models. We evaluate the effectiveness of these approaches and benchmark them against existing models using the public Twitter-US dataset, and introduce a new dataset derived from an extensive Twitter data collection in Latin America. Lastly, our study examines the constraints and relevance of comparisons between methods, considering varying definitions of labels and evaluation metrics.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have garnered significant interest due to their impressive results in tasks like node classification. Despite this, the mechanisms behind their operation, particularly in node representation learning, remain poorly understood. This paper introduces a theoretical framework to elucidate the functioning of GNNs, focusing on spectral graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks through the lens of graph signal denoising. Our analysis reveals that GNNs implicitly address graph signal denoising challenges: spectral graph convolutions serve to denoise node features, whereas graph attentions focus on denoising edge weights. Additionally, we demonstrate that a linear self-attention approach can perform comparably to leading graph attention techniques. These theoretical insights have inspired the development of two novel models, GSDN-F and GSDN-EF, which are adept at handling graphs with noisy node features and/or edges. We substantiate our theoretical conclusions and the efficacy of these new models through experiments on benchmark datasets. The source code for these models is accessible at \url{https://github.com/fuguoji/GSDN}.

The structure of three-dimensional (3D) graphs, composed of nodes and edges, is vital for numerous significant applications. A prime example is molecular graphs, where the spatial arrangement impacts critical molecular characteristics such as reactivity and biological function. To enhance deep learning applications on 3D graphs by integrating spatial features, we introduce three distinct geometric graph representations: positional, angle-geometric, and distance-geometric. As a demonstration, we apply the distance-geometric representation in geometric graph convolutions. Additionally, to adapt standard graph convolution networks for this purpose, we implement a straightforward correlation scheme between edge weights and distances, with parameters that can either be preset based on benchmark data or optimized via Bayesian hyperparameter techniques. The outcomes of using geometric graph convolutions on the ESOL and Freesol datasets reveal a marked improvement compared to traditional graph convolutions. This study confirms the potential and effectiveness of embedding geometric aspects, specifically through distance-geometric representations, into deep learning frameworks for 3D graphs.

In this study, we demonstrate the application of the Operational Space Control (OSC) framework with joint and Cartesian constraints for reinforcement learning in Cartesian space. Our approach enables rapid learning with customizable degrees of freedom, and facilitates policy transfer without the need for further dynamics randomization, as evidenced by experiments with a KUKA LBR iiwa on a peg-in-hole task. Prior to initiating learning in simulation, we conduct system identification to closely match the simulation environment to the dynamics of an actual robot. By integrating constraints into the OSC controller, we ensure safe learning on the real robot and develop a versatile, goal-conditioned policy that can be seamlessly transferred from simulation to reality.

Deep reinforcement learning techniques have demonstrated exceptional, super-human capabilities across various settings. However, these approaches are highly inefficient, often requiring vastly more data than humans to reach acceptable performance levels. We introduce Neural Episodic Control, a deep reinforcement learning agent designed to quickly integrate and respond to new experiences. This agent employs a semi-tabular approach to represent the value function, utilizing a memory buffer of previous experiences with gradually evolving state representations and swiftly updated value estimates. Our findings demonstrate that across diverse environments, our agent learns much more rapidly than other leading, general-purpose deep reinforcement learning agents.

Various techniques exist for achieving $\epsilon$-differential privacy (DP), but determining the right value for $\epsilon$ remains a challenge. There is no universal consensus on what constitutes a "sufficiently small" $\epsilon$, and its appropriateness varies based on the specific query and data involved. In this paper, we demonstrate a method to calculate $\epsilon$ in relation to $\delta$, which represents the adversary's advantage in terms of the probability of correctly guessing a particular property of the output. The attacker's objective can be expressed as a Boolean statement concerning the prediction of specific attributes, potentially with a certain level of precision. These attributes, when combined, must be independent of one another. We also assume that both the input and output distributions are characterized by corresponding probability density functions or probability mass functions.

Likely so. Supervised Deep Learning excels in performance metrics across numerous computer vision tasks, setting the benchmark for excellence. Yet, in the realm of medical image analysis, progress trails behind that of natural image applications. A key factor contributing to this disparity is the scarcity of well-annotated medical image data accessible to researchers. It is often emphasized to researchers that interpreting and labeling such data demands substantial expertise to ensure reliability and accuracy. There is notable variability in annotations even among expert annotators, both between different experts and within the same expert over time. Despite this, it is commonly believed that novice annotators are incapable of providing valuable annotations for clinical Deep Learning models. In this study, we question this belief and explore the consequences of employing a minimally trained novice labeling team to annotate a complex medical image dataset. We analyze the time and cost factors associated with novice annotators, their raw performance relative to gold-standard expert annotations, and the impact on the performance of a Deep Learning segmentation model trained to detect a specific congenital heart condition—hypoplastic left heart syndrome—in fetal ultrasound images.

Machine Learning for Software Engineering (ML4SE) is a rapidly expanding field of research dedicated to creating methods that support programmers in their tasks. To ensure these methods are practical, they must achieve a sufficient level of quality to assist developers without becoming a hindrance. Although advancements in code representation and data collection enhance the overall performance of these models, they often overlook valuable insights available from the specific project being worked on. In this study, we explore how tailoring a model to a particular project can enhance its effectiveness. We introduce a framework to evaluate the quality improvements achieved through fine-tuning models for the task of method name prediction on a specific project. We assess three models of varying complexity, comparing their performance across three scenarios: training on a broad dataset of Java projects, additional fine-tuning with data from a specific project, and training solely on the project-specific data from the ground up. Our findings demonstrate that fine-tuning on a per-project basis significantly boosts model performance by incorporating the project's unique domain and naming conventions. Additionally, we have made the data collection tool and the experimental code publicly available at: https://zenodo.org/record/6040745.

The majority of industrial robotic assembly tasks currently demand specific starting conditions to achieve successful outcomes, resulting in elevated production expenses and limited flexibility for new tasks. In this study, our goal is to enhance the versatility and adaptability of robotic assembly through the utilization of 3D CAD models for all components involved in the process. Our focus is on a universal assembly task known as the Siemens Innovation Challenge, where a robot is required to construct a gear-like mechanism with exceptional precision within a functional system. To meet the millimeter precision necessary for this challenge and similar industrial applications, we employ a depth camera positioned close to the robot's end-effector. We introduce a precise two-stage pose estimation method grounded in deep convolutional neural networks, encompassing detection, pose estimation, refinement, and the management of near and complete symmetries of components. These networks are trained using simulated depth images, with strategies implemented to guarantee effective application to the actual robot. Our approach yields an average pose estimation error of just 2.16 millimeters and 0.64 degrees, achieving a 91% success rate in the robotic assembly of randomly positioned parts. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance in which the Siemens Innovation Challenge has been fully tackled, with all components assembled at high success rates.

Self-supervised learning has emerged as an effective strategy for acquiring image representations without requiring extensive labeled datasets. In the context of underwater robotics, developing computer vision algorithms to enhance perception abilities, such as sonar image classification, is highly valuable. However, the sensitive nature of sonar imaging and the complexity of interpreting sonar images make it difficult to compile large, public labeled datasets for training supervised learning models. In this study, we explore the effectiveness of three self-supervised learning techniques—RotNet, Denoising Autoencoders, and Jigsaw—in generating robust sonar image representations without human-labeled data. We showcase results from pre-training and transfer learning on authentic sonar image datasets. Our findings reveal that self-supervised pre-training achieves classification performance on par with supervised pre-training in a few-shot transfer learning scenario across all three approaches. The code and pre-trained self-supervised models are accessible at https://github.com/agrija9/ssl-sonar-images.

Test Input Prioritizers (TIP) for Deep Neural Networks (DNN) play a crucial role in efficiently managing the often vast test datasets, thereby reducing computation and labeling expenses. This is especially relevant for large-scale, operational systems where inputs from production are logged to potentially serve as test or training data for future iterations of the system. Feng et al. introduce DeepGini, a notably fast and straightforward TIP, demonstrating its superiority over more complex methods like neuron- and surprise coverage. Through an extensive study involving 4 case studies, 8 test datasets, and 32,200 trained models, we confirm their results. Nevertheless, we also discover that other similar or even simpler baselines from uncertainty quantification, such as the predicted softmax likelihood or the entropy of these likelihoods, achieve comparable performance to DeepGini.

We present an innovative framework for developing a model capable of segmenting objects from a set of images without requiring human annotation. Our approach is grounded in the insight that the position of object segments can be slightly altered relative to a background without compromising the scene's realism. The methodology begins with training a generative model of a layered scene, which includes a background image, a foreground image, and the foreground's mask. A synthesized image is created by superimposing the masked foreground onto the background. This generative model is trained adversarially against a discriminator, compelling the generator to create lifelike composite images. To ensure that the generator learns a representation where the foreground layer represents an object, we introduce a random displacement to the generative model's output, shifting both the foreground image and its mask relative to the background. Since the generator does not know the extent of the shift prior to generating its output, it is forced to create layered representations that remain realistic under any random alteration.
