Extensive research has explored data augmentations to enhance the accuracy and resilience of classifiers. Yet, the role of image augmentation in advancing GAN models for image synthesis remains underexplored in prior work. In this study, we comprehensively evaluate the impact of various established augmentation methods on GAN training across diverse scenarios. We offer valuable insights and recommendations for augmenting images in both standard GANs and GANs with regularization techniques, significantly boosting the quality of synthesized images. Notably, we discover that vanilla GANs can achieve generation quality comparable to recent cutting-edge results when augmentations are applied to both real and generated images. Furthermore, when this training approach is paired with other augmentation-driven regularization methods, like contrastive loss and consistency regularization, the quality of generated images improves even more. We present new benchmark results for conditional generation on CIFAR-10, incorporating both consistency and contrastive losses as additional regularization strategies.

We investigate sequential decision-making challenges with the goal of maximizing the expected total reward while adhering to a constraint on the expected total utility. To address the discounted infinite-horizon optimal control problem for Constrained Markov Decision Processes (constrained MDPs), we utilize the natural policy gradient approach. Specifically, we introduce a novel Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual (NPG-PD) method that updates the primal variable through natural policy gradient ascent and the dual variable through projected sub-gradient descent. Despite the maximization problem involving a nonconcave objective function and a nonconvex constraint set, we demonstrate that, under softmax policy parametrization, our method achieves global convergence at sublinear rates for both the optimality gap and constraint violation. Notably, this convergence is dimension-free, meaning it is unaffected by the size of the state-action space. Additionally, for log-linear and general smooth policy parametrizations, we establish sublinear convergence rates, accounting for a function approximation error due to restricted policy parametrization. We further provide convergence guarantees and finite-sample complexity results for two sample-based NPG-PD algorithms. Lastly, we demonstrate the strengths and effectiveness of our approach through computational experiments.

High-throughput mRNA sequencing, commonly known as RNA-Seq, is extensively utilized for quantifying transcript levels of gene isoforms. However, RNA-Seq data by itself often falls short in precisely determining the origins of reads from specific isoforms for accurate quantification. To address this, we suggest incorporating protein domain-domain interactions as prior knowledge in an integrative analysis with RNA-Seq data. We present a novel Network-based method for RNA-Seq-based Transcript Quantification, termed Net-RSTQ, which combines a protein domain-domain interaction network with short read alignments to estimate transcript abundance. Observing that the abundances of neighboring isoforms linked by domain-domain interactions in the network tend to be positively correlated, Net-RSTQ employs Dirichlet priors to model the expression of these neighboring transcripts based on the likelihood of observed read alignments to the transcripts within a single gene. The transcript abundances across all genes are subsequently estimated through an alternating optimization approach involving multiple Expectation-Maximization (EM) problems. In simulations, Net-RSTQ significantly enhanced the accuracy of isoform transcript quantification, particularly when isoform co-expressions were aligned with their interactions. Additionally, qRT-PCR experiments on 25 multi-isoform genes across a stem cell line, an ovarian cancer cell line, and a breast cancer cell line demonstrated that Net-RSTQ provided more consistent isoform proportion estimates with RNA-Seq data. Further analysis of RNA-Seq data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) also confirmed the reliability of transcript abundance estimations by Net-RSTQ.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be viewed as a sequence modeling challenge, where a model, provided with a history of state-action-reward interactions, autoregressively forecasts a series of future actions. Recently, Transformers have been effectively utilized to tackle this issue. In this study, we introduce the State-Action-Reward Transformer (StARformer), which explicitly captures local causal relationships to enhance action prediction over extended sequences. StARformer initially derives local representations, termed StAR-representations, from small clusters of state-action-reward tokens within a brief timeframe. These local representations, alongside state representations, are then leveraged to predict actions across a prolonged duration. Experimental results demonstrate that StARformer surpasses the leading Transformer-based approach on both Atari (image) and Gym (state vector) benchmarks in offline-RL and imitation learning scenarios. Additionally, StARformer shows greater adaptability to longer input sequences compared to the baseline. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/elicassion/StARformer.

This paper introduces a new type of convolutional layer named perturbed convolution (PConv), designed to simultaneously enhance the performance of generative adversarial networks (GANs) and mitigate the issue of memorization, where the discriminator learns to recall all images from a dataset during training. PConv operates by randomly altering an input tensor prior to the convolution process, creating perturbed features. This method, though straightforward, proves to be highly effective. Initially, to maintain consistent output despite the altered tensor, each discriminator layer must develop robust features with a minimal local Lipschitz value. Additionally, as the input tensor undergoes random perturbation during training—akin to dropout in neural networks—the problem of memorization is reduced. To validate the versatility of this approach, we performed comprehensive tests using various loss functions and datasets such as CIFAR-10, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, LSUN, and tiny-ImageNet. Quantitative assessments reveal that PConv significantly improves the performance of both GAN and conditional GAN, as measured by the Frechet Inception Distance (FID).

Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is a widely recognized and effective technique for likelihood-free inference, utilized across various fields. The success of ABC hinges significantly on the selection of effective summary statistics. Traditionally, choosing these statistics depends on expert domain knowledge and the meticulous creation of features, often proving to be a tedious and time-intensive task. Given ABC's sensitivity to data dimensionality, the selection process must carefully weigh the inclusion of useful statistics against the size of the feature vector.

This paper introduces a novel approach by framing the dynamic selection of suitable summary statistics from a pool of candidates as a multi-armed bandit problem. This method enables ABC rejection sampling to adaptively concentrate on a distribution of high-performing summary statistics rather than adhering to a predetermined set. Unique in its design, this approach requires no preliminary processing and can handle a vast array of candidate statistics. It supports the efficient application of an extensive collection of time series summary statistics without the need for prior feature engineering. The effectiveness of this method is evaluated against leading techniques for selecting summary statistics, using a demanding test case from systems biology literature.

The typical perspective on code smells suggests a causal relationship: detect a smell, eliminate it, and thereby enhance the code's quality. We conducted an empirical study to assess their suitability for this purpose. We compiled a set of characteristics that code smells should exhibit if they genuinely contribute to reduced quality. Our analysis covered 31,687 Java files across 677 GitHub repositories, specifically those with over 200 commits in 2019. We examined the impact of smells on four key metrics related to quality, productivity, and bug detection efficiency. Of the 151 code smells identified by the CheckStyle tool, fewer than 20% showed potential causality, with only a small number demonstrating consistent reliability. The most significant smells were linked to simplicity, defensive programming, and abstraction. Files lacking these potentially causal smells were 50% more likely to be of superior quality. Regrettably, most smells remain unaddressed, and developers often prioritize removing the simpler ones over the more impactful ones.

We propose an efficient computational framework designed to accelerate various machine learning algorithms while maintaining nearly the same level of accuracy. This framework utilizes projections through structured matrices, termed Structured Spinners, which are constructed as products of three structured matrix blocks incorporating rotations. The approach is highly versatile, as it allows for: i) the use of either fully-randomized or learned structured matrices, ii) the inclusion of all previously explored structured schemes as special cases within our structured family, iii) applicability to non-linear scenarios where projections are succeeded by non-linear functions, and iv) a wide range of applications such as kernel approximations through random feature maps, dimensionality reduction techniques, innovative fast cross-polytope LSH methods, deep learning, convex optimization using Newton sketches, quantization via random projection trees, and more. Accompanied by theoretical guarantees, our framework assesses the capability of the structured model compared to its unstructured equivalent, grounded in a broad theoretical principle outlined in the paper. As a result of our theoretical exploration, we offer the first theoretical assurances for one of the most efficient LSH algorithms utilizing the HD3HD2HD1 structured matrix [Andoni et al., 2015]. Comprehensive experimental results validate the effectiveness of our approach.

We introduce any-precision deep neural networks (DNNs), trained using an innovative approach that enables adaptability in numerical precision during inference. This allows the same model to be seamlessly adjusted to various bit-widths at runtime by simply truncating the least significant bits, facilitating dynamic trade-offs between speed and accuracy. When configured to lower bit precision across all layers, our model maintains accuracy levels comparable to those of models specifically trained at that precision. This advantageous feature supports flexible implementation of deep learning models in real-world scenarios, where balancing model accuracy and runtime efficiency is frequently necessary. Unlike prior research, which focused on training models for specific efficiency/accuracy trade-off points, the challenge of creating a model with runtime precision flexibility remains largely unaddressed. In situations where efficiency/accuracy requirements fluctuate or dynamically shift during operation, retraining models becomes impractical, and storing multiple versions may exceed storage limits. Our proposed framework delivers this adaptability without compromising performance. Furthermore, we show that this capability is independent of model architecture and extends to various vision tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/SHI-Labs/Any-Precision-DNNs.

We examine a population divided into distinct communities and address the challenge of identifying the largest community through sequential, random sampling of individuals. The population is also segmented into various sampling domains, termed "boxes," each of which may contain members from different communities, while each community might extend across several boxes. At any point, the learning agent can select a box and sample a random individual (with replacement); upon sampling, the agent discovers the community affiliation of the individual and whether they have been sampled previously. The agent's objective is to reduce the likelihood of incorrectly identifying the largest community within a fixed budget scenario by refining both the sampling approach and the decision criteria. We introduce and evaluate new algorithms for this issue and establish information-theoretic lower bounds on the error probability for any algorithm. In many significant scenarios, the exponential decay rates of error probability under our algorithms are demonstrated to be nearly optimal, differing only by constant factors. Additionally, the effectiveness of these proposed algorithms is confirmed through simulations using real-world datasets.

Rectified Linear Units, commonly known as ReLUs, are now the go-to activation functions in artificial neural networks. This paper explores two fundamental learning challenges by assuming the data is generated from a ReLU-based neural network, which incorporates ReLU activation functions. As a theoretical analysis, our focus is restricted to a single-layer network. The initial problem we address relates to dictionary learning influenced by nonlinearity, which is represented by ReLU functions. With a collection of observation vectors $\mathbf{y}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d, i =1, 2, \dots , n$, our goal is to reconstruct the $d\times k$ matrix $A$ and the hidden vectors $\{\mathbf{c}^i\} \subset \mathbb{R}^k$ based on the model $\mathbf{y}^i = \mathrm{ReLU}(A\mathbf{c}^i +\mathbf{b})$, where $\mathbf{b}\in \mathbb{R}^d$ represents a random bias. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions related to the distribution of $\mathbf{b}$, the column space of $A$ can be recovered with an error margin of $O(d)$ in terms of the Frobenius norm. The second issue we tackle is the robust recovery of a signal amidst outliers, characterized by significant but sparse noise. Here, we aim to retrieve the latent vector $\mathbf{c}$ from its noisy, nonlinear representations given by $\mathbf{v} = \mathrm{ReLU}(A\mathbf{c}) + \mathbf{e}+\mathbf{w}$, where $\mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

We explore a data-driven method for creating uncertainty sets in robust optimization problems, where the uncertain parameters are treated as random variables with an unknown joint probability distribution. Using only independent samples from this distribution, we propose a nonparametric technique to estimate uncertainty sets, ensuring that their probability mass closely matches a specified target mass within a defined tolerance, with high confidence. The nonparametric estimators we employ also demonstrate distribution-free, finite-sample performance guarantees, indicating their probabilistic convergence to the target mass. Furthermore, these estimators are computationally efficient and produce uncertainty sets that lead to solvable robust optimization problems across a wide range of constraint functions.

Inspired by the learned iterative soft thresholding algorithm (LISTA), we present a versatile class of neural networks designed for sparse reconstruction from limited linear measurements. These networks accommodate varying levels of weight-sharing across layers, facilitating a comprehensive analysis of diverse neural network architectures, from recurrent models to those resembling traditional feedforward neural networks. Through empirical risk minimization using training data, we strive to determine the ideal network parameters and, consequently, the most effective network for reconstructing signals from their low-dimensional linear measurements. We establish generalization bounds by examining the Rademacher complexity of hypothesis classes composed of these deep networks, incorporating the thresholding parameters into our analysis. Our findings reveal that the sample complexity scales nearly linearly with both the number of parameters and the network depth. We leverage our primary findings to derive specific generalization bounds for various practical scenarios, including different algorithms for (implicit) dictionary learning and convolutional neural networks.

Evaluating the top $k$ elements across multiple ranked lists is a frequent task in various scenarios. While several methods have been developed to compare these top $k$ lists, offering desirable mathematical attributes, they often encounter practical limitations and drawbacks. In this study, we propose a novel approach to assess the similarity between any pair of top $k$ lists by analyzing the information they represent. Our technique focuses on the compressibility of the lists, using the length of the message required for lossless encoding as a reliable and intuitive indicator of their differences. This information-theoretic approach effectively addresses key factors in evaluating (dis-)similarity between lists, including the proportion of non-overlapping elements, the degree of disorder among shared elements, and the differences in the actual rankings of overlapping elements.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is commonly employed to optimize non-convex functions. However, traditional convergence theory for SGD in the smooth non-convex context indicates a slow sublinear convergence rate to a stationary point. In this study, we present several convergence theorems for SGD that demonstrate convergence to a global minimum for non-convex problems under specific additional structural conditions. Specifically, we examine two significant categories of structured non-convex functions: (i) Quasar (Strongly) Convex functions, which extend the concept of convex functions, and (ii) functions that adhere to the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, a broader interpretation of strongly-convex functions. Our analysis hinges on an Expected Residual condition, which we prove to be a less restrictive assumption compared to earlier conditions such as growth conditions, expected smoothness, or bounded variance. We offer theoretical assurances for the convergence of SGD across various step-size strategies, including constant, diminishing, and the innovative stochastic Polyak step-size. Moreover, our analysis applies to the arbitrary sampling approach, providing insights into the complexities of minibatching and identifying an optimal minibatch size. Lastly, we demonstrate that for models that perfectly fit the training data, the Expected Residual condition can be omitted, yielding cutting-edge results in this scenario.

The issue of data imbalance often hinders the classification performance of neural networks. In this study, we introduce a new supervised discriminative feature generation (DFG) approach specifically designed for minority class datasets. The DFG method modifies the framework of a generative adversarial network, incorporating four distinct components: a generator, a discriminator, a feature extractor, and a classifier. By implementing an attention mechanism, the generator enhances the discriminative features of the minority class data for the imbalanced target task. Additionally, the feature extractor and classifier are refined using pre-trained features derived from a substantial source dataset. Our experimental findings demonstrate that the DFG generator successfully boosts the creation of label-preserved and varied features, leading to notable improvements in classification performance on the target task. This feature generation model holds significant potential for advancing data augmentation techniques through the generation of discriminative features and the application of supervised attention strategies.

We investigate the challenge of determining the optimal arm in a stochastic multi-armed bandit scenario. Consider a collection of $n$ arms, labeled from 1 to $n$, where each arm $i$ has an unknown reward distribution bounded between 0 and 1, characterized by a mean $\theta_i$ and variance $\sigma_i^2$. It is given that $\theta_1 > \theta_2 \geq \cdots \geq \theta_n$. We introduce an adaptive algorithm that analyzes the reward gaps and variances across the arms, utilizing this data to inform subsequent choices through a novel method termed \textit{grouped median elimination}. Our algorithm ensures the identification of the best arm with a probability of $(1-\delta)$ while requiring no more than $O \left(\sum_{i = 1}^n \left(\frac{\sigma_i^2}{\Delta_i^2} + \frac{1}{\Delta_i}\right)(\ln \delta^{-1} + \ln \ln \Delta_i^{-1})\right)$ samples, where $\Delta_i$ (for $i \geq 2$) represents the reward difference between arm $i$ and the optimal arm, and $\Delta_1$ is set equal to $\Delta_2$. This approach offers a substantial improvement over variance-agnostic algorithms in certain advantageous conditions and marks the first instance of eliminating the additional $\ln n$ factor for the best arm relative to existing leading methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that a minimum of $\Omega \left( \sum_{i = 1}^n \left( \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\Delta_i^2} + \frac{1}{\Delta_i} \right) \ln \delta^{-1} \right)$ samples are required for any algorithm to attain the same objective, thus highlighting the efficiency of our method.

Belief propagation serves as a core message-passing algorithm for probabilistic reasoning and inference within graphical models. Although it delivers exact results on tree-structured graphs, it is frequently applied to graphs containing cycles in practical scenarios. The behavior of "loopy" belief propagation presents a significant challenge for machine learning researchers, with positive convergence outcomes for BP established only under stringent conditions that suggest the underlying graphical model demonstrates a decay of correlations. We demonstrate that with a suitable initialization, BP rapidly converges to the global optimum of the Bethe free energy for Ising models across any graph type, provided the Ising model is \emph{ferromagnetic} (meaning neighboring elements tend to align). This result persists despite the potential for long-range correlations in such models and the existence of multiple suboptimal BP fixed points. Additionally, we present a comparable finding for the iteration of (naive) mean-field equations; remarkably, both findings are independent of dimension, indicating that a fixed number of iterations yields a reliable approximation to the Bethe/mean-field free energy.

This paper introduces a novel 2-order graphic neighbor information feature extraction technique for improving the precision of protein-protein interaction function prediction. This method builds upon the existing 1-order graphic neighbor feature extraction approach by utilizing an undirected simple graph framework. Additionally, a chi-square test statistical approach is incorporated for feature combination. To evaluate the efficacy of the proposed 2-order graphic neighbor feature, four logistic regression models—namely logistic regression (LR), diffusion kernel logistic regression (DKLR), polynomial kernel logistic regression (PKLR), and radial basis function (RBF) based kernel logistic regression (RBF KLR)—are tested on two distinct feature sets. The experiments, conducted using protein-protein interaction data from the Munich Information Center for Protein Sequences (MIPS) on the Yeast Proteome Database (YPD), reveal that the 2-order graphic neighbor information significantly boosts the average overall accuracy of protein function prediction, particularly when paired with RBF KLR. Furthermore, employing a newly developed 5-top chi-square feature combination method, RBF KLR achieves an impressive average overall accuracy of 99.05% on the 2-order neighbor feature combination set.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are effective machine-learning techniques for solving and identifying partial differential equations (PDEs). In this study, we utilize PINNs to address the Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) equations for incompressible turbulent flows, without relying on specific turbulence models or assumptions, and using solely the data from the domain boundaries. Initially, we demonstrate the suitability of PINNs for solving the Navier–Stokes equations in laminar flow scenarios by tackling the Falkner–Skan boundary layer problem. Subsequently, we extend the application of PINNs to simulate four turbulent flow cases: zero-pressure-gradient boundary layer, adverse-pressure-gradient boundary layer, and flows over a NACA4412 airfoil and the periodic hill. Our findings indicate that PINNs perform exceptionally well for laminar flows with significant pressure gradients, achieving predictions with errors below 1%. For turbulent flows, PINNs also deliver high accuracy in simulation outcomes, including for the Reynolds-stress components.

Deep convolutional networks have achieved significant success in various image classification tasks. Current techniques for explaining the predictions of pre-trained models often depend on gradient information, producing saliency maps that highlight the foreground object in its entirety. In contrast, humans tend to analyze images by breaking them down into smaller, distinct concepts and determining the overall result based on the presence or absence of these elements. In this study, we introduce MACE: a Model Agnostic Concept Extractor, designed to elucidate the functioning of convolutional networks through these smaller concepts. The MACE framework analyzes the feature maps produced by a convolutional network for a given image to derive concept-based prototypical explanations. Additionally, it assesses the significance of these extracted concepts in relation to the predictions of the pre-trained model, addressing a crucial gap in existing methods for explaining specific class predictions. We evaluate our framework using the VGG16 and ResNet50 CNN architectures on datasets such as Animals With Attributes 2 (AWA2) and Places365. Our results show that the concepts identified by the MACE framework enhance the human interpretability of the explanations while remaining true to the underlying pre-trained black-box model.

In this study, we introduce a modified neural network model designed to simulate Markov Chains. We explain the process of constructing and training this network, ensuring it captures specific statistical properties from the training data. Additionally, we showcase various applications where the network generates non-deterministic results. For instance, it can be applied to a random walker model, which is valuable for simulating Brownian motion, or to a Tic-Tac-Toe network that promotes non-deterministic gameplay behavior.

A wide range of deep learning architectures have been created to handle the variety of time series datasets found in different fields. This article reviews the typical encoder and decoder structures employed in both single-step and multi-horizon time series forecasting, explaining how each model integrates temporal data into its predictions. Additionally, we discuss recent advancements in hybrid deep learning approaches that merge traditional statistical models with neural network elements to enhance the performance of standalone methods from either domain. Finally, we explore several ways deep learning can support decision-making processes using time series data.

Advancements in deep learning are rapidly simplifying and reducing the cost of creating video forgeries, underscoring the urgent need for effective detection methods. This paper presents a robust approach to identify such forgeries across diverse tampering situations. The issue is framed as a binary classification task for each frame. We suggest employing transfer learning from face recognition to enhance the detection of various facial manipulation techniques. Additionally, in scenarios with low resolution where single-frame detection is less effective, we incorporate data from adjacent frames to improve classification of the central frame. Both strategies are tested on the widely recognized FaceForensics benchmark, where they deliver top-tier accuracy.

This study examines character-level machine translation models employed in pivot-based translation, focusing on their performance with sparse and noisy datasets like crowdsourced movie subtitles. Our experiments reveal that these character-level models reduce the count of untranslated words by more than 40% and show particular strength (yielding 2-3 BLEU point improvements) when training data is scarce. We investigate the effects of character alignment, phrase table filtering, bitext volume, and pivot language selection on translation accuracy. Additionally, we compare cascaded translation systems with the application of synthetic training data through multiple pivots, finding the latter to be substantially more effective. Lastly, we note that neither word- nor character-BLEU metrics align perfectly with human evaluations, primarily due to BLEU’s sensitivity to output length.

Ultra-short laser pulses, ranging from femtosecond to attosecond durations, represent the briefest controlled events humanity can produce. Determining the amplitude and phase of these pulses is crucial for ultrafast science applications, such as studying chemical reactions and electronic phase transitions. In this work, we introduce and validate, through both simulations and experiments, the first deep neural network method for reconstructing ultra-short optical pulses. We believe this technique will broaden the spectrum of ultrashort laser pulses that can be analyzed, potentially allowing the characterization of extremely faint attosecond pulses.

Earlier versions of face recognition algorithms exhibit varying levels of accuracy across different racial groups, a phenomenon known as race bias. This paper explores potential contributing factors—namely data-driven elements and scenario modeling—as well as methodological approaches to evaluate race bias in these algorithms. We examine data-driven aspects such as image quality, population statistics of images, and algorithm design, alongside scenario modeling factors which account for the algorithm's "user" (e.g., decisions on thresholds and demographic limitations). To demonstrate these concepts, we analyze data from four face recognition algorithms, including one older-generation model and three deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs), focusing on East Asian and Caucasian faces. Our findings reveal that, firstly, the difficulty of the dataset influences both overall recognition accuracy and the extent of race bias, with bias intensifying as item difficulty rises. Secondly, the level of bias in all four algorithms fluctuates based on the identification decision threshold; to maintain equal false accept rates (FARs), higher thresholds were necessary for East Asian faces compared to Caucasian faces across all algorithms. Thirdly, demographic constraints affecting the composition of test distributions also influence perceived algorithm accuracy. We conclude that race bias must be assessed specific to each application, and we offer a checklist for evaluating this bias in face recognition algorithms.

sktime is an open-source, Python-based toolkit for time series analysis that is compatible with sklearn and was created by researchers from the University of East Anglia (UEA), University College London, and the Alan Turing Institute. One of the primary objectives of sktime was to replicate the time series classification capabilities found in tsml, a related Java package also developed at UEA. This paper discusses the integration of six classifiers in sktime and compares them to their counterparts in tsml. We verify their accuracy by testing them on various standard datasets and also evaluate the build times of these implementations. Our findings reveal a notable accuracy discrepancy in only one of the six algorithms examined (Proximity Forest), which poses challenges in debugging. Additionally, we observed a broader disparity in efficiency across the implementations. While not entirely surprising, these results underscore potential areas for enhancement in both toolkits.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are a unique type of learning system inspired by biological neural processes, with a notable inclination towards Hebbian learning, encapsulated by the principle "neurons that wire together, fire together." Unlike their biological equivalents, ANNs feature a tight and rigid connection between neuronal modules within the network. This rigid interlinking creates a fixed structure that restricts layers in the network from updating their weights until a complete feed-forward and backward pass is executed. While this limitation may have been tolerable previously, it is increasingly impractical in the current landscape of large-scale machine learning, where there is a growing need for parallelized learning across various computing platforms. To address this challenge, synthetic gradients (SG) combined with decoupled neural interfaces (DNI) are proposed as a compelling substitute for the traditional backpropagation algorithm. This paper conducts a speed benchmark to evaluate the performance and precision of SG-DNI compared to a conventional neural interface using a multilayer perceptron (MLP). The results indicate that SG-DNI holds significant potential, not only effectively addressing the learning challenge but also achieving speeds more than three times faster due to its asynchronous learning capabilities.

It is well-established that greedy approaches excel at maximizing monotone submodular functions, yet they falter when faced with non-monotonicity. In this study, we demonstrate—somewhat unexpectedly—that repeatedly applying the traditional greedy algorithm $O(\sqrt{k})$ times results in the fastest deterministic algorithm to date, termed Repeated Greedy, for maximizing a general submodular function under $k$-independent system constraints. Repeated Greedy delivers a $(1 + O(1/\sqrt{k}))k$ approximation with $O(nr\sqrt{k})$ function evaluations, where $n$ represents the size of the ground set and $r$ indicates the maximum size of a feasible solution. Furthermore, we introduce a refined sampling technique that allows the greedy algorithm to be executed just once, yielding the fastest randomized algorithm currently available, named Sample Greedy, for maximizing a submodular function under $k$-extendible system constraints (a subset of $k$-independent system constraints). Sample Greedy attains a $(k + 3)$-approximation using merely $O(nr/k)$ function evaluations. Additionally, we establish a near-matching lower bound, proving that no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve an approximation ratio less than $k + 1/2 - \varepsilon$. To substantiate our theoretical findings, we evaluate the performance of Repeated Greedy and Sample Greedy against existing methods in a specific application involving movie recommendations.

In this paper, we introduce three novel error bounds for covariance estimation under differential privacy, measured in the Frobenius norm: (1) a worst-case bound of $\tilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$, which surpasses the conventional Gaussian mechanism $\tilde{O}(d/n)$ when $d>\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{2/3})$; (2) a trace-sensitive bound that enhances the current best result by a factor of $\sqrt{d}$; and (3) a tail-sensitive bound that provides a more tailored, instance-specific outcome. The associated algorithms are straightforward and efficient. Experimental findings demonstrate that these approaches substantially outperform previous methods.

In parallel systems, communication overhead often becomes a critical bottleneck in parallel machine learning. To address this issue, we introduce EventGraD, an innovative algorithm that incorporates event-triggered communication for stochastic gradient descent in parallel machine learning environments. Unlike traditional implementations that require communication at every iteration, EventGraD communicates only during specific, necessary iterations. We offer a theoretical analysis to demonstrate the convergence properties of our algorithm. Furthermore, we have applied EventGraD to the data-parallel training of a well-known residual neural network for the CIFAR-10 dataset, achieving a reduction in communication overhead by up to 60% without compromising accuracy. Additionally, EventGraD can be integrated with other techniques like Top-K sparsification to further minimize communication while preserving accuracy.

Although traditional statistical inference methods and machine learning generalization bounds typically presume that tests are conducted on data chosen independently of the hypotheses, real-world data analysis and machine learning often involve iterative and adaptive processes. In these scenarios, the same holdout data is repeatedly used to test a series of hypotheses or models, each potentially influenced by the results of prior tests on the same dataset. In this study, we introduce RadaBound, a robust, efficient, and practical approach to manage generalization error when a holdout sample is used for multiple adaptive tests. Our method leverages a novel adaptation of the Rademacher Complexity generalization bounds tailored for dependent tests. We validate the statistical effectiveness and practicality of our approach through comprehensive simulations and comparisons with other methods.

Biology serves as both a crucial field for applying and a driving force behind the advancement of cutting-edge machine learning methods. While significant focus has been directed toward the vast and intricate data sets produced by high-throughput sequencing, recent progress in high-quality video recording technology has started to yield equally complex data sets that demand advanced approaches in computer vision and time-series analysis. Furthermore, just as analyzing gene expression patterns in a single organism can uncover universal principles applicable to others, examining complex social interactions in a manageable experimental model, such as a laboratory ant colony, can offer insights into the dynamics of various social groups. In this context, we highlight a specific case involving reproductive regulation in small laboratory colonies of over 50 Harpegnathos ants. These ants can be prompted artificially to initiate a roughly 20-day process of hierarchy restructuring. Although the outcome of this process is evident to a human observer, the specific behaviors during the transitional phase that influence this process remain ambiguous. To tackle this uncertainty, we investigate the potential use of One-class Classification (OC) for identifying abnormal states in ant colonies where only behavioral data is accessible.

The vast availability of healthcare data repositories underscores the need for effective tools to advance data-driven medicine. We present a distributed system based on Stratified Locality Sensitive Hashing designed for rapid similarity-based predictions on extensive medical waveform datasets. Tailored for an ICU setting, our implementation emphasizes reduced latency over high throughput and is optimized for cloud environments. We showcase the system's capabilities in predicting Acute Hypotensive Episodes using Arterial Blood Pressure waveforms. Testing on a dataset comprising 1.37 million data points, our system scales effectively up to 40 processors, achieving a 21-fold increase in comparison speed compared to parallel exhaustive search, with a trade-off of a 10% reduction in Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). Moreover, if a greater loss in MCC is acceptable, the system can deliver speedups of up to two orders of magnitude.

The global spread of the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) has presented unprecedented challenges to the research community. Leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising approach to forecasting the parameters, risks, and impacts of such outbreaks. These AI-driven predictions could play a crucial role in curbing and preventing the proliferation of such diseases. However, the primary obstacles in utilizing AI include the limited availability of data and its inherent unpredictability. In this study, we introduce a shallow long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network designed to assess the risk category of individual countries. We employed a Bayesian optimization framework to fine-tune and autonomously develop networks tailored to specific countries. Our findings demonstrate that this proposed pipeline surpasses existing top-tier methods across data from 180 countries, establishing it as an effective tool for risk classification. Additionally, we explored the integration of trend and weather data for predictive purposes, concluding that weather factors do not significantly influence outcomes. This tool holds potential for forecasting prolonged outbreaks, enabling earlier implementation of preventive measures.

Implementing machine learning for molecular analysis presents challenges due to the inherent graph structure of molecules, as opposed to vector formats. While various architectures for deep learning from molecular graphs have emerged recently, they often encounter information bottlenecks by limiting data exchange to immediate neighboring nodes. In response, we propose a novel approach featuring a route-based multi-attention mechanism that captures characteristics from paths connecting node pairs. We term this innovation Graph Informer. This allows a single network layer to reach nodes several connections away. Our empirical results indicate that this method outperforms existing solutions in two significant tasks: (1) predicting 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectra with an improved mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.35 ppm, setting a new benchmark, and (2) forecasting drug bioactivity and toxicity. Additionally, we introduce a variant, the injective Graph Informer, which matches the discriminative power of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test for graph isomorphism. Moreover, by leveraging route data, our method gains insights into the graph's nonlocal topology, surpassing even the capabilities of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.

Numerous data types encountered in data mining applications can be represented as bipartite graphs, such as terms and documents in textual datasets, customers and products in market basket analysis, and reviewers and films in movie recommendation systems. In this study, we introduce a novel data clustering technique that involves partitioning the corresponding bipartite graph. This partitioning is achieved by minimizing a normalized sum of the edge weights between unpaired vertices in the graph. We demonstrate that an approximate solution to this minimization challenge can be derived through a partial singular value decomposition (SVD) of the graph’s associated edge weight matrix. Additionally, we highlight the relationship between our clustering approach and correspondence analysis, a method used in multivariate analysis. We also touch on the concept of allocating data objects to multiple clusters. Through experimental results, we apply our clustering method to document clustering, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency.

Deep Reinforcement Learning represents a promising approach for robotic control, demonstrating the ability to develop policies for complex, high-dimensional, and continuous control of systems that lack predefined models. Despite its potential, the field of Robotic Reinforcement Learning suffers from the absence of standardized benchmark tasks, complicating the ability of researchers to replicate and evaluate previous studies. "Reacher" tasks, essential to robotic manipulation, often serve as benchmarks; however, the absence of a formal specification obscures critical details necessary for accurate reproduction. In this paper, we offer a new empirical analysis revealing that the unspecified spatial constraints in prevalent implementations of Reacher tasks significantly simplify the process of learning an effective control policy using Deep Deterministic Policy Gradients (DDPG), a cutting-edge Deep RL algorithm. Our findings indicate that Reacher tasks with fewer constraints pose much greater learning challenges, suggesting that current informal benchmarks fail to accurately reflect the complexities inherent in general robotic manipulation.

We introduce an innovative Stochastic Frank-Wolfe (also known as conditional gradient) algorithm tailored for constrained smooth finite-sum minimization with generalized linear prediction or structure. This problem category encompasses empirical risk minimization under sparse, low-rank, or other structured constraints. Our algorithm is straightforward to implement, eliminates the need for step-size adjustments, and maintains a constant cost per iteration, unaffected by the dataset's size. Additionally, a useful byproduct of our approach is a stochastic estimator of the Frank-Wolfe gap, which serves as an effective stopping criterion. Depending on the specific context, our method either matches or surpasses the best computational guarantees of existing Stochastic Frank-Wolfe algorithms. Comparative benchmarks across multiple datasets reveal scenarios where our method demonstrates superior empirical convergence compared to similar approaches. Lastly, we offer an open-source package that includes implementations of all methods discussed.

The transfer of knowledge across multiple streaming processes is a largely unexplored area in current research, presenting distinct challenges: the absence of labeled instances in the target domain, covariate shifts between source and target domains, and varying drift periods in both domains. This paper introduces Autonomous Transfer Learning (ATL), a versatile deep learning method designed for online unsupervised transfer learning across numerous streaming processes. ATL implements an online domain adaptation approach through generative and discriminative phases, integrated with a KL divergence-based optimization technique to create a domain-invariant network. Additionally, it features an adaptable network structure that evolves autonomously from the ground up, with or without ground truth, to address independent concept drifts in both source and target domains. A thorough numerical evaluation has been performed, alongside comparisons with recently published studies, revealing that ATL not only achieves superior performance but also offers significantly faster training times compared to its peers.

Machine learning models are susceptible to data-poisoning attacks, where an attacker deliberately alters the training data to manipulate the predictions of the trained model. In a trigger-less attack, the attacker can tamper with the training data but not the test inputs, whereas in a backdoor attack, the attacker has the ability to alter test inputs as well. Current model-agnostic defense methods are either ineffective against backdoor attacks or fail to offer reliable guarantees (i.e., proof of defense). We introduce BagFlip, a model-agnostic certified method that robustly counters both trigger-less and backdoor attacks. We assessed BagFlip using datasets for image classification and malware detection. BagFlip matches or surpasses the performance of leading methods for trigger-less attacks and outperforms the top methods for defending against backdoor attacks.

Mouse dynamics offers a promising avenue for user authentication. Traditionally, this process relies on conventional machine learning methods, though deep learning approaches have recently emerged in this field. While previous studies have shown that both machine learning and deep learning systems can be deceived by meticulously designed adversarial samples, research on adversarial threats in the realm of behavioral biometrics remains scarce. To bridge this gap, we developed a series of attacks using various generative techniques to create adversarial mouse trajectories capable of fooling authentication systems. These fabricated mouse movements act as adversarial samples in our experiments. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the attack methods we investigated, highlighting their constraints. Unlike earlier studies, we examine these attacks under a more realistic and stringent scenario where the attacker possesses access to logged user data but lacks knowledge of the authentication model or its outputs. We investigate three distinct attack strategies: 1) statistics-driven, 2) imitation-driven, and 3) surrogate-driven, demonstrating their ability to undermine the authentication models and negatively affect their reliability.

Federated learning is a widely adopted approach for training machine learning models on decentralized data sources while preserving data privacy. Vertical federated learning, also known as feature-based federated learning, is applicable when multiple data sources have overlapping sample IDs but distinct feature sets. To maintain data owners' sustained participation, it is essential to fairly evaluate each data source's contribution and provide appropriate compensation. The Shapley value (SV), a well-established fairness metric from cooperative game theory, offers a provably equitable way to assess contributions. However, calculating the SV demands repeated model retraining on various data source combinations, leading to excessively high communication overhead in federated learning environments. To address this, we introduce a novel contribution assessment metric called the vertical federated Shapley value (VerFedSV), derived from SV. We demonstrate that VerFedSV upholds key fairness properties, is computationally efficient, and seamlessly integrates with both synchronous and asynchronous vertical federated learning frameworks. Through theoretical analysis and comprehensive experiments, we confirm the fairness, efficiency, and versatility of VerFedSV.

The hallmark of a Bayesian approach is marginalization, which prioritizes integrating over various weight configurations rather than relying on a fixed set. This technique of Bayesian marginalization significantly enhances the precision and calibration of contemporary deep neural networks, which often lack sufficient data specification and can embody numerous plausible yet distinct solutions. Our findings demonstrate that deep ensembles serve as a potent tool for approximate Bayesian marginalization. Additionally, we introduce a complementary method that boosts the quality of the predictive distribution by marginalizing within attraction basins, achieving this without notable additional cost. We further explore the prior distribution over functions suggested by an ambiguous spread of neural network weights, shedding light on the generalization capabilities of these models through a probabilistic lens. Through this lens, we clarify phenomena previously seen as enigmatic and unique to neural network generalization—like the capacity to fit randomly labeled images—and illustrate that such outcomes are replicable with Gaussian processes. Moreover, we reveal that Bayesian model averaging mitigates the issue of double descent, leading to consistent performance gains as model flexibility increases. Lastly, we offer a Bayesian viewpoint on tempering as a means to refine predictive distribution calibration.

Building on MacKay (1992), we contend that traditional model-based active learning approaches, such as BALD, suffer from a critical limitation: they do not explicitly consider the test-time distribution of input variables. This oversight can result in flawed acquisition strategies, as maximizing information about model parameters does not necessarily equate to maximizing predictive utility. For instance, discrepancies may arise when the pool set data is more spread out than the data in the final prediction task or when the distributions of pool and test samples differ. To address this issue, we propose revisiting an acquisition approach focused on maximizing the expected information gained regarding future predictions, which we term Expected Predictive Information Gain (EPIG). However, since EPIG struggles to scale effectively for batch acquisition, we also explore a hybrid strategy combining elements of BALD and EPIG, which we name Joint Expected Predictive Information Gain (JEPIG). We evaluate the application of both methods in active learning with Bayesian neural networks across various datasets, specifically investigating their performance under conditions of distribution shift in the pool set.

In recent years, video action recognition systems and models have garnered considerable attention. Yet, the ability to directly compare their accuracy and computational performance is often obscured by variations in training environments, hardware setups, hyperparameters, processing pipelines, and inference techniques. This article offers a head-to-head comparison of fourteen ready-to-use and cutting-edge models by standardizing these training variables, thereby delivering a clear and insightful evaluation of diverse video action recognition algorithms. The models' accuracy is assessed using conventional Top-1 and Top-5 metrics, alongside a newly introduced accuracy measure. Furthermore, we analyze the computational efficiency of distributed training across a range of two to sixty-four GPUs on a leading-edge High-Performance Computing (HPC) system.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) seeks to apply knowledge gained from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. The majority of current UDA approaches concentrate on developing domain-invariant feature representations at either the domain or category level, utilizing frameworks based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). A key challenge in category-level UDA is the generation of pseudo labels for target domain samples, which often contain significant noise, hindering precise domain alignment and ultimately degrading UDA performance. Given the effectiveness of Transformers across various applications, we have discovered that the cross-attention mechanism in Transformers is resilient to noisy input pairs, facilitating improved feature alignment. Consequently, in this paper, we employ Transformers to address the complex task of UDA. To create reliable input pairs, we introduce a two-way center-aware labeling algorithm to assign pseudo labels to target samples. Additionally, we propose a weight-sharing triple-branch Transformer framework that leverages self-attention and cross-attention for learning source/target features and aligning source-target domains, respectively. This structure specifically compels the framework to simultaneously capture both discriminative domain-specific and domain-invariant representations. Named CDTrans (cross-domain Transformer), our approach represents one of the initial efforts to tackle UDA challenges using a purely Transformer-based model.

Probabilistic hierarchical time-series forecasting plays a crucial role in the field of time-series analysis, focusing on modeling and predicting multivariate time-series data with inherent hierarchical structures. Many existing methods primarily target point predictions and fail to deliver well-calibrated probabilistic forecast distributions. Moreover, cutting-edge probabilistic forecasting techniques often enforce hierarchical constraints solely on point predictions and distribution samples, overlooking the coherency of the entire forecast distribution. Additionally, prior research tends to implicitly assume that datasets consistently align with predefined hierarchical relationships, without adapting to real-world data that may deviate from such assumptions. To address these shortcomings, we introduce PROFHIT, a comprehensive probabilistic hierarchical forecasting model that captures the forecast distribution across the complete hierarchy. Employing a versatile probabilistic Bayesian framework, PROFHIT incorporates a novel Distributional Coherency regularization to leverage hierarchical relationships across the full forecast distribution. This approach ensures robust and well-calibrated forecasts while accommodating datasets with inconsistent hierarchical structures. Evaluations of PROFHIT across diverse datasets demonstrate a significant improvement in accuracy and calibration, ranging from 41% to 88%. Furthermore, by modeling coherency over the entire distribution, PROFHIT maintains reliability in forecasting even when up to 10% of the input time-series data is absent.

In the healthcare sector, patients must utilize wearable devices to enable remote data collection and real-time monitoring of health metrics and conditions. This reliance on wearable technology leads to a substantial rise in the amount of data gathered and shared. However, since these devices operate on limited battery power, their energy can be rapidly depleted due to the intensive processing demands of data collection and transmission. Considering the critical nature of medical data, it is essential that all transmitted information meets stringent standards of integrity and availability. Decreasing the volume of healthcare data and the frequency of transmissions can extend device battery life through the implementation of inference algorithms. A key challenge lies in optimizing transmission metrics like accuracy and efficiency, which often conflict—improving accuracy can compromise efficiency. This paper explores how machine learning can address this trade-off by analyzing intricate health data metrics, using the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm to improve both accuracy and efficiency. This is achieved by reducing the number of samples transmitted while preserving accuracy. The algorithm's effectiveness is evaluated using a standard heart rate dataset for comparison.

With the emergence of 5G wireless standards and the growing need for greater data rates, enhancing the spectral efficiency of wireless systems has gained critical importance. In the realm of cognitive radio, significant throughput improvements can be achieved if the secondary user intelligently decides which channel to monitor and the timing or frequency of such monitoring. In this study, we introduce an algorithm designed to both select a channel for data transmission and estimate the duration the channel will remain free, thereby reducing the time dedicated to channel sensing. Our algorithm operates in two phases: a reinforcement learning strategy for choosing the channel and a Bayesian method to calculate the ideal period during which sensing can be omitted. We present comparisons with other learning approaches through comprehensive simulations. Our findings demonstrate that the frequency of sensing is significantly reduced with only a minimal increase in primary interference, indicating that the secondary user expends less energy on sensing while also achieving greater throughput by cutting down on sensing time.

We explore model-free reinforcement learning in the context of infinite-horizon discounted Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) featuring a continuous state space and an unknown transition kernel, utilizing only a single sample path from any given policy of the system. Our focus is on the Nearest Neighbor Q-Learning (NNQL) algorithm, which employs the nearest neighbor regression method to estimate the optimal Q function. The primary contribution of this work is a detailed finite sample analysis of the algorithm's convergence rate. Specifically, for MDPs with a $d$-dimensional state space and a discount factor $\gamma \in (0,1)$, we demonstrate that, given a sample path with a "covering time" $L$, the algorithm can produce an $\varepsilon$-accurate approximation of the optimal Q-function with a sample complexity of $\tilde{O}\big(L/(\varepsilon^3(1-\gamma)^7)\big)$. For example, in a well-structured MDP, the covering time under a completely random policy is $\tilde{O}\big(1/\varepsilon^d\big)$, resulting in a sample complexity of $\tilde{O}\big(1/\varepsilon^{d+3}\big)$. Additionally, we provide a lower bound showing that a sample complexity of $\tilde{\Omega}\big(1/\varepsilon^{d+2}\big)$ is essential.

Despite significant progress in graph neural networks (GNNs) for handling graph data, training these models on large datasets remains challenging due to overfitting. Adversarial training, which enhances data with worst-case adversarial examples, has been extensively shown to bolster a model's resilience against malicious attacks and improve its ability to generalize. However, while prior adversarial training efforts have primarily aimed at safeguarding GNNs from hostile attacks, the impact of such training on enhancing GNNs' generalization in graph analytics tasks is still not well understood. In this study, we explore GNNs through the perspective of weight and feature loss landscapes, examining how loss varies with changes in model weights and node features. Our findings suggest that GNNs tend to get trapped in sharp local minima within these landscapes, leading to suboptimal generalization performance. To address this issue, we formulate the co-adversarial perturbation (CAP) optimization problem concerning both weights and features, and propose an alternating adversarial perturbation algorithm to smooth out the loss landscapes of weights and features in turn. Additionally, we split the training into two phases: the first focuses on standard cross-entropy minimization to guarantee rapid convergence of GNN models, while the second implements our alternating adversarial approach.

UMAP has emerged as the leading method for visualizing high-dimensional datasets across various fields, surpassing t-SNE, though the reasons behind its success remain unclear. In this study, we thoroughly examine UMAP's sampling-based optimization process. We derive its effective loss function in a closed form and discover that it deviates from the one originally published. Consequently, we demonstrate that UMAP does not strive to replicate the theoretically derived high-dimensional similarities it is based on. Rather, it focuses on replicating similarities that solely represent the shared $k$ nearest neighbor graph, which contradicts prior interpretations of UMAP's efficacy. We argue instead that UMAP's success stems from its implicit balancing of attractive and repulsive forces achieved through negative sampling. This balance plays a crucial role in enabling effective optimization through gradient descent. Our theoretical insights are supported by experiments on toy datasets and single-cell RNA sequencing data.

Advancements in deep learning are fueling a wide array of rapidly evolving models, accompanied by a surging need for computational resources. Yet, as frameworks focus on optimizing performance for common network patterns, they often limit the development of innovative and diverse models critical to research progress. To support deep learning researchers, we introduce a versatile and customizable pipeline for optimizing the training of any deep neural network, emphasizing the minimization of data movement. This pipeline starts with standard networks in PyTorch or ONNX, transforming computations via a process of progressive lowering. We implement four levels of broad transformations, ranging from localized intra-operator enhancements to comprehensive data movement reduction. These transformations are applied to a data-centric graph intermediate representation that captures both computation and data movement across various abstraction levels, including breaking down fundamental operators like convolutions into their core computations. A key feature of this design is its interactive and introspectable framework. Every component can be extended via a Python API and fine-tuned interactively through a graphical user interface. We showcase comparable performance or accelerated results across ten distinct networks, with interactive optimizations uncovering new potential in EfficientNet.

The requirement for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to remain invariant to permutations of the adjacency matrix, known as graph isomorphism, is fundamental. Typically, this condition is met through invariant operations over node permutations during message aggregation. However, this invariant approach can overlook the connections between neighboring nodes, thus limiting the expressiveness of GNNs. In this study, we introduce an effective permutation-sensitive aggregation method using permutation groups to capture pairwise interactions among adjacent nodes. We demonstrate that our method surpasses the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman (2-WL) graph isomorphism test in power and is at least as powerful as the 3-WL test. Additionally, we establish that our approach maintains linear sampling complexity. Extensive experiments across various synthetic and real-world datasets highlight the exceptional performance of our model.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking collaborative distillation meta learning (CDML) framework tailored for simulation-intensive hardware design challenges. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has demonstrated impressive results in hardware design tasks, yet prior DRL applications have been limited to scenarios with overly simplified goals, rendering them impractical. In reality, evaluating real-world electrical performance via simulation is both time-consuming and computationally expensive, rendering traditional DRL approaches with frequent reward computations unsuitable. Here, we implement the CDML framework to address the decoupling capacitor placement problem (DPP), a critical issue in simulation-intensive hardware design. The CDML framework integrates a context-based meta learner and a collaborative distillation mechanism to develop a versatile solver. The context-based meta learner identifies the probing port's location (i.e., the target circuit block) and enhances generalization ability. Meanwhile, the collaborative distillation mechanism, incorporating equivariant label transformation, embeds the action-permutation (AP)-equivariant characteristics of placement issues, boosting both sample efficiency and generalization. Comprehensive experiments confirm that our CDML approach surpasses neural baselines and traditional iterative design techniques in achieving real-world objectives and power integrity, while also demonstrating zero-shot transferability.

Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) is widely recognized as a valuable tool for data analysis across various fields. However, its application in real-world scenarios has faced difficulties in recent times, primarily due to the ever-increasing volume of datasets in the information sciences. To tackle this issue, we introduce the use of structured random compression, specifically random projections that leverage data structure, for two NMF variants: classical and separable. In separable NMF (SNMF), the left factors consist of a subset of the input matrix's columns. We propose tailored formulations for each variant, addressing different key algorithms within them. Our findings demonstrate that the compressed methods are not only faster than their uncompressed counterparts but also significantly reduce memory usage without notable performance loss. The structured random projections designed for SNMF enable handling of large matrices of any shape, moving beyond the conventional constraints of tall-and-skinny matrices, and facilitating highly efficient computations in a broader context. Alongside the algorithmic framework, we provide theoretical support and a range of diverse examples to validate the effectiveness of these proposed methods.

We address the challenge of counterfactual inference in sequentially designed experiments, where a set of $\mathbf{N}$ units is subjected to a series of interventions over $\mathbf{T}$ time periods, guided by policies that evolve dynamically. Our objective is to perform counterfactual inference, meaning we aim to predict the outcomes that would have occurred under different policies. This task is complex due to the variability in outcomes across units and over time. To address this, we propose a latent factor model in which potential outcomes are influenced by latent factors specific to units and time periods. Under certain assumptions, we demonstrate that missing (potential) outcomes can be estimated using a straightforward nearest neighbors approach. First, by adopting a bilinear latent factor model and accommodating any adaptive sampling policy, we provide a distribution-free, non-asymptotic guarantee for estimating the missing outcome of any unit at any given time; with appropriate regularity conditions, this guarantee ensures the consistency of our estimator. Second, for a general non-parametric latent factor model, we prove that the estimate of the missing outcome for any unit at time $\mathbf{T}$ adheres to a central limit theorem as $\mathbf{T} \to \infty$, given certain regularity conditions.
