This research represents an initial effort to experimentally investigate the various performance bottlenecks that 5G mobile networks may encounter. We utilize an extensive set of data collected from a prototype testbed designed to emulate the critical components of a cloud-based mobile network. Our study examines the significance of different metrics and explores multiple methods to precisely and effectively pinpoint bottlenecks at various network locations and across different layers of the system architecture. Our results underscore the challenges posed by the intricate, multi-layered structure of these networks and emphasize the necessity for innovative monitoring strategies that smartly integrate metrics from diverse network layers and functions. Notably, we discovered that distributed analytics offers a satisfactory balance, achieving decent accuracy in identifying bottlenecks while maintaining manageable levels of computational and communication overhead.

Distillation serves as a potent method for transferring knowledge, utilizing the predicted distributions from a robust teacher model as soft targets to educate a smaller, less complex student model. Often, a pre-trained, high-capacity teacher model isn't readily available. Recent online adaptations have shifted to using aggregated intermediate predictions from several student models as training targets for each student. While these group-sourced targets provide a viable approach for distillation without a teacher, the rapid homogenization of group members through basic aggregation methods results in prematurely saturated outcomes. In this study, we introduce Online Knowledge Distillation with Diverse Peers (OKDDip), which implements a two-tier distillation process during training involving multiple auxiliary peers and a single group leader. At the first level of distillation, each auxiliary peer utilizes a unique set of aggregation weights, crafted through an attention-based mechanism, to create personalized targets from the predictions of fellow peers. This learning from varied target distributions enhances diversity among peers, improving the efficacy of group distillation. The second level of distillation transfers the collective knowledge from the ensemble of auxiliary peers to the group leader, which is the model deployed for inference. Experimental findings demonstrate that this approach consistently outperforms leading methods without increasing training or inference complexity, underscoring the potency of OKDDip.

We have introduced a model inspired by flocking behavior within a complex network framework and subsequently developed two clustering algorithms derived from this model. In these algorithms, we first construct a k-nearest neighbor (knn) graph, which is both weighted and directed, encompassing all data points in a dataset. Each data point is treated as an agent capable of spatial movement. Following this, a dynamic complex network is formed by incorporating long-range links for each data point. Additionally, each data point is influenced not only by its k nearest neighbors but also by r long-range neighbors through collective spatial fields, prompting it to move in the direction of the resultant vector of these combined fields. Crucially, these long-range links deliver hidden information to each data point during movement, simultaneously enhancing the speed at which it converges toward a central point. As the data points navigate through space according to our model, those belonging to the same class gradually congregate at a common location, while points from different classes drift apart. Ultimately, experimental outcomes confirm that data points within datasets are clustered effectively.

Metal artifacts in computed tomography (CT) result from discrepancies between the actual physics of image creation and the simplified assumptions made during tomographic reconstruction. These artifacts are especially pronounced near metal implants, which has limited the broader use of 3D cone-beam CT (CBCT) despite its potential for intra-operative confirmation of implant placement, such as in spinal fusion procedures. Through synthetic and real data analysis, we show that a significant portion of these artifacts can be mitigated by collecting improved data for reconstruction in a way that is both task-specific and tailored to the individual patient. We also outline the initial phase of developing a task-aware CBCT protocol. Conventionally, the short-scan CBCT trajectory is confined to a single plane, offering minimal flexibility for adaptation to specific scenarios. We enhance this trajectory by autonomously modifying the out-of-plane angulation. This adjustment allows for C-arm source paths that are customized to the scene, avoiding the capture of suboptimal images plagued by issues like beam hardening, photon starvation, and noise. The optimal out-of-plane angulation is determined in real-time using a deep convolutional neural network, which predicts a detectability rank based on principles of imaging physics.

We introduce semi-random features for approximating nonlinear functions, offering a balance between the adaptable units of deep learning and the fixed random features of kernel methods. For single hidden layer models employing semi-random features, we demonstrate, without making unrealistic assumptions, that these models can approximate any function with increasing accuracy as the layer width grows (universality). Additionally, despite the challenge of non-convexity, we can identify an effective function (optimization theory) that performs well on new, unseen data (generalization bound). For deeper models, we establish, also without unrealistic assumptions, the capability for universal approximation, a minimum approximation error threshold, a partial guarantee on optimization, and a bound on generalization. Notably, the generalization bound for deep semi-random features can be significantly superior to existing bounds for deep ReLU networks, potentially independent of factors like depth, the number of adjustable weights, or input dimensionality. Experimental results indicate that semi-random features can rival the performance of neural networks with a modest increase in units and surpass random features with considerably fewer units. Furthermore, we propose a novel implicit ensemble approach utilizing semi-random features.

We present a novel category of lower bounds for the log partition function of a Markov random field, employing a reversed form of Jensen's inequality. Specifically, our approach estimates the intractable distribution through a linear combination of spanning trees with negative weights. This method serves as a lower-bound complement to the tree-reweighted belief propagation algorithm, which utilizes a convex combination of spanning trees with positive weights to establish corresponding upper bounds. We have created algorithms to refine and strengthen these lower bounds across the non-convex set of valid parameter values. Additionally, our algorithm extends mean field methods, encompassing both naive and structured mean field approximations as special cases.

We investigate efficient algorithms for statistical regression challenges within the strong contamination model, aiming to approximately optimize generalized linear models (GLMs) using adversarially corrupted data. Previous research in this area relied on the robust gradient descent framework by Prasad et al., which employs a first-order method with biased gradient queries, or the Sever framework by Diakonikolas et al., which uses an iterative outlier-removal technique with a stationary point finder. We introduce nearly-linear time algorithms for robust regression that offer enhanced runtime or estimation accuracy compared to existing methods. For the broad category of smooth GLMs, such as logistic regression, we demonstrate that the robust gradient descent approach by Prasad et al. can be made faster, and we extend our algorithm to optimize Moreau envelopes of Lipschitz GLMs, like support vector machines, addressing multiple unresolved issues in the field. For the extensively studied problem of robust linear regression, we propose a different method that achieves better estimation rates than previous nearly-linear time algorithms. Notably, our approach begins with a proof of identifiability originally presented in the sum-of-squares algorithm context by Bakshi and Prasad, which delivered optimal error rates but demanded significant polynomial runtime and sample complexity. We reinterpret their proof within our framework to advance the solution.

Reinforcement learning has demonstrated remarkable success across a range of applications. However, learning an effective policy for an agent typically demands extensive data collection through environmental interactions, which can be both computationally expensive and time-intensive. To address this issue, a framework known as Reinforcement Learning with Expert Demonstrations (RLED) was introduced to leverage guidance from expert demonstrations. While RLED methods can decrease the number of required learning iterations, they often operate under the assumption that the demonstrations are flawless, making them vulnerable to being misguided by imperfect or noisy demonstrations in practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a new framework that adaptively learns the policy by simultaneously interacting with the environment and utilizing expert demonstrations. Specifically, we treat each step of a demonstration trajectory as an instance and design a joint loss function to maximize the expected reward while minimizing the discrepancy between the agent’s actions and the demonstrations. Crucially, by estimating the expected gain of the value function, we assign a weight to each instance to gauge its potential usefulness, allowing us to prioritize more beneficial demonstrations and disregard those that are noisy. Experimental outcomes across various environments using several well-known reinforcement learning algorithms demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method.

The majority of artificial neural networks designed for object detection and recognition are trained using a fully supervised approach. This method demands significant resources, as it relies on extensive datasets of labeled examples, and contrasts sharply with human learning processes. We propose a novel framework where an artificial agent initially learns in a simulated environment via self-supervised exploration. Subsequently, the representations developed through these interactions with the environment can be utilized to link semantic concepts, such as various door types. To achieve this, we employ a technique called fast concept mapping, which identifies and defines semantic concepts through the correlated firing patterns of neurons. This mapping occurs instantly and requires only a minimal number of labeled examples, mirroring the human ability known as fast mapping. Remarkably, this approach can recognize objects with just a single labeled example, underscoring the effectiveness of the self-supervised encoding achieved through curiosity-driven exploration in a physical context. Thus, it offers a practical method for concept learning with minimal supervision and demonstrates that meaningful environmental representations can be developed solely through interaction with the world.

The Box-Cox transformation stands out as a distinctive method within the family of power transformations. This mathematical technique involves determining the optimal lambda (λ) value that maximizes the log-likelihood function, thereby transforming data to approximate a normal distribution and minimize heteroscedasticity. Many statistical test models in data analytics rely on the assumption of normality. While this method is primarily recognized in statistical analysis for processing one-dimensional data, this paper focuses on its application as a pre-processing tool for transforming two-dimensional data, specifically digital images, and evaluating its impact. To address time complexity issues, we propose estimating the lambda parameter in real-time for large two-dimensional matrices by using their probability density function as a statistical representation of the data distribution. We compare the performance of this streamlined Box-Cox transformation against leading state-of-the-art techniques for low-light image enhancement. Additionally, we showcase the efficacy of our method through various test-bed datasets, demonstrating improvements in the visual quality of images and enhancing the performance of a color pattern classification algorithm as a practical example. The outcomes, with and without the proposed method, are evaluated to highlight its benefits.

Hottopixx, introduced by Bittorf et al. at NIPS 2012, is an algorithm designed to address nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) problems under the separability condition. Separable NMFs are crucial in applications like topic modeling from text data and hyperspectral image unmixing, where the algorithm’s resilience to noise is vital for success. Hottopixx has demonstrated strong noise tolerance, which can be further improved through postprocessing. However, a significant limitation exists: both Hottopixx and its postprocessing require an upfront estimation of the noise level in the matrix to be factorized, as this value is a necessary input. Estimating noise levels is often challenging. In this paper, we address this limitation by proposing a refined version of Hottopixx and its postprocessing that operates without prior knowledge of the noise level. We demonstrate that this refined approach maintains nearly the same level of noise robustness as the original algorithm.

With the swift expansion of mobile applications and cloud computing, mobile cloud computing has garnered significant attention from academic and industrial sectors alike. Nonetheless, security challenges such as data integrity, user privacy, and service availability continue to plague mobile cloud applications. A proactive strategy to mitigate these issues involves identifying and neutralizing cyber threats before they severely impact the mobile cloud computing infrastructure. In this paper, we introduce an innovative framework that employs deep learning techniques to identify cyberattacks within the mobile cloud environment. Experimental outcomes reveal that our framework not only detects a wide range of cyberattacks but also boasts an impressive accuracy rate of up to 97.11% in attack detection. Additionally, we compare our approach with existing machine learning-based methods to highlight the superior efficacy of our proposed solution.

Creating new image-text pairs is a challenge that merges computer vision with natural language processing. In this paper, we introduce methods for producing fresh image and caption combinations using existing captioning datasets. Our approach leverages the latest developments in generative adversarial networks and sequence-to-sequence modeling. We extend our techniques to create paired samples across various domains. Additionally, we explore cycles—converting from image to text and back to image, and vice versa—and examine their relationship with autoencoders.

Diabetes ranks among the most prevalent, hazardous, and expensive diseases globally, stemming from elevated blood sugar levels or reduced insulin production in the body. Late diagnosis of diabetes can severely impact individuals' health. It poses a significant challenge for health and government authorities today. Prioritizing prevention and ensuring people's well-being without sacrificing their comfort is crucial. This research employs an Ensemble training approach, utilizing genetic algorithms to precisely diagnose and forecast the outcomes of diabetes mellitus. The study leverages experimental and real data on Indian diabetic patients, sourced from the University of California website. Advancements in information and communication technology, including the Internet of Things, machine learning, and data mining, enable the development of smarter health strategies. These technologies enhance the ability to predict disease outcomes in everyday settings and hospitals, thereby helping to halt the disease's progression and its numerous complications. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving a diagnostic accuracy of 98.8% and an overall accuracy of 99% in this study.

We examine vector-valued non-linear dynamical systems defined by the equation $X_{t+1} = \phi(A^* X_t) + \eta_t$, where $\eta_t$ represents unbiased noise and $\phi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a known link function possessing a specific {\em expansivity property}. Our objective is to estimate $A^*$ using a single trajectory of dependent or correlated samples, $X_1,\cdots,X_T$. Although the linear case, where $\phi$ is the identity function, has been extensively studied with optimal error rates even for non-mixing systems, current results for the non-linear case are limited to mixing systems. In this research, we advance the understanding of learning non-linear systems in several key areas: a) we introduce the first offline algorithm capable of learning non-linear dynamical systems without assuming mixing, b) we achieve a substantial reduction in sample complexity compared to previous results for mixing systems, c) in the more challenging one-pass, streaming context, we explore a SGD with Reverse Experience Replay ($\mathsf{SGD-RER}$) approach, showing that for mixing systems, it matches the sample complexity of our offline algorithm, d) we validate the expansivity assumption by demonstrating that for the widely used ReLU link function—a non-expansive yet easily learnable function with i.i.d. samples—any learning method would require

We examine a scenario where a seller manages a vast network of $N$ products across a time span of $T$ periods. Unfamiliar with the parameters of the linear demand model for these products, the seller dynamically modifies prices to deduce the demand model from sales data. The objective is to minimize pseudo-regret, defined as the anticipated revenue shortfall compared to an omniscient entity aware of the true demand model. We explore a sparse set of demand interactions among products to analyze different connectivity traits of the product network. Specifically, we investigate three sparsity models: (1) $L_0$ sparsity, which limits the number of network connections, (2) off-diagonal sparsity, which restricts the intensity of cross-product price sensitivities, and (3) a novel concept of spectral sparsity, which limits the rate of decline of a similarity measure across network nodes. We introduce a dynamic pricing-and-learning strategy that integrates the optimism-in-the-face-of-uncertainty principle with PAC-Bayesian methods, demonstrating that this approach yields asymptotically optimal results relative to $N$ and $T$. Furthermore, we establish that under spectral and off-diagonal sparsity conditions, the seller can achieve a pseudo-regret that scales linearly with $N$, even in dense networks.

We show that language models, when pre-trained on codified (discretely-encoded) music audio, develop representations that prove valuable for various Music Information Retrieval (MIR) tasks. In particular, we investigate the representations produced by Jukebox (Dhariwal et al. 2020), a music generation system with a language model trained on codified audio from 1 million songs. To assess whether Jukebox's representations hold meaningful information for MIR, we utilize them as input features for training shallow models across multiple MIR tasks. Compared to representations from traditional MIR models pre-trained on tagging, Jukebox's representations as input features result in an average performance improvement of 30% across four MIR tasks: tagging, genre classification, emotion recognition, and key detection. Notably, for key detection, Jukebox's representations significantly outperform those from tagging-based pre-trained models, indicating that pre-training with codified audio language modeling might overcome limitations in traditional methods. We interpret the robust performance of Jukebox's representations as evidence that directly modeling audio, rather than relying on tags, yields more comprehensive representations for MIR.

In this study, we present Symplectic ODE-Net (SymODEN), a deep learning approach designed to deduce the dynamics of a physical system, described by an ordinary differential equation (ODE), using observed state trajectories. To enhance generalization with limited training data, SymODEN integrates specific inductive biases by constructing its computation graph with a physics-informed perspective. Specifically, we impose Hamiltonian dynamics with control to transparently capture the underlying dynamics, enabling insights into critical physical properties of the system, such as mass and potential energy. Furthermore, we introduce a parametrization method that maintains this Hamiltonian structure even when the generalized coordinate data resides in a high-dimensional space or when only velocity data, rather than generalized momentum, is available. By providing interpretable and physically consistent models for physical systems, this framework paves the way for developing innovative model-based control strategies.

We present the chi-square test neural network, a single hidden layer backpropagation neural network that employs the chi-square test theorem to reformulate both the cost function and the error function. The weights and thresholds are adjusted through the conventional backpropagation algorithm. This novel method offers the benefit of ensuring uniform data distribution across training and testing sets. It is applicable to binary classification tasks. Experimental outcomes using real-world datasets demonstrate that this algorithm markedly enhances classification accuracy when compared to similar methods.

Current machine translation systems, whether phrase-based or neural, predominantly depend on word-level modeling with explicit segmentation. This paper poses a critical question: is it possible for neural machine translation to produce a character sequence without explicit segmentation? To explore this, we assess an attention-based encoder-decoder framework featuring a subword-level encoder and a character-level decoder across four language pairs—En-Cs, En-De, En-Ru, and En-Fi—utilizing parallel corpora from WMT'15. Our findings reveal that models equipped with a character-level decoder consistently surpass those with a subword-level decoder across all four language pairs. Moreover, ensembles of neural models with character-level decoders surpass the top-performing non-neural machine translation systems for En-Cs, En-De, and En-Fi, and show comparable results for En-Ru.

Random feature maps are a common tool in contemporary statistical machine learning, extending the concept of random projections through complex, often challenging-to-analyze nonlinear operators. In this study, we utilize the "concentration" effect from random matrix theory to conduct a spectral analysis of the Gram matrix associated with these random feature maps, specifically for Gaussian mixture models that are both high-dimensional and large in sample size. Our findings contribute to a more profound insight into how nonlinearity interacts with data statistics, thus enabling improved optimization of random feature-based methods.

The partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) serves as a robust foundational model for robotic decision-making in uncertain environments. However, the computational demands of POMDP planning escalate significantly when extended planning periods are necessary. Although temporally-extended macro-actions can reduce the planning horizon and enhance computational efficiency, the challenge lies in developing effective macro-actions. This paper introduces the Macro-Action Generator-Critic (MAGIC), a novel approach for offline learning of macro-actions tailored for online POMDP planning. MAGIC trains a macro-action generator from end to end, utilizing feedback from an online planner’s performance. During real-time planning, this generator dynamically produces context-specific macro-actions based on the robot’s belief and environmental factors. Evaluations of MAGIC in simulated environments and on an actual robot across various long-term planning tasks demonstrate that these learned macro-actions substantially outperform both basic actions and manually designed macro-actions in online planning scenarios.

Creating text from structured data, such as tables, plays a crucial role in numerous natural language processing applications, including question answering and dialogue systems. Recent research has leveraged neural language models and encoder-decoder architectures for converting tables into text. Nevertheless, these neural network approaches often overlook the sequencing of content during the text generation process. In contrast, when humans compose a summary from a table, they typically prioritize the order of information before crafting their sentences. For instance, in a biographical text, a person’s nationality is usually mentioned prior to their profession. In this study, we introduce a novel order-planning text generation model that accounts for the relationships between various data fields, utilizing these connections to produce more coherent and fluid text. Our experiments on the WikiBio dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior methods, as evidenced by substantially improved BLEU, ROUGE, and NIST scores.

This paper introduces the Pressure Ulcers Online Website, a pioneering platform designed to assist individuals in detecting, understanding, and managing pressure ulcers. It explains the motivations behind the project's creation and serves as a primary hub for pressure ulcer analysis and continuous research. By integrating cutting-edge technologies such as convolutional neural networks and transfer learning, combined with comprehensive web technologies, the platform enables the analysis of pressure ulcers and the dissemination of results. Through ongoing collaborations, future iterations of the system will incorporate decision support tools to detail the intricate features of pressure ulcers and offer guidance on wound care across diverse user groups. Ultimately, this initiative aims to increase awareness and provide support for those affected by or caring for individuals with pressure ulcers.

This paper introduces a novel Grounded Language-Image Pre-training (GLIP) model designed to develop object-level, language-aware, and semantically rich visual representations. GLIP integrates object detection and phrase grounding during pre-training, offering two key advantages: 1) it enables learning from both detection and grounding datasets, enhancing performance in both areas and establishing a robust grounding model; 2) by autonomously generating grounding boxes through self-training, GLIP utilizes vast image-text pairs to enrich the semantic depth of the learned representations. For our experiments, GLIP was pre-trained on 27 million grounding data points, comprising 3 million human-annotated and 24 million web-sourced image-text pairs. The resulting representations exhibit exceptional zero-shot and few-shot transfer capabilities across various object-level recognition tasks. Specifically: 1) When assessed directly on COCO and LVIS datasets (without prior exposure to COCO images during pre-training), GLIP records 49.8 AP and 26.9 AP respectively, outperforming numerous supervised benchmarks. 2) Post fine-tuning on COCO, GLIP reaches 60.8 AP on the validation set and 61.5 AP on the test-dev set, exceeding previous state-of-the-art results. 3) When applied to 13 downstream object detection tasks, a 1-shot GLIP performs comparably to the fully-supervised Dynamic Head. The code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/GLIP.

The integration of automated condition monitoring and workpiece inspection is crucial for ensuring both high quality and high efficiency in manufacturing processes. Recent advancements in machine learning have significantly enhanced autonomous process oversight. However, as these models grow in complexity and capability, they often become less transparent and harder to interpret. A key challenge lies in monitoring these machine learning systems during live operation and issuing alerts for events that could degrade model performance. Specifically, supervised classifiers are generally designed with the expectation of a stable data distribution. For instance, a visual inspection system trained to identify specific material surface defects may fail to adapt to or even detect gradual shifts in data distribution—known as "data drift"—such as the appearance of new defect types. This can result in harmful misclassifications, like categorizing samples from new defect categories as defect-free. Therefore, it is critical to implement real-time performance tracking for classifiers to detect the potential emergence of new error categories and to address them promptly.

Are machine learning models used for recommendations susceptible to manipulation? Although this issue has been examined with manually crafted fake user profiles, the impact of machine-learned adversarial attacks remains uncharted. This paper seeks to address this gap by introducing a framework for creating fake user profiles that, when integrated into the training process of a recommendation system, fulfill an adversarial purpose while appearing identical to genuine profiles. We conceptualize this approach as a recurring general-sum game involving two entities: an unaware recommendation system, denoted as $R$, and an adversarial fake user generator, denoted as $A$, with dual objectives. The first objective (G1) is to ensure that the rating distribution of fake users closely mirrors that of real users, while the second objective (G2) focuses on optimizing a specific adversarial intent, $f_A$, such as degrading the top-K recommendation accuracy of $R$ for a selected group of users. We present a learning framework designed to meet both objectives and conduct comprehensive experiments across various attack scenarios to demonstrate the susceptibility of recommendation systems.

Acoustic monitoring for detecting machine faults is a burgeoning field of research that has shown significant promise for industrial applications. However, gathering sufficient data to identify every possible fault in a machine remains a challenge. To address this, innovative algorithms have been developed that rely solely on data from normal operating conditions to conduct unsupervised anomaly detection. A major obstacle in creating these algorithms is the presence of noise in the signals, which can degrade the effectiveness of anomaly detection. In this study, we introduce a robust, data-driven, and quasi non-parametric denoising technique for spectral data, utilizing a tensor decomposition method known as Non-negative Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition. This approach is especially suitable for machines producing consistent sound patterns. Through a case study using the Malfunctioning Industrial Machine Investigation and Inspection (MIMII) baseline, we illustrate how our denoising method significantly enhances the performance of unsupervised anomaly detection. Such techniques contribute to making sound-based monitoring of industrial processes more dependable.

Deep learning classifiers play a crucial role in supporting human decision-making, making user trust in these models paramount. Trust often stems from predictable behavior, meaning that users expect consistent outputs for identical inputs, particularly when the outputs are correct. This paper explores model behavior during periodic retraining of deployed models, where successive model generations may assign different labels to the same input. We introduce formal definitions for consistency and correct-consistency in learning models. Our analysis demonstrates that the consistency and correct-consistency of an ensemble learner are at least as high as the average of individual learners, and correct-consistency can be enhanced with a certain probability by combining learners whose accuracy matches or exceeds the average accuracy of the ensemble's components. To substantiate this theory, we utilize three datasets and two cutting-edge deep learning classifiers, while also proposing an efficient dynamic snapshot ensemble method to highlight its effectiveness.

In the realm of modern large-scale data analysis, there is a critical need to strategically select samples for manual review. This process often focuses on identifying significant mislabeled samples or critical weaknesses that could be exploited in adversarial attacks. To address the challenge of pinpointing these crucial samples amidst vast datasets—akin to finding a needle in a haystack—we have developed an innovative, scalable adaptation of Cook's distance. This traditional statistical method is used to detect samples that have a disproportionately large effect on the fit of a regression model and, consequently, its predictions.

To adapt this method for handling extremely large and high-dimensional datasets, we introduce a novel algorithm named "influence sketching." This approach integrates random projections into the calculation of influence, specifically by computing influence scores using a randomly projected pseudo-dataset derived from a post-convergence Generalized Linear Model (GLM). We demonstrate the efficacy of influence sketching in identifying influential samples through its application to a malware detection dataset comprising over 2 million executable files, each characterized by nearly 100,000 features. Our findings reveal that randomly removing about 10% of the training samples results in a minimal drop in predictive accuracy, from 99.47% to 99.45%. In stark contrast, removing the same proportion of samples based on high influence sketch scores significantly diminishes predictive accuracy.

The application of machine learning for network traffic classification has been extensively explored. However, most current methods focus on classifying complete traffic flows, which poses significant practical challenges. At a network router, packets must be processed with minimal delay, meaning the classifier cannot afford to wait for a flow to conclude before making a decision. Additionally, implementing a complex machine learning algorithm directly within the router can be computationally prohibitive. In this paper, we proposes the Flow-Packet Hybrid Traffic Classification (FPHTC) approach, where the router decides on a per-packet basis using a routing policy crafted by transferring knowledge from an external flow-based classifier. We examine the generalization bound of FPHTC and demonstrate its superiority over traditional packet-based traffic classification methods. Experimental results using a real-world traffic dataset are presented to showcase FPHTC's classification effectiveness. The findings indicate that FPHTC adapts well to changes in traffic patterns and can be implemented with constrained computational resources.

In this work, we introduce a fresh method for reconstructing multivariate functions from training data by determining an appropriate network architecture and initialization through polynomial-based approximations. Training deep neural networks with gradient descent can be seen as navigating the network's parameters across the loss landscape to reduce the loss function. The choice of initial parameters is crucial for descent-based iterative training methods. Our approach results in a network that starts from a polynomial representation of the training data. The primary benefit of this method is that, from this starting point, the network can be further refined using conventional training techniques. As the network initially approximates the data, subsequent training is more likely to yield parameters that correspond to a favorable local minimum. We elaborate on the theoretical framework required to build such networks and explore various numerical examples, demonstrating that our method successfully generates networks that can be effectively trained from the initialized state to achieve better approximations for a wide range of target functions.

Biological perception often employs attention mechanisms to focus on specific subsets of sensory data for detailed processing, as it would be impractical to analyze all inputs equally. In the field of computer vision, while soft attention—which adjusts the importance of information through re-weighting and aggregation without discarding any data—has seen considerable success, hard attention, which deliberately excludes certain information, remains underexplored. In this study, we present a novel hard attention approach that demonstrates highly competitive results on a newly released visual question answering dataset, matching or even exceeding the performance of comparable soft attention models by completely disregarding some features. Despite the common belief that hard attention mechanisms are non-differentiable, we discovered that the magnitude of features corresponds to their semantic importance, offering a valuable indicator for our attention selection process. Additionally, since hard attention prioritizes critical input features, it proves to be more efficient than similar soft attention methods. This efficiency is particularly crucial for recent techniques involving non-local pairwise operations, where both computational and memory demands increase quadratically with the number of features.

We investigate the optimization of finite sums of geodesically smooth functions on Riemannian manifolds. While variance reduction techniques for finite-sum optimization have gained significant interest in recent years, prior studies have been confined to vector space problems. We propose Riemannian SVRG (RSVRG), a novel variance-reduced optimization method tailored for Riemannian settings. Our analysis of RSVRG covers both geodesically convex and nonconvex (smooth) functions, demonstrating that RSVRG retains the benefits of the standard SVRG approach, albeit with convergence influenced by the manifold's curvature. To the best of our knowledge, RSVRG represents the first provably efficient stochastic Riemannian optimization method. Additionally, this work provides the first non-asymptotic complexity analysis for nonconvex Riemannian optimization, a contribution that is original even in the batch context. These findings have broad implications, including a Riemannian viewpoint on variance-reduced PCA, which facilitates a concise and clear convergence analysis.

In this research, we explore the challenge of identifying cluster heads in a two-tier unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarm network (USNET) comprising multiple UAV clusters, where the inherent follow strategy (IFS) of lower-tier follower UAVs (FUAVs) relative to upper-tier cluster head UAVs (HUAVs) remains unknown. Initially, we introduce a graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (GASSL) designed to identify HUAVs within a single UAV cluster, simultaneously adapting to the IFS. Subsequently, to address HUAV detection across multiple UAV clusters in the USNET, we extend GASSL into a multi-cluster graph attention self-supervised learning algorithm (MC-GASSL). This advanced algorithm employs a gated recurrent unit (GRU)-based metric learning approach to segment the USNET into clusters and applies GASSL to pinpoint HUAVs within each cluster. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that GASSL achieves an average accuracy of over 98% in detecting HUAVs in single clusters across diverse IFSs. Additionally, simulation outcomes reveal that MC-GASSL enhances clustering purity in the USNET by at least 10% compared to conventional clustering methods. Moreover, MC-GASSL effectively identifies all HUAVs in USNETs with varying IFSs and cluster counts, maintaining low detection redundancy.

Machine learning models are frequently utilized with human brain imaging data to link brain function or structure to behavior, health, or other personal characteristics. These models often depend on simplified, low-dimensional maps created through intricate processing pipelines. Yet, the numerical instabilities in these pipelines can compromise the accuracy of these maps and introduce computational bias. To address this, Monte Carlo Arithmetic was employed to add controlled numerical noise to a structural connectome estimation pipeline, generating a variety of plausible networks for each sample. The diversity among these altered networks was incorporated into an expanded dataset used for age classification. Our analysis revealed that resampling brain networks through multiple numerically perturbed versions enhanced performance across all classifiers, preprocessing methods, and dimensionality reduction approaches tested. Notably, this improvement does not require extensive perturbations, indicating that even slight numerical disturbances can introduce valuable variability, which can be effectively utilized in the models developed afterward.

Variable selection plays a pivotal role in analyzing high-dimensional data, prompting the creation of numerous algorithms. While an ideal variable selection algorithm should be flexible, scalable, and theoretically robust, most current methods struggle to embody all these traits simultaneously. This article introduces a novel three-step variable selection algorithm that incorporates kernel-based estimation of the regression function and its gradients, alongside hard thresholding. A primary benefit of this approach is its lack of specific model assumptions, accommodation of diverse predictor effects, computational scalability, and achievement of asymptotic sparsistency. The algorithm is versatile enough to be applied within any reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) using various kernel functions and can be easily modified for interaction selection. Its computational demand grows linearly with data dimension and can be enhanced through parallel computing. Under mild conditions, the algorithm's sparsistency is proven for general RKHS, encompassing linear and Gaussian kernels as specific instances. The efficacy of this method is further demonstrated through an array of simulated and real-world examples.

Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) excel at extracting distinctive features, they frequently struggle to adapt to new, unseen domains. Domain generalization seeks to overcome this limitation by training a model on multiple source domains to perform effectively on any unfamiliar domain. This paper introduces a unique method called MixStyle, which probabilistically blends instance-level feature statistics from training samples across different source domains. The inspiration for MixStyle stems from the recognition that a visual domain is often tied to the stylistic elements of images (such as photos versus sketches). These stylistic elements are typically encoded in the lower layers of a CNN, where our style-mixing technique is applied. By blending the styles of training samples, MixStyle implicitly creates new domains, enhancing the variety of source domains and improving the model's ability to generalize. Seamlessly integrating with mini-batch training, MixStyle is also remarkably simple to implement. Its efficacy is validated across diverse applications, including category classification, instance retrieval, and reinforcement learning.

In computed tomography (CT), automatic exposure control (AEC) is commonly employed to minimize radiation dose exposure for patients. For organ-specific AEC, an initial CT reconstruction is required to determine organ shapes for dose optimization, allowing only a limited number of projections for real-time reconstruction. This study explores the effectiveness of automated transform by manifold approximation (AUTOMAP) in these scenarios. As a preliminary evaluation, we assess its performance using the MNIST dataset, randomly dividing the dataset of all 10 digits into training and test sets. The AUTOMAP model is trained for image reconstruction using either 2 or 4 projections directly. Test outcomes show that AUTOMAP successfully reconstructs most digits, achieving false rates of 1.6% and 6.8% respectively. In a follow-up experiment, the MNIST dataset is divided such that the training set includes only 9 digits, while the test set comprises solely the excluded digit, for example, "2". Results from the test reveal that the digit "2" is often misidentified as "3" or "5" when reconstructed from 2 projections, resulting in a false rate of 94.4%. For its application in medical imaging, AUTOMAP is similarly trained on patient data.

Deep learning holds immense promise for medical imaging applications. However, the varying incidence rates of different diseases result in imbalanced class frequencies within medical image datasets, which often leads to reduced accuracy for rarer conditions. A potential remedy involves augmenting data for these less common classes with synthetic images generated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Nevertheless, traditional GANs still need a substantial number of images to train effectively. To address this challenge, we introduce the General-to-detailed GAN (GDGAN), which consists of two sequentially linked GANs—one handling general labels and the other focusing on detailed labels. The GDGAN successfully generated a variety of medical images, and the model trained on the enhanced dataset surpassed other networks employing conventional techniques in terms of the Area-Under-Curve (AUC) of the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve.

Deep convolutional networks frequently incorporate additive constants, known as "bias" terms, into their convolution processes to allow for a broader array of functional mappings. These biases also aid in training by adjusting for the average response across batches of training images, a technique integral to "batch normalization." Cutting-edge blind denoising approaches, such as DnCNN, appear to depend on these terms for effective results. However, our findings reveal that these networks tend to overfit to the specific noise levels they are trained on, resulting in significant performance drops when applied to noise levels beyond the training spectrum. On the other hand, a network without biases—achieved by eliminating constant terms from all layers, including those in batch normalization—demonstrates strong adaptability across various noise levels while maintaining top-tier performance within the trained range. At a local level, the bias-free network processes the noisy image linearly, facilitating straightforward analysis of network behavior using conventional linear-algebraic methods. Such analyses offer insights into the network's operations, portraying them as nonlinear adaptive filtering and projection onto a combination of low-dimensional subspaces, thereby linking this learning-based approach to traditional denoising techniques.

Recent studies on overparametrized learning theory have aimed to provide generalization guarantees within the interpolating regime. While such guarantees have been proven for several standard method categories, ensemble methods have remained unaddressed until now. We introduce an ensemble classification approach that not only interpolates the training data but also maintains consistency across a wide range of data distributions. For this purpose, we introduce the manifold-Hilbert kernel, tailored for data on a Riemannian manifold. We demonstrate that kernel smoothing regression employing the manifold-Hilbert kernel achieves weak consistency as per the framework of Devroye et al. 1998. Specifically on the sphere, we illustrate that the manifold-Hilbert kernel can be expressed as a weighted random partition kernel, which emerges as an infinite collection of classifiers based on partitioning.

In this research, we address the challenge of constrained robust (min-max) optimization within a black-box scenario, where the optimizer lacks access to the objective function's gradients but can evaluate its values. We introduce a systematic optimization framework that combines a zeroth-order (ZO) gradient estimator with an alternating projected stochastic gradient descent-ascent approach. The ZO estimator demands only a limited number of function evaluations, while the descent/ascent method requires merely a single-step update. We demonstrate that our proposed framework, named ZO-Min-Max, achieves a sub-linear convergence rate under moderate conditions and effectively handles increasing problem sizes. On the application front, we uncover a significant link between black-box min-max optimization and black-box evasion and poisoning attacks in adversarial machine learning (ML). Our empirical tests in these scenarios confirm the efficacy of our method and its ability to scale to problem dimensions that render recent black-box solvers impractical.

To keep pace with the explosion of available data, there has been a growing focus on enhancing the efficiency of data analysis and machine learning libraries. While significant progress has been made in conventional array-based computing, these methods are often constrained by the limitations of a single computational node. As a result, new strategies are needed to leverage distributed resources, such as distributed memory architectures. In response to this need, we present HeAT, a numerical programming framework designed for large-scale parallel processing with a user-friendly, NumPy-like API. HeAT employs PyTorch as a local eager execution engine on each node and manages workload distribution across vast high-performance computing systems using MPI. It supports both fundamental array operations and a variety of advanced algorithms. With HeAT, users familiar with NumPy can fully utilize their computational resources, greatly simplifying distributed data analysis. Compared to similar frameworks, HeAT delivers performance improvements of up to two orders of magnitude.

This paper aims to evaluate and contrast various popular Bayesian model selection techniques in real-world model selection scenarios, identifying their distinctions and suggesting optimal strategies. Our analysis centers on variable subset selection for regression and classification tasks, incorporating multiple numerical tests with both synthetic and actual data. The findings indicate that optimizing a utility measure like the cross-validation (CV) score often results in overfitting, primarily due to the high variance in utility estimates when data is limited. Such optimization can introduce significant selection-induced bias and overly optimistic performance assessments for the chosen model. From a predictive perspective, superior outcomes are achieved by embracing model uncertainty through the creation of a comprehensive encompassing model, exemplified by the Bayesian model averaging approach across potential models. If this encompassing model proves overly intricate, it can be effectively streamlined using the projection method, where the comprehensive model's information is transferred to simpler submodels. This technique demonstrates markedly less susceptibility to overfitting compared to CV-score-based selection. In general, the projection method seems to surpass both the maximum a posteriori model and the selection of the most probable model in performance.

Extracting features directly from data has proven more effective than relying on manually designed features for numerous machine learning applications. In the field of music information retrieval (MIR), features derived from windowed spectrograms often exhibit significant variability under transformations such as transposition or time-shifting. These variations are problematic when they are not relevant to the specific MIR task at hand. To address this, we introduce a novel architecture called the Complex Autoencoder (CAE), designed to learn features that remain unchanged under orthogonal transformations. By projecting signals onto complex basis functions derived through the CAE, we create a "magnitude space" that is invariant to transformations and a "phase space" that varies with them. The phase space proves valuable for deducing transformations between pairs of data. Leveraging the invariance of the magnitude space, we have achieved top-tier performance in tasks like audio-to-score alignment and the identification of repeated sections in audio. A PyTorch implementation of the CAE, along with the method for repeated section discovery, is accessible online.

This study focuses on the challenge of learning real-time occupancy levels in dynamic settings and forecasting future occupancy. Given the intricacies of many real-world scenarios, like urban roads or densely populated zones, integrating temporal dynamics into static occupancy models in an effective and resilient manner is difficult. We introduce a technique to account for the spatial uncertainty of moving entities and embed this uncertainty data into a continuous occupancy map, depicted within a detailed, high-dimensional feature space. Tests conducted with LIDAR data have confirmed the algorithm's capability to perform in real time.

This research presents a method for learning a policy for a dynamical system that ensures both safety and goal attainment with provable guarantees. Safety, in this context, refers to a policy that prevents the system from entering unsafe states, while goal attainment implies that the trajectory of the controlled system will eventually converge to a designated goal region, extending the concept of stability. We achieve this dual objective by simultaneously learning two certificate functions: a barrier function to ensure safety and a specialized Lyapunov-like function to meet the goal-reaching condition, both implemented using neural networks. The effectiveness of this approach in developing policies that are both safe and goal-oriented is demonstrated across various systems, including pendulums, cart-poles, and UAVs.

In this research, we introduce a more challenging and realistic framework for intent detection within natural language understanding, termed Generalized Few-Shot Intent Detection (GFSID). GFSID is designed to identify intents from a combined label space that includes both well-represented existing intents with ample labeled data and new intents with limited examples per category. To tackle this issue, we present a new model called Conditional Text Generation with BERT (CG-BERT). This model capitalizes on a robust pre-trained language model to produce text based on specified intent labels. Through the use of variational inference to model utterance distributions, CG-BERT is capable of creating varied utterances for new intents, despite having access to only a small number of examples. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that CG-BERT delivers top-tier performance on the GFSID task in both 1-shot and 5-shot scenarios across two authentic datasets.

Customers frequently encounter various online digital advertising platforms, including email marketing, display ads, and paid search engine marketing, as they progress towards making a purchase or subscription (commonly referred to as conversion). Marketers collect comprehensive data on customer journeys to evaluate the effectiveness of each advertising medium. Understanding the impact of these channels is crucial for decisions related to budget distribution and inventory pricing. While numerous simplistic rule-based and data-driven algorithmic approaches are common in the marketing industry, they often fail to account for complexities such as channel interactions, temporal dynamics, and individual user traits. In this paper, we introduce a cutting-edge attribution algorithm leveraging deep learning to analyze the influence of each advertising channel. We unveil the Deep Neural Net With Attention Multi-Touch Attribution (DNAMTA) model, which operates in a supervised learning framework to predict whether a sequence of interactions culminates in conversion. This approach provides profound insights into the dynamic interplay among media channels. Additionally, DNAMTA integrates user-context data, including demographics and behavioral patterns, as control variables to minimize biases in estimating media impacts. We conducted computational experiments using a vast real-world marketing dataset to validate the efficacy of our proposed model.

Spatial clustering methods excel in reducing multi-channel noise across diverse microphone setups, yet struggle to integrate comprehensive speech and noise models. Conversely, LSTM neural networks have proven effective in distinguishing speech from noise in single-channel audio, but they often fail to fully utilize the data from multi-channel recordings. This paper combines these two methodologies by training LSTM speech models to refine the masks produced by the Model-based EM Source Separation and Localization (MESSL) spatial clustering technique. This integration harnesses both the robust spatial separation and adaptability of multi-channel clustering and the detailed signal modeling capabilities of multiple parallel single-channel LSTM speech enhancers. Experiments conducted on the CHiME-3 dataset, which consists of noisy tablet recordings, demonstrate that our approach enhances speech quality, as evaluated by the Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) metric, and lowers the word error rate of the baseline CHiME-3 speech recognition system compared to the standard BeamformIt beamformer.

Noise significantly contributes to the poor quality of Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) images. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have shown exceptional capability in image denoising. Nevertheless, denoising OCT images remains a formidable challenge as many existing neural network approaches depend on extensive labeled data, which can be time-consuming and costly to acquire. Additionally, these CNN-based methods often require a large number of parameters and sophisticated tuning techniques, demanding substantial hardware resources. To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach called Dual-Merged Cycle-WGAN, based on Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Networks, for retinal OCT image denoising. This method excels even with limited unlabeled training data. Our model integrates two Cycle-GAN networks with enhanced generators, discriminators, and Wasserstein loss to ensure training stability and superior performance. By employing an image merge technique between the two Cycle-GAN networks, our model captures finer details, leading to improved training outcomes. The efficacy and versatility of our proposed network are validated through ablation studies and comparative analyses. When benchmarked against other leading techniques, our unsupervised approach achieves the best subjective visual quality and superior objective evaluation metrics.

When a neural network is used in real-world scenarios, it might encounter inputs that differ from the distribution of its training data. Numerous studies have shown that it is relatively simple to identify or create inputs for which a neural network shows high confidence but is incorrect. Generative models are often considered resistant to such erroneous confidence, as they can model the density of input features to identify novel, out-of-distribution inputs. However, this paper questions that belief. Our findings reveal that the density representations learned by flow-based models, VAEs, and PixelCNNs fail to differentiate between images of everyday objects like dogs, trucks, and horses (from CIFAR-10) and images of house numbers (from SVHN), often assigning higher likelihood to the latter despite being trained on the former. Additionally, this pattern holds true across various well-known image datasets, including FashionMNIST versus MNIST, CelebA versus SVHN, and ImageNet versus CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, or SVHN. To explore this surprising trend, we specifically analyze flow-based generative models, which are trained and assessed using exact marginal likelihood. End-to-end (E2E) models are frequently paired with language models (LMs) through shallow fusion to enhance their overall performance and improve the recognition of uncommon words. However, previous research indicates that LMs can inadvertently retain rare or unique sequences from their training data. In this study, we develop a framework to identify the memorization of arbitrary textual sequences (referred to as canaries) within the LM training data, using only black-box (query-based) access to an LM-integrated speech recognizer, rather than direct access to the LM itself. We demonstrate that, in a production-level Conformer RNN-T E2E model combined with a Transformer LM, it is feasible to detect the memorization of canaries that appear only once in a training dataset of 300 million examples. With a focus on privacy protection, we further illustrate that such memorization can be substantially diminished through per-example gradient clipping during LM training, without sacrificing overall performance.

We investigate the issue of universal function approximation using two-layer neural networks with random weights that are "almost Gaussian" as measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence. This inquiry is inspired by recent studies on lazy training, where stochastic gradient descent results in minimal deviation of weights from their initial i.i.d. Gaussian distribution. Initially, we explore the mean-field limit, substituting the finite set of neurons in the hidden layer with a continuous ensemble, and demonstrate that our issue translates into a global minimization problem of a free-energy functional within the realm of probability measures over weights. This functional balances the $L^2$ approximation error with the KL divergence relative to a centered Gaussian prior. We identify the sole global minimizer and subsequently develop a controlled nonlinear dynamic within the space of probability measures over weights, addressing a McKean--Vlasov optimal control problem. This control challenge bears similarity to the Schrödinger bridge (or entropic optimal transport) problem, and its value corresponds proportionally to the free energy's minimum. Lastly, we illustrate that in the lazy training regime, SGD—achievable through combined adjustment of the Gaussian prior's variance and the entropic parameter—maintains this behavior.

A key underlying objective in research on deep generative models is to enable the creation of new samples that differ from those encountered during training. In this study, we explore the extent to which this capability is present in popular variational autoencoder (VAE) frameworks. VAEs are designed to optimize a lower bound on the log marginal likelihood, suggesting that, with a sufficiently powerful decoder, they are prone to overfitting the training data. In the extreme scenario of a decoder with limitless capacity, the ideal generative model becomes a uniform mixture of the training data. More broadly, an optimal decoder would produce a weighted average of training examples, with weights influenced by their closeness in the latent space. This observation prompts the hypothesis that, with high-capacity encoders and decoders, the VAE decoder will essentially perform nearest-neighbor matching based on latent space coordinates. To validate this hypothesis, we examine generalization using the MNIST dataset. We assess generalization both to novel instances of familiar classes and to entirely unseen classes excluded from the training set. In this article, we introduce CANDIES (Combined Approach for Novelty Detection in Intelligent Embedded Systems), an innovative method for identifying novelty in technical systems. We posit that multiple processes interact within a technical system. By monitoring these processes through sensors, we can represent the collected data (samples) using a probabilistic model. Ideally, the components of the parametric mixture density model we employ align with the actual processes in the real world. Over time, during operation, unforeseen processes, such as unexpected failures, may arise within these systems. This results in the observation of new types of samples, necessitating model updates. CANDIES utilizes Gaussian mixture models, which are also applicable for classification tasks. New processes might appear in areas of the model's input space with sparse prior data (low-density regions) or in areas abundant with data (high-density regions). The latter scenario poses greater challenges, although most current approaches target the former. Detecting novelty in both low- and high-density regions demands distinct strategies. Through CANDIES, we present a novel technique for identifying new processes in high-density regions using a rapid online approach.

Mini-batch Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with momentum is a crucial method for training large predictive models. In this study, we introduce a novel analytical framework to examine mini-batch SGD applied to linear models, considering various momenta and batch sizes. Central to our approach is the representation of the loss value sequence through its generating function, which we express in a simplified form by assuming a diagonal approximation for the second moments of model weights. Through analysis of this generating function, we derive insights into convergence conditions, the model's phase structure, and optimal learning configurations. For instance, we demonstrate that 1) the optimization path can transition from a "signal-dominated" to a "noise-dominated" phase at a predictable time scale; 2) during the "signal-dominated" phase (but not the "noise-dominated" phase), opting for a high effective learning rate is advantageous, though it must be capped for any given batch size to prevent divergence; 3) the best convergence rate is attainable with a negative momentum. Our theoretical findings are substantiated by thorough experiments on MNIST and synthetic datasets, showing strong quantitative correlation.

We present a model-free relax-and-round algorithm for k-means clustering, building on a semidefinite relaxation proposed by Peng and Wei. This algorithm treats the SDP output as a refined, noise-reduced version of the input data and subsequently converts this output into a definitive clustering. We offer a general approach to establishing performance guarantees for this method and evaluate its effectiveness within the framework of subgaussian mixture models. Additionally, we explore the inherent challenges in estimating Gaussian centers using k-means clustering to benchmark our approximation guarantee against the theoretically ideal k-means clustering solution.

Supervised learning approaches for segmentation generally demand a substantial volume of annotated training data to perform effectively during testing. However, in medical contexts, assembling such extensive datasets is impractical due to the high cost and time required to obtain annotated samples from experts. As a result, various strategies have been explored in the literature to facilitate learning with fewer annotated examples. Despite these efforts, the methods proposed have not significantly surpassed the results of basic random data augmentation in image segmentation, where even random augmentations fail to achieve high precision. In this study, we introduce a novel task-oriented data augmentation technique tailored for scenarios with scarce labeled data. This method employs a synthetic data generator specifically fine-tuned for the segmentation task. Our approach incorporates a generator that accounts for variations in intensity and shape through two types of transformations: additive intensity adjustments and deformation fields. These transformations are refined using both labeled and unlabeled data within a semi-supervised framework. Our tests on three medical datasets—cardiac, prostate, and pancreas—demonstrate that this method markedly improves upon traditional augmentation and semi-supervised techniques for image segmentation under limited annotation conditions. The code for this project is publicly accessible at https://github.com/krishnabits001/task$\_$driven$\_$data$\_$augmentation.

In recent years, machine learning has gained significant traction within the realm of lattice field theories. A key aspect of these theories is the incorporation of symmetries into neural network designs, which can greatly enhance performance and generalizability. One critical symmetry often present in physical systems on a lattice with periodic boundary conditions is equivariance under spacetime translations. This study explores the benefits of using translationally equivariant neural networks compared to non-equivariant ones. We focus on a complex scalar field with quartic interaction on a two-dimensional lattice in the flux representation, where the networks perform various regression and classification tasks. Through a systematic search, we identify promising architectures for both equivariant and non-equivariant models. Our findings reveal that, in most tasks, the top-performing equivariant architectures consistently outperform and generalize better than their non-equivariant counterparts. This advantage extends not only to physical parameters outside the training set but also to varying lattice sizes.

This paper illustrates the application of a Transformer Neural Network in learning a Generative Model from a single path-based example image. Additionally, it explores the creation of a dataset from this example image and demonstrates how the model can produce a diverse collection of altered images that maintain the style and essence of the original.

The newly introduced "generalized min-max" (GMM) kernel can be effectively linearized, offering valuable applications in large-scale statistical learning and rapid near neighbor search. A thorough comparison was conducted between the linearized GMM kernel and the linearized radial basis function (RBF) kernel. Across numerous classification tasks, the tuning-free GMM kernel surprisingly holds its own against the finely tuned RBF kernel. However, it is reasonable to anticipate further enhancements to the GMM kernel by incorporating tuning parameters. This paper explores three straightforward designs of adjustable GMM kernels: (i) the exponentiated-GMM (eGMM) kernel, (ii) the powered-GMM (pGMM) kernel, and (iii) the exponentiated-powered-GMM (epGMM) kernel. The pGMM kernel retains the ability to be efficiently linearized by adapting the original hashing method used for the GMM kernel. Testing on approximately 60 publicly accessible classification datasets confirms that these tunable GMM kernels generally outperform the standard GMM kernel. On certain datasets, the performance gains are remarkably substantial. For instance, on 11 well-known datasets commonly used to evaluate deep learning algorithms and tree-based methods, our experiments demonstrate that the tunable GMM kernels are formidable rivals to both tree methods and deep networks.
