In the context of the Electronic Health Record (EHR), research ranks as a tertiary concern behind the primary focuses of patient care and billing. Consequently, the data within EHRs lacks standardization and is not formatted in a way that readily supports machine learning methodologies. Variability in data can arise from numerous factors, including diverse input styles among individuals and variations in clinical decision-making, such as the selection of specific lab tests. Only a small number of patient records meet research-quality annotation standards, which restricts sample sizes and creates an evolving benchmark for quality. Understanding disease progression over time is critical for many conditions, yet numerous machine learning algorithms depend on data captured at a single point in time to form usable vectors. Additionally, algorithms that yield opaque, "black box" outcomes fail to offer the transparency necessary for clinical acceptance. This chapter explores these obstacles and other issues related to the application of machine learning to structured EHR data, encompassing elements like Patient Demographics, Family History, Medication Information, Vital Signs, Laboratory Tests, and Genetic Testing. While the discussion excludes feature extraction from supplementary sources such as imaging data or unstructured patient notes, the methods considered can incorporate features derived from these additional data types.

Chemical kinetics and reaction engineering provide a phenomenological framework for unraveling reaction mechanisms, enhancing reaction efficiency, and systematically designing chemical processes. In this study, we employ feed-forward artificial neural networks as basis functions to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) constrained by differential algebraic equations (DAEs) that represent microkinetic models (MKMs). We introduce an algebraic framework for the mathematical representation and categorization of reaction networks, types of elementary reactions, and chemical species. Within this framework, we show that simultaneously training neural networks and kinetic model parameters in a regularized multi-objective optimization context enables solving the inverse problem by estimating kinetic parameters from synthetic experimental data. We evaluate various scenarios to determine the retrievability of kinetic parameters from transient kinetic data and test the methodology's robustness against statistical noise. This approach to solving inverse kinetic ODEs supports the clarification of reaction mechanisms using transient data.

In recent times, the learning management system (LMS) has become a cornerstone in educational environments ranging from primary to higher education, facilitating student administration, documentation, tracking, reporting, and the delivery of educational courses, training initiatives, and learning and development programs. With a focus on enhancing learning outcome evaluations, the challenge of generating exam scripts has garnered significant interest and research in recent years. However, this area of study remains in its nascent phase, presenting numerous opportunities for enhancing the quality of automatically generated exam scripts in various dimensions. Notably, two critical challenges have been largely overlooked by current methodologies. Firstly, for a given course, there is still no clear method to create an exam script that achieves a targeted distribution of student scores within a single class or across multiple classes. Secondly, despite its common occurrence in real-world scenarios, there remains a lack of understanding on how to produce a pair of high-quality exam scripts that are equivalent in terms of assessment (meaning student scores are comparable regardless of which script they take) yet feature distinctly different sets of questions. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces ExamGAN (Exam Script Generative Adversarial Network), a novel approach for crafting superior quality exam scripts. Furthermore, we extend this framework to T-ExamGAN (Twin-ExamGAN) to specifically tackle the generation of paired exam scripts.

Collaborative personalization, achieved through learned user representations (embeddings), can substantially enhance the prediction accuracy of neural-network-based models. We introduce Federated User Representation Learning (FURL), a straightforward, scalable, privacy-preserving, and resource-efficient method to apply existing neural personalization techniques within the Federated Learning (FL) framework. FURL categorizes model parameters into federated and private types. Private parameters, like individual user embeddings, are trained on local devices and, unlike federated parameters, are neither uploaded to nor averaged on the central server. We provide theoretical evidence that this division of parameters does not impede training for most personalization methods. Keeping user embeddings on local devices not only safeguards user privacy but also enhances memory locality for personalization compared to server-based training. Our evaluation of FURL on two datasets reveals significant improvements in model quality, with performance boosts of 8% and 51%, and results nearly equivalent to centralized training, showing only minor reductions of 0% and 4%. Additionally, we demonstrate that user embeddings developed in FL mirror those in centralized settings in structure, suggesting that FURL effectively learns collaboratively via shared parameters while maintaining user privacy.

Rural electrification requires cost-effective solutions like single wire earth return (SWER) networks. However, the increasing energy needs of remote users may soon outstrip the capacity of current lines. Additionally, high impedance arcing faults (HIF) in SWER systems pose a severe risk, as evidenced by devastating bushfires like the 2009 Black Saturday disaster. To address these challenges, a viable solution is to reconfigure existing systems into microgrids, using current SWER lines to link them. Creating such dependable networks with improved energy demand management hinges on implementing a comprehensive, network-wide condition monitoring system. As the primary contribution of this thesis, a distributed online monitoring platform is introduced, featuring power quality monitoring, real-time HIF detection, and transient classification for SWER networks. Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques are employed to identify faults and transients, achieving a remarkable HIF detection accuracy of 98.67% and a reduced detection latency of 115.2 ms. Additionally, a methodology for identifying remote consumer load types based on their transients is developed. An edge computing-based framework is proposed to support high-frequency analysis for load identification, with the approach being tested in real-time.

The effectiveness of semi-supervised learning hinges on its ability to scale to vast quantities of unlabeled data, which are essential for discerning the underlying manifold structure to enhance classification accuracy. However, calculating pairwise similarities across training data is often computationally infeasible for most input types, resulting in a lack of accessible semi-supervised learning methods or tools capable of handling tens of millions of data points or more. In this study, we embraced the concepts behind two low-rank label propagation algorithms, namely Global Linear Neighborhood Propagation (GLNP) and Kernel Nyström Approximation. We developed parallelized versions of these algorithms, enhanced by Nesterov's accelerated projected gradient descent, to create Big-data Label Propagation (BigLP). These parallel algorithms were evaluated on five real-world datasets, varying in size from 7,000 to 10,000,000, and a simulated dataset comprising 100,000,000 samples. Experimental results show that our BigLP implementation can efficiently scale to datasets with up to 100,000,000 samples and numerous features, while also markedly boosting prediction accuracy with only a minimal fraction of labeled data. These findings affirm that the BigLP implementation is not only highly scalable for big data applications but also proficient in leveraging unlabeled data for semi-supervised learning.

In numerous scientific domains, the need for high-dimensional integration is paramount. To address this, various numerical techniques have been devised for solving these intricate integrals. We present i-flow, a Python package designed for high-dimensional numerical integration through the use of normalizing flows. These flows are machine-learned, bijective transformations that bridge two distinct distributions. Additionally, i-flow enables the sampling of random points from complex, high-dimensional distributions. Comparative analysis reveals that i-flow surpasses other algorithms in the realm of high-dimensional numerical integration, particularly with correlated integrals. The i-flow package is openly accessible on GitLab at https://gitlab.com/i-flow/i-flow.

In the field of machine learning, likelihood-free inference pertains to conducting data-driven analysis without relying on an analytical formula. This discussion focuses on the use of Neural Spline Flows, a type of neural density estimation algorithm, in addressing the likelihood-free inference challenge for measuring neutrino oscillation parameters in Long Baseline neutrino experiments. A tailored approach for inferring physics parameters is introduced and implemented in the context of the muon neutrino disappearance analysis at the T2K experiment.

We introduce a unified framework that extends several loss functions, including Cauchy/Lorentzian, Geman-McClure, Welsch/Leclerc, generalized Charbonnier, Charbonnier/pseudo-Huber/L1-L2, and L2. By incorporating robustness as a flexible parameter, our proposed loss function enables the generalization of algorithms focused on robust loss minimization, leading to enhanced performance in fundamental vision tasks like registration and clustering. When viewed as the negative log of a univariate density, our loss function translates into a versatile probability distribution that encompasses normal and Cauchy distributions as specific instances. This probabilistic perspective facilitates the training of neural networks where the robustness of the loss dynamically adjusts during the process, thereby boosting performance in learning-driven tasks such as generative image synthesis and unsupervised monocular depth estimation, all without the need for manual parameter adjustments.

We introduce Sparse Sinkhorn Attention, an innovative and efficient sparse technique for learning attention mechanisms. This approach relies on the differentiable sorting of internal representations. Specifically, we develop a meta sorting network that acquires the ability to create latent permutations across sequences. By utilizing these sorted sequences, we achieve near-global attention using only local windows, thereby enhancing the memory efficiency of the attention mechanism. For this purpose, we present novel algorithmic advancements like Causal Sinkhorn Balancing and SortCut, a dynamic method for sequence truncation tailored for Sinkhorn Attention in encoding and decoding tasks. Through comprehensive testing on algorithmic seq2seq sorting, language modeling, pixel-level image generation, document classification, and natural language inference, we show that our memory-efficient Sinkhorn Attention method holds its own against traditional attention mechanisms and regularly surpasses the performance of recently introduced efficient Transformer models, such as Sparse Transformers.

Sum-Product Networks featuring complex probability distributions at their leaves have proven to be highly effective probabilistic models for tractable inference. Although the learning of internal parameters has been extensively explored, the challenge of learning complex leaf distributions remains largely unresolved, with limited solutions available only in specific scenarios. In this paper, we present a novel and efficient approach for learning a broad range of leaf distributions using Expectation-Maximization (EM). The EM updates are formulated as straightforward weighted maximum likelihood problems, enabling the incorporation of any distribution learnable via maximum likelihood, even if only approximately. The algorithm's complexity is linear with respect to the model size and achieves convergence even with partial optimizations. We validate this method through experiments on twenty real-world datasets for density estimation, employing tree graphical models as leaf distributions. Our approach surpasses cutting-edge techniques in parameter learning, despite utilizing SPNs with significantly fewer parameters.

Deep reinforcement learning has proven to be an effective method for developing policies that map complex, high-dimensional sensory inputs to actions in intricate tasks, such as those in the Atari domain. In this study, we investigate output representation modeling through temporal abstraction to enhance the convergence and reliability of deep reinforcement learning methods. Our focus is on macro-actions, which we test across various Atari 2600 games. The results demonstrate a notable increase in learning speed. Furthermore, we find that these macro-actions can outperform DQN in terms of final scores. We provide a detailed analysis and explanation of both the convergence process and the outcomes, highlighting a challenge that deep reinforcement learning faces with sparse reward signals.

In this paper, we examine both physics-based and data-driven reconstruction methods for integrated positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems, which offer substantial benefits for clinical imaging in areas such as cancer, neurological conditions, and cardiovascular diseases. These methods incorporate structural or statistical priors alongside a physics-informed model of the PET system's response. Nevertheless, the nested nature of the forward problem renders direct PET/MRI reconstruction inherently nonlinear. We explore how a comprehensive strategy that blends data-driven and physics-guided machine learning enables effective 3D PET/MRI reconstruction, highlighting key advancements in deep learning over the past five years related to attenuation correction, scatter management, low photon counts, and data consistency. Additionally, we discuss how these multi-modal techniques extend their utility beyond PET/MRI, contributing to enhanced precision in radiation therapy planning. We wrap up by considering future possibilities for advancing the field, leveraging the latest developments in physics- and deep learning-based computational imaging, as well as innovations in next-generation detector technology.

Addressing inverse problems, like parameter estimation and optimal control, is crucial in scientific research. Numerous experiments continuously gather data and utilize machine learning algorithms to rapidly deduce solutions to these inverse challenges. However, we observe that cutting-edge training methods are often inadequate for problems involving physical processes due to significant variations in the magnitude and direction of gradients. To overcome this, we introduce an innovative hybrid training strategy that integrates advanced optimization techniques with machine learning approaches. We substitute the traditional gradient related to the physical process with a novel concept we call the physical gradient. This substitution also enables the integration of domain-specific knowledge into the training process by embedding assumptions about the solution space directly into the gradients. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through applications on various fundamental physical systems, demonstrating that physical gradients substantially enhance performance across a broad spectrum of optimization and learning tasks.

In the field of optimization, it is well-established that gradient-based methods are highly effective when dealing with strictly convex and well-conditioned objective functions, often achieving an exponential convergence rate. Conversely, traditional Lasso-type estimators typically fail to reach the optimal convergence rate due to the problematic behavior of the absolute function at the origin. To address this, a homotopic approach employs a series of surrogate functions to approximate the $\ell_1$ penalty inherent in Lasso-type estimators. These surrogate functions are designed to progressively resemble the $\ell_1$ penalty of the Lasso estimator while maintaining strict convexity, which supports a demonstrably faster numerical convergence rate. In this study, we illustrate that by carefully crafting these surrogate functions, a superior numerical convergence rate can be achieved compared to existing methods for Lasso-type estimators. While current leading algorithms are limited to convergence rates of $O(1/\epsilon)$ or $O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$, our proposed algorithm achieves an impressive $O([\log(1/\epsilon)]^2)$ rate. Furthermore, our numerical experiments confirm that this new algorithm also outperforms others in practical applications.

A novel approach for training variational autoencoders (VAEs) has been introduced, utilizing Stein variational gradient descent. This method offers a significant benefit by eliminating the need for specific parametric assumptions regarding the encoder distribution. Its effectiveness is further improved by combining the proposed encoder with importance sampling. The approach showcases outstanding results in various unsupervised and semi-supervised tasks, including the semi-supervised analysis of the ImageNet dataset, proving the model's ability to handle large-scale data efficiently.

We develop a low-complexity decentralized learning algorithm to train a recently introduced large neural network across distributed processing nodes, referred to as workers. We operate under the assumption that the communication network among these workers is synchronized and can be represented by a doubly-stochastic mixing matrix, eliminating the need for a central master node. In our framework, the training data is distributed across the workers and is not exchanged during the training phase to protect privacy and security. By integrating the alternating-direction-method-of-multipliers (ADMM) with a layer-wise convex optimization strategy, we introduce a decentralized learning algorithm that offers reduced computational complexity and minimized communication overhead among workers. We demonstrate that this approach can achieve learning performance comparable to a scenario where all data is centralized. Lastly, we provide experimental results to highlight the algorithm's time complexity and convergence characteristics.

In his 2013 PhD thesis, Maillard introduces a relatively obscure algorithm for the $K$-armed bandit problem, which we refer to as Maillard Sampling (MS). Unlike the widely-used Thompson Sampling, prevalent in industry applications, MS calculates the probability of selecting each arm in a \textit{closed form}. This characteristic allows the data logged from MS to be directly utilized for counterfactual analysis, a capability not shared by Thompson Sampling. Inspired by this advantage, we re-examine MS and conduct an enhanced analysis, demonstrating that it attains both asymptotic optimality and a minimax regret bound of $\sqrt{KT\log{T}}$, where $T$ represents the time horizon. These results align with the established bounds for asymptotically optimal UCB algorithms. Furthermore, we introduce a variant of MS, named MS$^+$, which refines the minimax bound to $\sqrt{KT\log{K}}$. MS$^+$ also offers the flexibility to be adjusted for aggressiveness (i.e., reduced exploration) while preserving asymptotic optimality—a distinctive trait not found in other existing bandit algorithms. Our numerical assessments confirm the efficacy of MS$^+$.

In the context of end-to-end speech recognition using Recurrent Neural Network Transducer (RNN-T), the modeling unit and model architecture play crucial roles. To enhance the performance of RNN-T for Mandarin speech recognition, we introduce a novel transformer transducer that integrates a self-attention transformer with RNN architecture. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of various modeling units on the transformer transducer's effectiveness. Additionally, a new mix-bandwidth training approach is proposed to develop a versatile model capable of accurately recognizing Mandarin speech at different sampling rates simultaneously. Our experiments are based on approximately 12,000 hours of Mandarin speech data recorded at 8kHz and 16kHz sampling rates. The results reveal that the Mandarin transformer transducer, when utilizing syllables with tone as the modeling unit, delivers the best performance. It achieves a relative Word Error Rate (WER) reduction of 14.4% and 44.1% compared to models using syllable initial/final with tone and Chinese characters, respectively. Moreover, it surpasses the model employing syllable initial/final with tone by achieving a relative Character Error Rate (CER) reduction of 13.5% on average.

Patent data offers valuable insights into technical innovations but lacks information on the ethnic backgrounds of inventors. In this study, I employ supervised learning methods to deduce this information. I have assembled a dataset comprising 95,202 labeled names and trained an artificial recurrent neural network equipped with long-short-term memory (LSTM) to estimate ethnic origins from names. The trained model demonstrates a high accuracy of 91% across 17 different ethnic groups. Utilizing this model, I classified and analyzed the ethnic backgrounds of 2.68 million inventors, uncovering new descriptive insights into their ethnic composition across different time periods, countries, and technological sectors. Over recent decades, the global ethnic diversity among inventors has increased, largely due to a growing proportion of inventors of Asian descent. Additionally, the presence of inventors of foreign origin is particularly significant in the USA and has risen in other high-income economies as well. In the USA, this trend is predominantly fueled by an influx of non-western inventors into cutting-edge technology sectors, a pattern less evident in other high-income countries.

In the context of universal hypothesis testing, where the objective is to distinguish between a known null hypothesis distribution and an unknown alternative distribution, Hoeffding introduced a universal test in the 1960s. The test statistic for Hoeffding's universal test is expressed using the Kullback-Leibler (K-L) divergence between the empirical distribution of the observed data and the null hypothesis distribution. This paper examines a variation of Hoeffding's test that incorporates a relaxed version of the K-L divergence test statistic, termed mismatched divergence. The resulting mismatched test is demonstrated to be a generalized likelihood-ratio test (GLRT) when the alternative distribution belongs to a parametric family defined by a finite-dimensional parameter, effectively addressing the composite hypothesis testing challenge. It is further established that, for specific selections of the alternative distribution, both the Hoeffding test and the mismatched test exhibit equivalent asymptotic performance regarding error exponents. This finding implies that the GLRT is optimal for distinguishing a specific distribution from others within an exponential family. Additionally, the mismatched test is shown to offer a notable advantage over the Hoeffding test in terms of finite sample performance.

Dual decomposition offers a practical approach for developing algorithms to determine the most probable (MAP) configuration in graphical models. However, in many real-world inference scenarios, the standard decomposition exhibits a significant integrality gap due to frustrated cycles. A method to refine the relaxation involves adding constraints that explicitly ensure cycle consistency. Previous studies demonstrated that cluster-pursuit algorithms, which progressively incorporate cycle and other higher-order consistency constraints, can precisely resolve many challenging inference issues. Yet, these algorithms are constrained by explicitly listing a set of candidate clusters, restricting them to triplets or other short cycles. We address the challenge of identifying cycle constraints by proposing a nearly linear-time algorithm capable of detecting the most frustrated cycle of any length. We demonstrate how this search algorithm can be integrated with the dual decomposition framework and cluster-pursuit approach. This innovative algorithm successfully provides exact solutions to MAP inference problems encountered in relational classification and stereo vision.

In the supervised training context, we focus on developing task-specific word embeddings. We begin with initial embeddings derived from unlabeled data and refine them to create tailored embeddings for words within the supervised training dataset. Nonetheless, when encountering new words in the test set, we are constrained to using either their original embeddings or a generic unknown embedding, which frequently results in inaccuracies. To overcome this challenge, we employ a neural network to transform initial embeddings into the task-specific embedding space using a multi-loss objective function. This approach is versatile, and in this instance, we showcase its effectiveness in enhancing dependency parsing, particularly for sentences containing out-of-vocabulary words, while also achieving better results in sentiment analysis tasks.

The National Football League, in collaboration with Amazon Web Services, has initiated a groundbreaking sports injury surveillance and mitigation program through a Kaggle competition. The NFL aims to accurately associate specific players with their respective helmets to monitor each player's "exposures" during a football play. Our focus is on developing machine learning algorithms based on computer vision to assign detected helmet impacts to the correct players using tracking data. This paper will detail our methodology for automatically tracking player helmets and their collisions. Additionally, this approach will enable the review of past plays and the analysis of exposure trends over time.

In this study, we introduce DiCOVA-Net, a deep residual network approach designed to detect COVID-19 in patients by analyzing the acoustic patterns of their coughs. Given the significant disparity between the number of healthy individuals and those infected, this classification task grapples with the issue of imbalanced data. To enhance the model's capability to identify the minority class (infected patients), we incorporate data augmentation and cost-sensitive techniques. Additionally, due to the unique nature of this challenge, we employ specific fine-tuning strategies to adapt the pre-trained ResNet50 model. To boost the model’s adaptability across varied data, we apply ensemble learning, combining predictions from several base classifiers created with different random seeds. The effectiveness of DiCOVA-Net was tested using the DiCOVA challenge dataset, where it achieved an AUC of 85.43%, placing it among the leading entries in the competition.

Phase retrieval involves reconstructing images from measurements that capture only magnitude, often resulting in an underdetermined problem in practical scenarios. When training data is accessible, generative models offer a fresh approach to limit the potential solutions. However, these models do not encompass all possible solutions, leading to some degree of representation error. To address this error in phase retrieval, we first employ a unique adaptation of intermediate layer optimization (ILO) to broaden the generator's scope while ensuring the generated images align with the training data. Additionally, we propose innovative initialization methods that enhance reconstruction quality. Through comprehensive experiments on Fourier and Gaussian phase retrieval challenges, coupled with detailed ablation studies, we demonstrate the advantages of our modified ILO approach and the novel initialization techniques.

The proliferation of mobile malware has escalated alongside the increasing use of smartphones, with Android becoming the most widely used mobile platform and simultaneously experiencing a sharp rise in targeted malware. A concerning development is the growing ability of Android malware to bypass detection by conventional signature-based scanning tools. This poses a significant risk to Android app marketplaces, where malicious applications might go undetected until downloaded by unaware users. In response, this paper introduces a robust solution using Bayesian classification models derived from static code analysis. These models are constructed from a set of code and application features that signal potential malicious behavior. The effectiveness of this method is tested with actual malware samples collected from real-world scenarios, and the experimental outcomes are discussed to highlight the success of the proposed strategy.

Kernel ridge regression (KRR) is a widely used method for non-linear, non-parametric learning. However, current KRR implementations demand that all data be held in main memory, significantly restricting its applicability in scenarios where data volume surpasses memory capacity. Such scenarios are becoming increasingly prevalent in fields like data mining, bioinformatics, and control systems. A promising approach for handling oversized data sets is the streaming model of computation, which processes data one sample at a time and discards each sample after processing before proceeding to the next. In this paper, we introduce StreaMRAK, a streaming adaptation of KRR. StreaMRAK enhances traditional KRR methods by breaking down the problem into multiple resolution levels, enabling ongoing refinement of predictions. The algorithm minimizes memory usage by seamlessly and effectively incorporating new samples into the training model. Through an innovative sub-sampling technique, StreaMRAK lowers both memory and computational demands by generating a condensed sketch of the original data, with sub-sampling density adjusted according to the kernel's bandwidth and the data's local dimensionality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of StreaMRAK through a detailed study on two synthetic problems and the forecasting of a trajectory.

We introduce a novel estimation approach for topic models that diverges from traditional simplex finding algorithms and independently determines the number of topics, K, from the observed data. We establish new finite sample minimax lower bounds for estimating A, alongside updated upper bounds for our innovative estimator. We outline the conditions under which our estimator achieves minimax adaptability. Our analysis holds for any number of documents (n), individual document lengths (N_i), dictionary sizes (p), and number of topics (K), accommodating scenarios where both p and K increase with n—an aspect not adequately addressed in prior studies. We support our theoretical findings with an extensive simulation study, demonstrating that our new algorithm outperforms existing methods in speed and accuracy. This is noteworthy, as we operate under the initial computational and theoretical challenge of not knowing the true number of topics K, whereas competing methods in our simulations are provided with the correct K value.

In the worst-case scenario, the junction tree algorithm stands out as the most comprehensive approach for exact MAP inference, offering polynomial run-time guarantees. However, its primary limitation lies in the requirement that the treewidth of the associated Markov Random Field (MRF) must be bounded, severely restricting the scope of applicable problems. Many real-world challenges in structured prediction necessitate the modeling of global dependencies, either through the direct incorporation of global factors or by imposing global constraints on prediction variables. This inevitably leads to a fully-connected graph, rendering exact inference using this algorithm computationally infeasible. Prior research [1]-[4] on loss-augmented inference has shown how effective inference can be achieved in models with specific global factors that represent non-decomposable loss functions within the training framework of Structural Support Vector Machines (SSVMs). In this work, we build upon the efficient exact inference framework introduced in [3], enabling more nuanced interactions between the core model's energy and the sufficient statistics of global terms without incurring additional computational overhead. We illustrate the efficacy of our approach through various use cases, including one that existing methods are unable to address. Additionally, we introduce a novel graph transformation method through node cloning, which ensures

Precise electricity demand predictions are vital for maintaining sustainable power systems. To support improved decision-making, particularly regarding end-user demand flexibility, forecasts must be not only precise but also clear and actionable. Global Forecasting Models (GFM), which are trained on multiple time series, have recently outperformed univariate forecasting methods in numerous demand forecasting challenges and real-world scenarios. Our goal is to bridge the gap between accuracy and interpretability in these global forecasting methods. To achieve this, we introduce Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Rule-based Explanations for Forecasting (LIMREF), a framework that generates k-optimal impact rules for specific forecasts by treating the global forecasting model as a black-box in a model-agnostic manner. This approach offers various types of rules that clarify the global model’s predictions and provides counterfactual rules, which offer actionable insights for making adjustments to achieve different outcomes in specific cases. We test this approach using a comprehensive electricity demand dataset that includes external factors like temperature and calendar effects. In this study, we assess the quality of explanations provided by the LIMREF framework through both qualitative and quantitative measures.

This paper explores the concept of multi-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) supported mobile edge computing (MEC), termed UAVE, where multiple UAVs serve as airborne MEC platforms to deliver computing resources to ground-based user equipment (UEs). Unlike traditional stationary MEC systems, UAVE proves especially beneficial for temporary events, emergencies, and on-demand services, thanks to its adaptability, cost-effectiveness, and straightforward deployment. Nevertheless, operating UAVE presents challenges, notably in managing 1) the connection between various UEs and UAVs, and 2) the distribution of resources from UAVs to UEs, all while aiming to reduce energy usage across all UEs. To tackle these issues, we model the scenario as a mixed integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, which poses significant solution difficulties, particularly in extensive setups. Consequently, we introduce a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based strategy for user Association and resource Allocation (RLAA) to address this challenge both efficiently and effectively. Simulation results demonstrate that the RLAA approach matches the optimal outcomes achieved by exhaustive search in smaller-scale settings and offers substantial performance improvements over other conventional methods in larger-scale scenarios.

In e-commerce platforms, providing prompt and precise answers to product-related questions is crucial. Relying on manual responses, such as those on community Q&A forums, is often slow and lacks scalability. Recent research highlights that product reviews can serve as an effective resource for real-time, automated product question answering (PQA). Within existing studies, PQA is approached as a retrieval task aimed at identifying the most pertinent reviews to address a specific product query. This paper delves into the challenges of answerability and the trustworthiness of responses in PQA systems using reviews. Our analysis stems from the understanding that many questions may remain unanswered due to the limitations of available reviews. In such cases, a system should ideally return no answer rather than presenting irrelevant reviews, as this can significantly degrade user experience. Additionally, for questions that can be answered, only the most relevant reviews that directly address the query should be provided. We introduce a framework based on conformal prediction to enhance the dependability of PQA systems. This approach filters out unreliable responses, ensuring that the answers provided are both succinct and precise, and includes the option to return no answer for questions that cannot be addressed.

We introduce an innovative neural topic model within the Wasserstein autoencoders (WAE) framework. In contrast to current variational autoencoder-based models, we directly impose a Dirichlet prior on the latent document-topic vectors. By leveraging the latent space's structure, we employ an appropriate kernel to minimize the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) for effective distribution matching. Our findings indicate that MMD outperforms the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) in aligning with high-dimensional Dirichlet distributions. Additionally, we observe that introducing randomness into the encoder output during training substantially enhances topic coherence. To assess topic diversity, we propose a straightforward metric for topic uniqueness. Combined with the commonly used coherence measure NPMI, this provides a more comprehensive assessment of topic quality. Our experiments across various real-world datasets demonstrate that our model generates notably superior topics compared to existing topic models.

Variational approaches to Gaussian processes (GPs) often rely on a limited set of inducing points to create a low-rank approximation of the covariance matrix. In contrast, this study focuses on a sparse approximation of the precision matrix. We introduce the variational nearest neighbor Gaussian process (VNNGP), which employs a prior that preserves correlations only among the K nearest-neighboring observations, thus enforcing a sparse structure in the precision matrix. Within the variational framework, the objective of VNNGP can be decomposed over both observations and inducing points, facilitating stochastic optimization with a time complexity of O($K^3$). This allows for flexible scaling of the inducing point size, including the possibility of placing inducing points at every observed location. Through a series of experiments, we evaluate VNNGP against other scalable GP methods, showing that VNNGP (1) significantly surpasses low-rank approaches in performance, and (2) is less susceptible to overfitting compared to other nearest neighbor techniques.

Online meta-learning is becoming a crucial approach for fostering edge intelligence within the IoT ecosystem. However, for a single agent to develop an effective meta-model for rapid adaptation within a task, it must train across numerous tasks, leading to the 'cold-start' issue. Recognizing that tasks across various agents in a multi-agent network often exhibit model similarities, we pose a key question: "Can online meta-learning be enhanced across agents through minimal communication, and if so, to what extent can performance be improved?" To address this, we introduce a multi-agent online meta-learning framework, formulating it as a dual-level nested online convex optimization (OCO) problem. By analyzing the upper limit of the agent-task-averaged regret, we demonstrate that the efficacy of multi-agent online meta-learning largely hinges on the benefits an agent gains from network-level OCO for meta-model updates through restricted communication, a concept that remains insufficiently explored. To overcome this obstacle, we develop a distributed online gradient descent algorithm incorporating gradient tracking. In this setup, each agent monitors the global gradient with just one communication exchange with neighboring agents per iteration, achieving an average regret of $O(\sqrt{T/N})$ per agent, suggesting significant improvement.

Answer-agnostic question generation presents a formidable challenge in automatically creating questions for a given sentence without a predefined answer. In this study, we introduce two innovative strategies to tackle this issue: question type prediction and a copy loss mechanism. The question type module predicts the kinds of questions to be posed, enabling our model to produce diverse question types from a single source sentence. Additionally, the novel copy loss improves the existing copy mechanism, ensuring that every key word in the source sentence is replicated during question generation. Our comprehensive model surpasses the leading method in answer-agnostic question generation, securing a BLEU-4 score of 13.9 on the SQuAD dataset. Human assessments further confirm the superior quality of the questions we generate. Our code will be made publicly accessible to support future research.

Langevin diffusion offers a robust approach to nonconvex optimization by introducing noise into the gradient, facilitating escape from local minima. The temperature parameter, which regulates the noise intensity, creates a balance between "global exploration" at high temperatures and "local exploitation" at low temperatures. To leverage the benefits of both states, we introduce replica exchange, a technique that alternates between two Langevin diffusions operating at different temperatures. We provide a theoretical analysis of the acceleration benefits of replica exchange from two angles: (i) convergence in \chi^2-divergence, and (ii) the large deviation principle. This acceleration enables a quicker approach to global minima. Additionally, by discretizing the replica exchange Langevin diffusion, we develop a discrete-time algorithm. We theoretically assess the discretization error of this algorithm and empirically validate its acceleration benefits.

Complex time-varying systems are frequently analyzed by focusing on population-level dynamics, often overlooking the behavior of individual components. In constructing these broad models, the specific contributions of each individual to the overall system can be obscured. This paper introduces a new transformer architecture tailored for time-varying data, which simultaneously captures both individual and collective dynamics. Instead of integrating all data into the model from the beginning, we propose a distinct architecture that processes individual time-series data before advancing them, ensuring permutation-invariance and enabling adaptability across systems of varying sizes and complexities. We first validate our model by accurately recovering intricate interactions and dynamics in many-body systems. Subsequently, we apply this methodology to neuronal populations within the nervous system. Using datasets of neural activity, we demonstrate that our multi-scale transformer not only achieves strong decoding results but also excels in transferability. Our findings indicate that it is feasible to train a model on the neural data of one animal and successfully apply it to another.

Deep learning models trained through full supervision often depend on "shortcut" features—inputs linked to the desired outcome in training data but absent or irrelevant in testing or deployment scenarios. Our experiments demonstrate that newer self-supervised models, trained on both images and text, yield more robust image representations and lessen dependence on visual shortcut features in a practical medical imaging context. Furthermore, we observe that these self-supervised models discard shortcut features more rapidly than fully supervised models during fine-tuning on labeled data. While not a definitive fix, our findings strongly suggest that self-supervised models incorporating images and text offer a degree of protection against reliance on visual shortcut features.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning frequently encounters challenges due to the exponentially vast action space resulting from numerous agents. This paper introduces HAVEN, an innovative value decomposition framework grounded in hierarchical reinforcement learning, specifically designed for fully cooperative multi-agent scenarios. To mitigate the instability from simultaneously optimizing high-level and low-level policies, as well as the concurrent optimization among agents, we implement a dual coordination mechanism that manages strategies both between layers and among agents. HAVEN operates without the need for domain-specific knowledge or pretraining and is adaptable to any value decomposition variant. Our approach yields promising outcomes across various decentralized partially observable Markov decision process environments and provides an effective method for implicitly dividing the decision space.

This paper focuses solely on the effectiveness of AIS-INMACA. AIS-INMACA has significantly contributed to addressing key challenges in bioinformatics, such as protein region identification and promoter region prediction, achieving results in a shorter time (Pokkuluri Kiran Sree, 2014). Additionally, AIS-INMACA has evolved with multiple variations (Pokkuluri Kiran Sree, 2014), positioning it as a valuable tool in bioinformatics for tackling a wide range of issues. Therefore, this paper will be highly beneficial for researchers in the field of bioinformatics, particularly those working with cellular automata.

In numerous academic environments, medical students begin engaging in scientific research during their coursework. At our institution, for instance, they frequently collaborate in interdisciplinary groups alongside researchers of varying experience levels, including postgraduate scholars in pharmaceutical sciences, general natural sciences, or biostatistics. It is essential that all these individuals are educated in good research practices as a fundamental component of their training, particularly in statistical analysis. A key element of modern research, reproducibility, must be emphasized. Recognizing that even instructors may lack familiarity with the components of a fully reproducible workflow, I agreed to deliver a lecture series on reproducible research (RR) tailored for medical students and postgraduate pharmacists engaged in various clinical research domains. Consequently, I developed a pilot lecture series to cover the definition of RR, its importance, its potential benefits, and methods to implement it effectively. While attempting to replicate a published analysis, I faced several practical challenges. This article centers on that specific example to highlight the diverse aspects of RR, offer potential explanations and solutions, and advocate for the inclusion of RR principles in standardized curricula for (quantitative) clinical researchers. I hope sharing these insights will increase awareness among both educators and students about the importance of adopting RR practices.

Robust reinforcement learning (RL) aims to identify a policy that maximizes performance under the worst-case scenario within a defined set of uncertain Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). This paper explores model-free robust RL, where the uncertainty set is centered on a misspecified MDP that sequentially produces a single sample trajectory and is considered unknown. We propose a sample-based method to estimate this unknown uncertainty set and develop two algorithms: a robust Q-learning algorithm for the tabular case and a robust TDC algorithm for settings with function approximation. Both algorithms are designed for online, incremental implementation. We establish that the robust Q-learning algorithm converges to the optimal robust Q function, while the robust TDC algorithm asymptotically approaches certain stationary points. In contrast to findings in [Roy et al., 2017], our algorithms do not require specific conditions on the discount factor to ensure convergence. Additionally, we analyze the finite-time error bounds for both algorithms, demonstrating that they converge at rates comparable to their standard versions (within a constant factor). Numerical experiments further validate the robustness of our proposed methods. Our framework is versatile and can be adapted to enhance the robustness of various other algorithms.

Contextual bandit algorithms, a subset of multi-armed bandit algorithms that utilize contextual data, have proven effective in addressing sequential decision-making challenges amid uncertainty. Typically, research assumes that the learner can observe the actual (ground truth) reward of a chosen action at no cost, an assumption that often does not hold in real-world situations. In scenarios where obtaining the ground truth reward incurs a cost, the learner faces the critical challenge of strategically acquiring this information by weighing the benefits against the expenses to optimize both learning efficiency and cost. From an information theory standpoint, a compelling question arises: how much efficiency is compromised due to these costs? In this paper, we introduce a new contextual bandit-based learning algorithm equipped with active learning capabilities. A distinguishing aspect of our algorithm is that, alongside requesting the ground truth from an annotator, it also provides prior information about the ground truth that the learner has deduced, thus lowering the cost of the query. We demonstrate that by meticulously selecting the algorithm's parameters, the learning regret of our proposed algorithm achieves

Twenty-three machine learning algorithms were trained and evaluated to determine baseline performance metrics and identify a suitable image classification algorithm for integration into critical satellite imaging systems. The Overhead-MNIST dataset, akin to the well-known MNIST handwritten digit dataset in machine learning research, comprises satellite images used for this purpose. Among the algorithms, the CatBoost classifier, Light Gradient Boosting Machine, and Extreme Gradient Boosting models achieved the highest accuracy, Area Under the Curve (AUC), and F1 scores in a general comparison using PyCaret. Additional assessments revealed a deep convolutional architecture as the most viable option. We report the results of the top-performing algorithm as a benchmark for edge deployment and future enhancements: a convolutional neural network (CNN) that achieved a categorical accuracy of 0.965 on unseen test data.

Forecasting the completion time of business process instances is a valuable tool for managing processes constrained by service level agreements. Being able to anticipate the progress of active process instances empowers business managers to take timely actions to avoid delays or unfavorable outcomes. However, achieving precise predictions is challenging due to the numerous factors that can affect the time needed to finalize a process instance. In this paper, we introduce a method utilizing deep Recurrent Neural Networks, particularly LSTMs, which leverages detailed event-specific data to deliver highly accurate predictions of completion times for ongoing instances. Testing on real-world datasets validates the effectiveness of our approach.

The high data requirements of deep neural networks (DNNs) compel practitioners to gather data from the Internet without thorough vetting, due to the prohibitive costs of manual curation. This practice introduces significant risks of backdoor attacks. A model compromised by a backdoor will consistently predict a specific target class whenever a predefined trigger pattern is present, a vulnerability that can be exploited by poisoning just a small subset of data. Adversarial training is often considered a potential defense against such attacks, as it trains models to maintain consistent predictions despite input perturbations within a certain range. However, prior research has largely failed to confirm its effectiveness in this context. To investigate the potential of adversarial training as a defense mechanism against backdoor attacks, we conducted comprehensive experiments across various threat models and perturbation levels. Our findings reveal that the choice of threat model in adversarial training is critical. For example, adversarial training using spatial adversarial examples demonstrates significant resilience against common patch-based backdoor attacks. Additionally, we propose a hybrid approach that offers robust protection across a range of backdoor attack types.

Detecting groups of similar entities within data is crucial across numerous fields. For clustering, we focus on the densest k-disjoint-clique problem as a foundational model. This problem aims to find a set of k disjoint cliques in a weighted complete graph that maximizes the total density of the complete subgraphs formed by these cliques. In this paper, we define conditions under which the densest k cliques of a graph can be precisely recovered using the optimal solution of a specific semidefinite program. Notably, this semidefinite relaxation proves accurate for graphs representing data with k sizable, distinct clusters alongside a minimal number of outliers. This methodology also extends to a semidefinite relaxation for the biclustering problem, offering comparable recovery assurances. Biclustering involves grouping a set of objects and their associated features based on expression levels simultaneously. This challenge can be framed as partitioning the nodes of a weighted bipartite complete graph to maximize the total density of the resulting bipartite complete subgraphs. Similar to our examination of the densest k-disjoint-clique problem, we demonstrate that the correct partition can be achieved.

Clustering plays a central role in data analysis, particularly when examining time series data. Its subjective nature means that different individuals might favor distinct clustering solutions for the same dataset. Semi-supervised clustering offers a solution by enabling users to specify examples of data points that should or should not be grouped together. This paper explores semi-supervised clustering specifically for time series data. We demonstrate that COBRAS, a leading semi-supervised clustering technique, can be tailored for this purpose, and we term this adaptation COBRAS-TS. Through comprehensive experimental analysis, we establish several key points: (1) COBRAS-TS significantly surpasses existing semi-supervised clustering methods for time series, establishing a new standard in the domain; (2) COBRAS-TS effectively detects clusters with distinct, separated elements; (3) COBRAS-TS excels at recognizing clusters defined by subtle, localized patterns; (4) even minimal semi-supervision can substantially enhance clustering accuracy for time series; (5) the selection of the clustering algorithm is crucial, challenging previous assertions in the research community.

With the swift growth of machine learning applications, designing reusable models has become increasingly important. This paper explores the potential for reusing pre-trained deep convolutional models. Rather than merely using these models as feature extractors, we uncover additional value within the convolutional layers, specifically that their activations can serve as detectors for identifying common objects in the image co-localization challenge. We introduce a straightforward yet powerful approach called Deep Descriptor Transforming (DDT) to assess descriptor correlations and pinpoint category-consistent regions, enabling precise localization of common objects across a group of images. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of the DDT method, showing that it significantly surpasses leading techniques on standard image co-localization datasets. Furthermore, DDT exhibits strong generalization to unfamiliar categories and resilience against noisy data.

The destruction inflicted by crypto-ransomware through encryption is often irreversible, leading to significant data loss. This paper presents the development of a machine learning (ML) classifier designed for the early detection of crypto-ransomware, which employs cryptographic techniques, by analyzing program behavior. When signature-based detection fails, a behavior-based detector serves as a critical final barrier to identify and mitigate damage. Our research indicates that the input/output operations of ransomware and the entropy of file content are distinctive indicators for identifying crypto-ransomware. Utilizing a deep-learning (DL) classifier, we achieved high detection accuracy with a minimal rate of false positives. We also conducted adversarial testing on the developed models, employing simulated ransomware programs in a gray-box analysis to uncover vulnerabilities in ML classifiers and enhance model durability. Beyond accuracy and resilience, trustworthiness is a vital attribute of an effective detector. Ensuring that accurate data is used for decision-making is crucial in security applications. We applied the Integrated Gradient method to interpret the deep learning model and understand the reasons behind false negatives evading detection. This paper demonstrates and explores the methodologies for constructing and assessing a practical detector in real-world scenarios.

When data storage and users are spread across different locations, strategically placing distributed data cache points is crucial to reduce data transfer. To address this, we are creating an adaptive distributed data caching framework designed to pinpoint optimal data segments for caching and transfer among a network of community cache sites.

Bibliographic reference parsers are designed to retrieve machine-readable metadata, including author names, titles, journals, and publication years, from reference strings. These parsers utilize either heuristic methods or machine learning techniques to perform metadata extraction. However, no single parser or algorithm universally outperforms others across all contexts. For example, a particular tool might excel at identifying titles in ACM citation format but rank only third when processing APA style. Similarly, one parser may be optimal for extracting English author names, while another is more effective with inconsistent or noisy citation data. In this extended version of our recent RecSys poster, we tackle the challenge of reference parsing through the lens of recommender systems and meta-learning. We introduce ParsRec, a meta-learning-based recommender system that identifies and suggests the most suitable parser for a specific reference string. ParsRec selects from a pool of 10 open-source parsers, including Anystyle-Parser, Biblio, CERMINE, Citation, Citation-Parser, GROBID, ParsCit, PDFSSA4MET, Reference Tagger, and Science Parse. We tested ParsRec using a dataset of 105,000 references from the field of chemistry. Our study explores two distinct meta-learning strategies for generating recommendations. The first strategy determines the most effective parser for an entire reference string as a whole.
